units.name: Data Protection and the EU GDPR

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: Why data protection law exists
slides.html:
Processing itself, not just secrecy, creates power over people, so data protection law regulates every stage of how personal data is used.

Where Part I fits. Part I follows the class GDPR deck (GDPR.pdf) and adds the syllabus.md entries the slides do not reach: the right to be forgotten, restriction, portability, objection, automated decisions and transfers. The GDPR is prescribed in its own right and is the benchmark for judging the DPDP Act. This chapter explains why data protection law exists, separates it from neighbouring ideas, and traces the EU framework from the OECD Guidelines to the GDPR.

Big data analytics (class slide 3) structures, models and visualises vast datasets. It turns trivial facts into knowledge about a person's habits, health, beliefs and finances, and links online identities to real people. The cartoon on class slide 2, a pupil asking how his name will be used before he writes it, captures the core idea: people care about how information is used, not only whether it stays secret.

A typical data flow has four actors:

  1. The individual generates data.
  2. The controller (GDPR) or Data Fiduciary (DPDP Act) decides why and how it is used.
  3. A processor handles it on the controller's behalf.
  4. Third parties, such as advertisers, receive data or inferences.

Each stage, from collection through combination and inference to disclosure, can create new information without the person's knowledge. Data protection law therefore regulates processing itself, asking whether there is a lawful basis, a defined purpose, minimal and accurate data, security, timely deletion and enforceable rights.

Class slide 6 states the structure. The law applies when personal data, including sensitive data, of an identifiable data subject is processed; a controller determines the nature and extent of processing; and a processor may carry it out under an outsourcing contract.

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: Four concepts that should not be merged
slides.html:
Privacy, confidentiality, data protection and data security overlap but differ: privacy is the broadest, and security is only one component of data protection.

ConceptWhat it protectsLegal home
PrivacyThe broadest: a sphere of autonomy and private life, including informational privacyIndia: Article 21 (Puttaswamy, 2017). Europe: Article 7 of the Charter and Article 8 ECHR
ConfidentialityInformation shared in relationships of trust (doctor and patient, lawyer and client)Usually ends once information becomes public
Data protectionA regulatory regime for the fair and lawful handling of personal data at every stage, whether or not secretEU: a separate Charter right (Article 8) implemented by the GDPR. India: the DPDP Act
Data securityOne component of data protection: technical and organisational measures that keep data confidential, intact and availableGDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32; DPDP s. 8(5) with Rule 6; IT Act s. 43A until its omission

Why the distinctions matter. A perfectly secure organisation can still breach data protection law by collecting too much or misusing data, because security answers only one of data protection's questions. And public information, though no longer confidential, remains regulated by the GDPR. The DPDP Act, by contrast, excludes data the Data Principal herself made public (Chapter 10).

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: Big Brother Watch: the challenge and the ruling
slides.html:
The State is often the most intrusive processor: in Big Brother Watch the Grand Chamber found two of three UK surveillance regimes in breach of the ECHR.

Class slide 4 uses this case to show that the State is often the most intrusive processor.

Big Brother Watch and Others v the United Kingdom (ECtHR, Applications nos. 58170/13, 62322/14 and 24960/15; Chamber, 13 September 2018; Grand Chamber, 25 May 2021)

Facts
After the Snowden disclosures, journalists and NGOs challenged three UK regimes: bulk interception by GCHQ (the TEMPORA programme); receipt of intelligence from foreign services (including NSA material from PRISM and Upstream); and acquisition of communications data from providers.
Held (Grand Chamber)
  1. The bulk interception regime under section 8(4) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 violated Articles 8 and 10 ECHR.
  2. The communications data regime violated Articles 8 and 10 because it was not in accordance with law.
  3. The intelligence sharing regime did not violate Article 8 (twelve votes to five).

Current law update. Class slide 4 describes the 2018 Chamber judgment. The Grand Chamber judgment of 25 May 2021 is final and should be cited.

Remember: two regimes failed (bulk interception; communications data), one survived (intelligence sharing, 12 to 5).

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: Big Brother Watch: end to end safeguards
slides.html:
Bulk interception is not unlawful in itself, but intrusion grows at each stage, so a lawful regime needs "end to end safeguards" from authorisation to review.

Reasoning. The Court did not condemn bulk interception as such. It reasoned that intrusion grows at each stage of the process:

  1. Interception
  2. Filtering
  3. Selection by selectors
  4. Examination by analysts

Because each stage intrudes further, safeguards must follow the data all the way through. A lawful regime therefore needs "end to end safeguards":

At every stage

Necessity and proportionality

At the outset

Independent authorisation

Afterwards

Supervision with independent review

Where the UK fell short.

  1. It lacked independent authorisation.
  2. It left selector categories out of warrant applications.
  3. It required no prior internal authorisation for selectors linked to individuals.
  4. It did not adequately protect journalistic material.

Use. The judgment is persuasive in India. It is the benchmark for any surveillance power or State exemption, read with Puttaswamy and the critique of DPDP s. 17(2)(a).

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: Sectoral and omnibus models
slides.html:
The United States regulates data sector by sector; the EU uses one omnibus law for all sectors, public and private; India's DPDP Act is omnibus in form.

FeatureSectoral: United StatesOmnibus: EU
How law is organisedSeparate statutes govern separate industriesOne law covers all sectors
Public and private sectorsFall under different lawsBoth covered by the same law
GapsSome areas are unregulated; coverage depends on who holds the dataA uniform baseline
EnforcementUnder each statute, such as the FTC's COPPA RuleIndependent supervisory authorities coordinated by the European Data Protection Board
PriceGaps in protectionComplexity and cost

Class slide 5 draws this contrast. Two US statutes show how the sectoral model works:

HIPAA (1996)
With its Privacy Rule, governs health information held by health plans, clearinghouses, providers transacting electronically and their business associates.
COPPA (1998)
With the FTC's COPPA Rule, requires operators of services directed to children under 13, or with actual knowledge of collecting from them, to obtain verifiable parental consent.

Because coverage depends on who holds the data, hospital records are protected while a health app outside HIPAA's categories may not be.

India. The DPDP Act is omnibus in form, binding the State too, but it preserves stricter transfer laws (s. 16(2)) and operates in addition to other laws (s. 38(1)).

Current law update. The FTC's COPPA Rule amendments were published on 22 April 2025, took effect on 23 June 2025 and required compliance by 22 April 2026: separate parental consent for disclosures to third parties, a written retention policy, and biometric identifiers as personal information. No comprehensive US federal privacy statute had been enacted by the review date.†

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: The OECD Guidelines and Convention 108
slides.html:
Two international instruments came first: the non binding OECD Guidelines (1980) and Council of Europe Convention 108 (1981), the first legally binding international instrument on data protection.

FeatureOECD GuidelinesConvention No. 108
Full nameGuidelines on the Protection of Privacy and Transborder Flows of Personal DataCouncil of Europe Convention No. 108 (Strasbourg, 28 January 1981)
Dates1980, revised 20131981, modernised 2018
Binding?Not bindingThe first legally binding international instrument; requires domestic implementation
ContentCovers the public and private sectors and manual and electronic processing; core principles (class slides 7 to 9)Principles set out in Chapter II (class slides 10 and 11)

The OECD core principles are usually listed as these eight:†

  1. collection limitation
  2. data quality
  3. purpose specification
  4. use limitation
  5. security safeguards
  6. openness
  7. individual participation
  8. accountability

A double motive. The OECD Preface (class slide 8) protects people against unlawful storage, inaccurate data and unauthorised disclosure, while preventing divergent national laws from obstructing the transborder flows on which banking and insurance depend. Convention 108's preamble likewise seeks to reconcile respect for privacy with the free flow of information, a tension that runs through every later instrument.

Caveat. The ratification status of the 2018 protocol was not verified.

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: How the EU framework was built
slides.html:
The EU moved from a Directive that fragmented in practice to the GDPR, a directly applicable Regulation adopted in 2016 and applicable from 25 May 2018.

Class slides 12 to 20 give the sequence:

  1. OECD Guidelines (1980).
  2. Convention 108 (1981).
  3. Treaty of Maastricht (signed 1992, in force 1993), with its three pillars: the European Communities, foreign and security policy, and justice and home affairs.
  4. Directive 95/46/EC (24 October 1995).
  5. Treaty of Amsterdam (signed 1997, in force 1999), creating the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice.
  6. Charter of Fundamental Rights (2000).
  7. Treaty of Lisbon (signed 2007, in force 2009), which made the Charter binding, collapsed the pillars and introduced Article 16 TFEU.
  8. The GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, adopted on 27 April 2016, applicable from 25 May 2018, repealing the Directive.
Directive 95/46/ECGDPR (a regulation)
Legal effectA directive leaves form and method to national lawA regulation is directly applicable
OutcomeRecital 9: sound in principle, but fragmentation and legal uncertainty obstructed data flows and distorted competitionArticle 1 aims to harmonise, and to strengthen and unify protection (class slides 19 and 20)

Where it applies. The GDPR applies in the 27 Member States and, through the EEA Agreement, in Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway (class slide 18).

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: Primary law: Charter Articles 7 and 8, Article 16 TFEU
slides.html:
In the EU, data protection is a fundamental right in its own name (Charter Article 8), separate from private life (Article 7), with Article 16 TFEU as the legislative base.

Charter Article 7. Protects private and family life, home and communications.

Charter Article 8. Protects personal data:

  1. everyone has the right to protection of personal data concerning them;
  2. data must be processed fairly, for specified purposes, on consent or another legitimate basis laid down by law;
  3. there are rights of access and rectification; and
  4. compliance is controlled by an independent authority.

Article 16 TFEU. Restates the right and gives the Union competence to legislate, with independent supervision (class slides 14 to 16).

Why it matters. Because data protection is a fundamental right in its own name, the Court of Justice invalidated adequacy decisions in Schrems I and II by reference to the Charter (Chapter 8). Limitations on the right must satisfy Article 52(1): they must be provided by law, respect the essence of the right, and be necessary and proportionate.

Indian law reaches a similar point through Article 21 and the Puttaswamy proportionality test (Chapter 9).

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: Key recitals for Chapter 1
slides.html:
Recitals are not binding and cannot override an Article, but the Court of Justice uses them to interpret the GDPR, and examiners expect them to be cited.

What recitals are. The GDPR has 173 numbered recitals, statements of reasons that precede its 99 Articles. They are not binding in themselves and cannot override an Article, but the Court of Justice relies on them to interpret the Articles. Those below were read from the supplied text.

Recital 1
Declares data protection a fundamental right, citing Charter Article 8(1) and TFEU Article 16(1).
Recital 4
Processing should serve mankind, and the right is not absolute: it must be balanced against other fundamental rights, such as private life, religion, expression, the freedom to conduct a business and a fair trial, in accordance with proportionality. This underpins every balancing exercise in the GDPR.
Recitals 6 and 7
Why a new framework was needed: technology and globalisation have vastly increased collection and sharing by companies and public authorities, so a strong, coherent and well enforced framework is needed to build trust in the digital economy, and individuals should control their own data.
Recital 9
Records the Directive's failure (class slide 20): sound principles but fragmented implementation, legal uncertainty and perceived online risks, which obstructed data flows and distorted competition.

slides.part: Chapter 1: Privacy, Data Protection and Regulatory Models
slides.title: Exam guidance: Chapter 1
slides.html:
Data protection regulates processing at every stage; in the EU it is a fundamental right, and in India it rests on Puttaswamy and the DPDP Act.

State the foundations precisely: in the EU, Charter Article 8 and TFEU Article 16; in India, Puttaswamy and the DPDP Act.

Exam focus. Common mistakes to avoid:

  1. Do not confuse Article 8 ECHR (private life) with Article 8 of the Charter (data protection).
  2. Do not cite the 2018 Chamber judgment in Big Brother Watch as final: cite the Grand Chamber judgment of 25 May 2021.
  3. Do not call the OECD Guidelines binding.
  4. Do not equate security with data protection.

Model problem: bulk interception in India

Answer it in this order:

  1. Apply Puttaswamy: legality, legitimate aim, proportionality.
  2. Add, persuasively, Big Brother Watch's stage by stage safeguards: independent authorisation, oversight and protection of journalistic sources.

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: The building blocks in Article 4
slides.html:
Before applying any GDPR obligation, decide whether the processing falls within the material scope (Article 2) and the territorial scope (Article 3); both rest on Article 4.

Five definitions in Article 4 recur in every later chapter, so learn their exact elements.

Personal data, Article 4(1)
Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person, identifiable directly or indirectly by an identifier (name, number, location data, online identifier) or by factors specific to physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity (class slide 23).
Processing, Article 4(2)
Any operation on personal data, automated or manual, from collection and storage to use, disclosure, combination, restriction and erasure; even mere storage counts (class slide 27).
Filing system, Article 4(6)
A structured set of personal data accessible by specific criteria.
Controller, Article 4(7)
Determines the purposes and means of processing, alone or jointly.
Processor, Article 4(8)
Processes personal data on the controller's behalf (class slide 31).

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: Material scope: Article 2
slides.html:
The GDPR covers automated processing and manual records in a filing system, but Article 2(2) carves out four kinds of activity, including purely personal or household activity.

Article 2(1). Covers processing wholly or partly by automated means, and manual processing of data forming part of, or intended for, a filing system (class slide 21).

Article 2(2) exclusions (class slide 28):

  1. activity outside Union law (Recital 16 places national security here);
  2. Member State activity under the Common Foreign and Security Policy;
  3. purely personal or household activity;
  4. processing by competent authorities for criminal law enforcement, which falls under the Law Enforcement Directive (EU) 2016/680.†

The household exemption is narrow. Recital 18 explains that household activity, including correspondence, addresses and social networking within such activity, is excluded, but the providers of the means, such as social networks, remain covered (class slide 29).

Two further provisions. Article 2(3) deals with EU institutions, and Article 2(4) preserves the intermediary liability rules of Directive 2000/31/EC on electronic commerce.

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: Jehovah's Witnesses: paper notes and joint control
slides.html:
Structured handwritten notes form a filing system, door to door preaching is not household activity, and joint control does not require access to the data.

Tietosuojavaltuutettu (Case C 25/17, Grand Chamber, 10 July 2018), called Jehovah's Witnesses v Finland in syllabus.md

Background
A reference from Finland after the Data Protection Supervisor acted against the Jehovah's Witnesses community (class slide 22).
Facts
Members preaching door to door took handwritten notes of names, addresses, religious beliefs and family circumstances. The community organised and encouraged the note taking but never saw the notes.
Held
  1. No household exemption: preaching is directed outside the members' private sphere.
  2. A filing system: the notes were structured by criteria such as geographical area for easy retrieval, whatever their physical form.
  3. Joint controller: the community was a joint controller with its members because it organised, coordinated and encouraged the collection; joint control does not require access to the data.
Use
Material scope of paper records, the narrowness of the household exemption, and joint controllership (with Fashion ID).

Correction. syllabus.md calls the case "Jehovah's Witnesses v Finland". That is an informal name: it is formally Tietosuojavaltuutettu, Case C 25/17, a preliminary reference.

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: Territorial scope: the establishment test in Article 3(1)
slides.html:
Article 3(1) applies the GDPR to processing in the context of an EU establishment's activities, wherever the processing occurs and wherever the data subjects are.

Article 3(1). The GDPR applies to processing in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or processor in the Union, regardless of where the processing occurs (class slide 30).

Establishment
The effective and real exercise of activity through stable arrangements, whatever the legal form (Recital 22, class slide 33).
"In the context of"
Read broadly, as Google Spain shows.

Google Spain (Google Spain SL v AEPD and Costeja González, Case C 131/12, Grand Chamber, 13 May 2014)

Processing by Google Inc. in the United States was in the context of Google Spain's advertising sales because the two activities were inextricably linked.

The class slide examples (hypotheticals, in the order the notes give them):

ExampleFactsResult
Example 1 (class slide 33)A US car maker's Brussels branch oversees its European operationsAn establishment, so Article 3(1) applies
Example 4 (class slide 34)A French company's car sharing app is offered only in Morocco, Algeria and TunisiaCovered: processing is in the context of an EU establishment; the location of data subjects is irrelevant under Article 3(1)
Example 3 (class slide 35)A South African hotel chain with no EU presence but a website in English, German, French and SpanishOutside Article 3(1); its position depends on Article 3(2), where EU languages are one sign of targeting

Caveat. The slides' examples carry the numbering of the EDPB's Guidelines 3/2018 and appear to be taken from them;† they are hypotheticals.

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: Targeting and monitoring: Article 3(2)
slides.html:
Article 3(2) reaches controllers and processors outside the Union that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people who are in the Union.

Article 3(2). Applies to controllers and processors outside the Union that process data of data subjects "who are in the Union" (location, not nationality) where processing relates to:

  1. Article 3(2)(a): offering goods or services to them, paid or free; or
  2. Article 3(2)(b): monitoring their behaviour in the Union.

Targeting (Recital 23, class slide 36). The question is whether the controller apparently envisages offering services to people in one or more Member States.

Insufficient on its ownMay suffice
Mere accessibility of a website or contact detailsUse of an EU language or currency with the possibility of ordering
Use of the controller's home languageMention of EU customers

Monitoring (Recital 24). Tracking people on the internet, including profiling to predict preferences and behaviour, is monitoring.

ExampleFactsCovered?
Example 10 (class slide 37)A US tourist in Europe uses a US news app aimed solely at the US market (dollar pricing)No: nothing targets people in the Union
Example 11A Taiwanese bank serves German citizens who live in TaiwanNo: they are not in the Union, and nationality is irrelevant
Example 14 (class slide 38)A Turkish photo album site in English, French, Dutch and German, priced in euros, delivering to France, the Benelux countries and GermanyYes: EU languages, the euro and EU delivery show targeting

Consequences. A controller caught by Article 3(2) must normally appoint an EU representative (Article 27). Separately, Article 3(3) covers places where Member State law applies by public international law, such as diplomatic missions.

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: Answering a scope question, step by step
slides.html:
Answer every scope question in the same order: personal data and processing, the Article 2 filters, an EU establishment, then targeting or monitoring, then a representative.

  1. Is there personal data and processing (Article 4(1) and (2))?
  2. Is the processing automated, or part of a filing system (Article 2(1))?
  3. Does any Article 2(2) exclusion apply?
  4. Is there an EU establishment (Article 3(1))?
  5. Otherwise, is there targeting or monitoring (Article 3(2))?
  6. Then, if Article 3(2) applies, a representative (Article 27).

The two territorial routes work differently, which is why the order matters:

Article 3(1)Article 3(2)
WhoA controller or processor with an EU establishmentA controller or processor outside the Union
TriggerProcessing in the context of the establishment's activitiesOffering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in the Union
Where data subjects areIrrelevantMust be in the Union (location, not nationality)
Extra duty—Normally an EU representative (Article 27)

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: Comparison with Section 3 of the DPDP Act
slides.html:
DPDP s. 3 is narrower than the GDPR: it covers only digital or digitised data, uses processing in India as its trigger, and has no monitoring limb.

What s. 3 covers. Digital personal data processed in India, whether collected digitally or collected physically and digitised later, and processing abroad connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India. It excludes personal or domestic processing and data made public by the Data Principal or under a legal obligation. The provision commences on 13 May 2027.

PointGDPRDPDP Act s. 3
Paper recordsCovered if part of a filing systemUndigitised paper files not covered
Main triggerAn EU establishment (Article 3(1))Processing in India
Reach abroadTargeting or monitoring (Article 3(2))Offering goods or services in India only: no monitoring limb
Public dataStill protectedData made public by the Data Principal excluded
Foreigners' dataCovered under Article 3(1) wherever the data subjects areProcessing in India of foreigners' data under foreign contracts exempt (s. 17(1)(d))

Why the gap matters. The missing monitoring limb lets foreign entities that profile Indians without selling to them escape the Act.

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: Key recitals for Chapter 2
slides.html:
Recitals 14 to 24 explain who is protected, which processing is covered, and when an establishment, targeting or monitoring brings a controller within the GDPR.

Recital 14
Protection applies to natural persons whatever their nationality or residence, but not to legal persons, so a company's name and contact details are not personal data.
Recital 15
Protection is technologically neutral to prevent circumvention; it covers automated processing and manual filing systems, but unstructured files and their cover pages fall outside. This is the basis of the Jehovah's Witnesses reasoning.
Recital 16
National security and Common Foreign and Security Policy activities are outside the Regulation (class slide 29).
Recital 18
Purely personal or household activity, including correspondence, addresses and social networking within such activity, is excluded, but providers of the means for such activity are covered (class slide 29).
Recital 22
Establishment means effective and real activity through stable arrangements, whatever the legal form, and the processing need not occur in the Union (class slide 33).
Recital 23
Non EU controllers offering goods or services to people in the Union are covered if an intention to target is apparent; accessibility or a home language is insufficient, while EU languages or currency with ordering, or mention of EU customers, may suffice (class slide 36).
Recital 24
Monitoring means tracking people online, including profiling to take decisions or to predict preferences, behaviour and attitudes.

slides.part: Chapter 2: When and Where the GDPR Applies
slides.title: Exam guidance: Chapter 2
slides.html:
The GDPR covers automated and structured manual processing, subject to Article 2's exclusions, through an EU establishment or by a non EU controller targeting or monitoring people in the Union.

Exam focus. Common mistakes to avoid:

  1. Do not treat nationality as decisive.
  2. Do not treat website accessibility as targeting.
  3. Do not forget that Article 3(1) applies even when every data subject is outside the Union.
  4. Do not stretch the household exemption to internet publication.

Model problem

A Bengaluru firm sells German language courses priced in euros and tracks EU visitors.

  1. Courses in an EU language, priced in euros: offering goods or services under Article 3(2)(a).
  2. Tracking EU visitors: monitoring under Article 3(2)(b).
  3. So the firm must appoint an EU representative (Article 27).
  4. The DPDP Act, by contrast, reaches foreign firms only through offering goods or services in India.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: The four elements of personal data
slides.html:
Personal data has four elements: any information, relating to, an identified or identifiable, natural person; identifiability is judged by all means reasonably likely to be used.

This chapter explains personal data (Article 4(1), Breyer, Nowak), anonymisation and pseudonymisation (EDPS v SRB), and controllership (Fashion ID). Article 4(1) (class slide 23) breaks into four elements:

"Any information"

Facts and opinions, in any form

"Relating to"

By content, purpose or effect

"Identified or identifiable"

Directly, or indirectly by combining information (class slide 24)

"Natural person"

A living human being: company data are not personal data, though a sole trader's may be

Recital 26: the identifiability test. All means reasonably likely to be used, such as singling out, by the controller or another person, considering cost, time and available technology.

The class slide 25 flowchart asks three questions. If all three answers are yes, the GDPR applies.

  1. Does the data relate to a person?
  2. Is the person alive?
  3. Can the person be identified, directly or by an identification number or physical, physiological, mental, economic, cultural or social factors?

The dead. Recital 27 excludes deceased persons and leaves them to Member States, while the DPDP Act lets a Data Principal nominate someone to exercise her rights after death (s. 14).

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: Breyer: dynamic IP addresses
slides.html:
A dynamic IP address is personal data for a website operator that has legal means to identify the user through data held by the internet service provider.

A dynamic IP address is assigned afresh at each connection. A website logs it, but only the internet service provider can link it to a subscriber. The question is whether it is personal data in the website's hands.

Patrick Breyer v Bundesrepublik Deutschland (Case C 582/14, 19 October 2016; class slide 24)

Facts
German federal websites stored visitors' dynamic IP addresses to defend against cyber attacks.
Held
  1. A dynamic IP address is personal data for the website operator where it has legal means to identify the user with additional data held by the provider. In Germany it could, after an attack, turn to the competent authority, which could obtain the subscriber's identity.
  2. Identification is not reasonably likely if prohibited by law or practically impossible because of disproportionate effort.
  3. National law may not categorically exclude the operator's interest in keeping its website operational from the legitimate interests balance.
Significance
Identifiability is judged from the holder's position, including lawful access to information held by others, and the reasoning extends to cookies and device identifiers (Recital 30).

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: Nowak: examination scripts
slides.html:
A candidate's answers and the examiner's comments are both personal data, because "relating to" covers content, purpose and effect.

Peter Nowak v Data Protection Commissioner (Case C 434/16, Grand Chamber, 20 December 2017, ECLI:EU:C:2017:994; class slide 26, not listed in syllabus.md)

Facts
A candidate sought access to his corrected script, and the Irish Commissioner refused to act, saying it was not personal data.
Held
  1. The candidate's answers are his personal data because they reflect his knowledge and competence.
  2. The examiner's comments are also his personal data because they evaluate his individual performance and affect him (paragraphs 42 and 43).
  3. They are simultaneously the examiner's personal data, because the same information may relate to several people (paragraphs 44 and 45).
Significance
"Relating to" covers content, purpose and effect, so opinions and assessments about a person are personal data, which supports access to appraisals and evaluations.

Remember: one script, two data subjects: the candidate (answers and comments) and the examiner (comments).

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: Anonymised and pseudonymised data
slides.html:
Anonymous information falls outside the GDPR, but pseudonymised data remain personal data for whoever holds the key.

AnonymisationPseudonymisation
MeaningInformation that does not relate to an identifiable person (Recital 26)Data attributable to a person only with separately kept additional information, protected by technical and organisational measures (Article 4(5))
AimMake reidentification not reasonably likely for anyoneReplace identifiers with codes or tokens
TechniquesAggregation, generalisation, suppression, added noiseKeyed hashing, tokenisation, encryption with a separate key
GDPR statusOutside the GDPRRemain personal data for the key holder (class slide 24)

Encryption versus hashing. Encryption is reversible with the key, while hashing is one way. Yet even a hash of a phone number can be reversed by hashing every possible number and matching the results, so hashing alone rarely anonymises.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: EDPS v SRB: identifiability depends on who holds the data
slides.html:
Pseudonymised data remain personal data for the key holder, but since EDPS v SRB (2025) they may not be personal data for a recipient unable reasonably to reidentify.

Current law update. In EDPS v Single Resolution Board (Case C 413/23 P, 4 September 2025, ECLI:EU:C:2025:645), the SRB sent coded comments to Deloitte and kept the key. The Court held that pseudonymised data are not personal data in all cases and for every person: for a recipient unable reasonably to reidentify, they may not be personal data, though they remain so for the key holder, whose information duties are judged from its own perspective at collection; personal opinions relate to their author. The Commission's Digital Omnibus proposal (COM(2025) 837, 19 November 2025) would make identifiability entity relative in Article 4(1); it is only a proposal, opposed by the EDPB and EDPS, and the Council's October 2026 mandate reportedly keeps the current definition. Class slide 24 remains correct for the key holder.

Who holds the coded dataPersonal data?
The SRB, which kept the keyYes: its information duties are judged from its own perspective at collection
Deloitte, the recipient without the keyMay not be, if it is unable reasonably to reidentify

The DPDP position. The DPDP Act defines neither concept. Personal data is any data about an individual identifiable by or in relation to it (s. 2(t)), and Rule 6(1)(a) treats encryption, masking, obfuscation and virtual tokens as security safeguards rather than exits from the Act.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: Controllers, processors and joint controllers
slides.html:
Controllership is functional: whoever actually decides why and how data are processed is the controller, whatever a contract says.

RoleTestProvision
ControllerActually decides why and how data are processed (purposes and means), alone or jointly, whatever a contract saysArticle 4(7)
ProcessorActs only on documented instructions, on the controller's behalfArticle 4(8), under an Article 28 contract
Joint controllersTwo or more controllers jointly determine purposes and meansArticle 26

Because the test is functional, a contract cannot turn a party that in fact decides purposes and means into a mere processor.

Joint controllers' duties (Article 26). They must:

  1. transparently allocate their responsibilities, especially for rights and information duties;
  2. make the essence of the arrangement available to data subjects; and
  3. remain answerable to each data subject individually.

Liability. Under Article 82(4), each party involved can be liable for the entire damage.†

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: Fashion ID: website plugins and joint control
slides.html:
A website that embeds a social plugin is a joint controller with the platform, but only for collection and transmission, not for the platform's later processing.

An embedded social plugin makes the visitor's browser send data such as the IP address and browser details to the platform as soon as the page loads, without any click or account.

Fashion ID GmbH & Co. KG v Verbraucherzentrale NRW eV (Case C 40/17, 29 July 2019; class slide 32)

Facts
An online retailer embedded Facebook's "Like" button, and a consumer association sued.
Held
  1. The Directive did not preclude consumer associations from bringing proceedings.†
  2. Fashion ID was a joint controller with Facebook Ireland only for the collection and disclosure by transmission of visitors' data, not for Facebook's later processing, over which it had no influence.
Reasoning
By embedding the plugin, Fashion ID decisively influenced collection and transmission for its own commercial benefit (publicity for its goods), while Facebook gained data. Each joint controller needs its own legitimate interest, and where consent is needed the website operator must obtain it and inform visitors for its share of the processing.
Significance
Governs cookies, pixels, analytics and embedded tools, and shows that joint control can be partial and stage specific.
StageController
Collection of visitors' dataFashion ID and Facebook Ireland jointly
Disclosure by transmissionFashion ID and Facebook Ireland jointly
Facebook's later processingFacebook alone: Fashion ID had no influence

Wirtschaftsakademie Schleswig Holstein (Case C 210/16, 5 June 2018)†

Earlier, a Facebook fan page administrator was held to be a joint controller with Facebook.†

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: The DPDP position on controllership
slides.html:
The DPDP Act mirrors controller and processor as Data Fiduciary and Data Processor, but has no joint controllership rule like Article 26.

Data Fiduciary, s. 2(i)
Any person who "alone or in conjunction with other persons" determines purpose and means.
Data Processor, s. 2(k)
Processes on the fiduciary's behalf.
  1. The fiduciary remains responsible for its processors' processing regardless of contract (s. 8(1)).
  2. It may use a processor only under a valid contract (s. 8(2)).
PointGDPRDPDP Act
Decision makerController (Article 4(7))Data Fiduciary (s. 2(i))
Acts for itProcessor (Article 4(8)), under an Article 28 contractData Processor (s. 2(k)), under a valid contract (s. 8(2))
Joint controlArticle 26 arrangement allocating responsibilitiesNo equivalent: joint fiduciaries need not allocate responsibilities
Sharing liability in a Fashion ID situationEach party can be liable for the entire damage (Article 82(4))†The Act is silent

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: Key recitals for Chapter 3
slides.html:
Recitals 26 to 30 supply the identifiability test, exclude deceased persons, present pseudonymisation as a safeguard and name online identifiers.

Recital 26
Treats pseudonymised data that can be attributed with additional information as data on an identifiable person; sets the test of all means reasonably likely to be used (singling out; cost, time and technology at the time of processing); and excludes anonymous information, including for statistical or research purposes. Breyer and EDPS v SRB apply it.
Recital 27
Excludes deceased persons and leaves rules to Member States (class slide 24).
Recital 28
Pseudonymisation reduces risk and helps compliance without excluding other measures, which explains its role as a safeguard in Articles 6(4), 25, 32 and 89.
Recital 30
Recognises online identifiers such as IP addresses, cookie identifiers and RFID tags, whose traces can be combined to profile and identify people: the legislative counterpart of Breyer.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Personal Data, Pseudonymisation and Controllership
slides.title: Exam guidance: Chapter 3
slides.html:
Personal data is any information relating to an identifiable living person; whoever determines purposes and means, alone or jointly, controls the operations it influences.

Exam focus. Common mistakes to avoid:

  1. Do not treat pseudonymised data as anonymous.
  2. Do not treat IP addresses as always, or as never, personal data.
  3. Do not make a website operator responsible for a platform's later processing.
  4. Do not invent a DPDP anonymisation exemption.

Model problem

An Indian retailer targets French customers and embeds a plugin and pixel on its site.

  1. Targeting French customers brings it within Article 3(2).
  2. Embedding the plugin and pixel makes it a joint controller for collection and transmission (Fashion ID).
  3. So it needs an Article 26 arrangement.

slides.title: The architecture of Chapter II
slides.html:
Every processing operation must comply with the seven principles in Article 5 and rest on one of the six lawful bases in Article 6.

Chapter II of the GDPR (class slide 39) contains seven Articles:

ArticleSubject
Article 5Principles
Article 6Lawfulness
Article 7Conditions for consent
Article 8Children's consent for information society services
Article 9Special categories
Article 10Criminal convictions
Article 11Processing not requiring identification

Seven principles. Article 5(1) lists six principles and Article 5(2) adds accountability (class slide 40). Infringements attract the highest tier of fines.

  1. Lawfulness, fairness and transparency: Article 5(1)(a)
  2. Purpose limitation: Article 5(1)(b)
  3. Data minimisation: Article 5(1)(c)
  4. Accuracy: Article 5(1)(d)
  5. Storage limitation: Article 5(1)(e)
  6. Integrity and confidentiality: Article 5(1)(f)
  7. Accountability: Article 5(2)

Remember: "Lawyers Prefer Minimal, Accurate, Short, Intact Answers": Lawfulness, Purpose, Minimisation, Accuracy, Storage, Integrity, Accountability.

slides.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
slides.html:
Article 5(1)(a) bundles three duties: a legal basis and compliance with other law, no unjustifiably detrimental or unexpected processing, and clear information.

Article 5(1)(a) (class slide 41) has three parts:

Lawfulness

An Article 6 basis (plus an Article 9 condition for special data) and compliance with other law

Fairness

Forbids processing that is unjustifiably detrimental, unexpected or misleading, and respects reasonable expectations

Transparency

Accessible, easily understood information in clear and plain language (Recital 39)

Article 12. Information must be concise and intelligible, and rights requests must be answered without undue delay and within one month, extendable by two months for complex or numerous requests if the data subject is told within the first month.

  1. A rights request arrives.
  2. Respond without undue delay, and within one month.
  3. If the requests are complex or numerous, tell the data subject within the first month, and the period extends by two months.

slides.title: The six lawful bases
slides.html:
Article 6(1) permits processing only on one of six bases; there is no hierarchy, consent is not the default, and the basis should be fixed before processing begins.

Article 6(1)BasisWhat it requires
(a)ConsentConsent for specific purposes (Chapter 5)
(b)ContractNecessity for a contract with the data subject, or for pre contract steps at her request, judged objectively: behavioural advertising is not necessary for a social network contract
(c)Legal obligationAn obligation laid down by Union or Member State law
(d)Vital interestsLife or death situations
(e)Public taskA public task or official authority with a basis in law
(f)Legitimate interestsOf the controller or a third party, unless overridden by the data subject's interests, especially a child's; unavailable to public authorities performing their tasks

The legitimate interests test has three steps, because the controller's interest must be weighed against the data subject's:

  1. A legitimate interest.
  2. Necessity of the processing for it.
  3. Balancing against the data subject's interests.

Class slide 42 lists the bases. Remember three rules: there is no hierarchy, consent is not the default, and the basis should be fixed before processing begins.

Remember: "Clever Cats Love Visiting Public Libraries": Consent, Contract, Legal obligation, Vital interests, Public task, Legitimate interests.

slides.title: Purpose limitation
slides.html:
Data collected for specified purposes may be reused only for compatible purposes; an incompatible new use needs its own basis, such as consent.

Article 5(1)(b) (class slide 47). Data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed incompatibly; archiving, research and statistics are deemed compatible with Article 89(1) safeguards.

The compatibility assessment, Article 6(4) (class slide 48). Without consent or a law, the controller must consider:

  1. the link between purposes;
  2. the context and relationship;
  3. the nature of the data (especially special or criminal data);
  4. the possible consequences; and
  5. safeguards such as encryption or pseudonymisation.
OutcomeWhat follows (class slide 47, Recital 50)
Compatible further processingNeeds no new basis
Incompatible further processingNeeds its own basis, such as consent

The class slide 2 cartoon, the pupil asking how his name will be used, is a purpose limitation story: he wants to know the purpose before he hands over his data.

Remember: the Article 6(4) factors: Link, Context, Nature, Consequences, Safeguards ("Lions Can Never Climb Stairs").

slides.title: Data minimisation, accuracy and storage limitation
slides.html:
Three principles control the data itself: hold only what is necessary, keep it accurate, and keep it in identifiable form no longer than needed.

PrincipleThe ruleHow it is applied
Minimisation: Article 5(1)(c), class slide 49Data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessaryProcessed only if the purpose cannot reasonably be achieved by other means (Recital 39)
Accuracy: Article 5(1)(d), class slide 50Data must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to dateInaccurate data erased or rectified without delay, enforced through the right to rectification (Article 16)
Storage limitation: Article 5(1)(e), class slide 51Identifiable data kept no longer than necessaryExcept archiving, research or statistics with safeguards; controllers should set time limits for erasure or periodic review (Recital 39)

Each principle shrinks risk in a different way: less data, correct data, and data kept for a shorter time.

slides.title: Integrity and confidentiality: security and breach notification
slides.html:
Article 5(1)(f) requires appropriate security; after a breach, the GDPR notifies according to risk, while the DPDP regime requires every breach to be intimated.

Article 5(1)(f) (class slide 52). Appropriate security against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, by technical and organisational measures.

Article 32 adds risk based measures such as pseudonymisation and encryption, resilience, restoration of access and regular testing.

RuleWho must be toldWhenException
GDPR Article 33The supervisory authorityWithout undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awarenessThe breach is unlikely to result in a risk
GDPR Article 34The data subjectsWithout undue delay, where the risk is highFor example, the data were encrypted
DPDP s. 8(6) and Rule 7The Board and each affected Data PrincipalWithout delay, with a detailed report to the Board within 72 hours (from 13 May 2027)None: no risk threshold

The key contrast: the GDPR filters notification by risk, while the DPDP regime requires every breach to be intimated.

slides.title: Accountability
slides.html:
Accountability (Article 5(2)) makes the controller responsible for compliance and able to demonstrate it; class slide 53 calls it a new principle that obliges the controller.

Accountability is implemented through:

  1. Article 24: appropriate measures;
  2. Article 25: protection by design and by default;
  3. Article 30: records of processing;
  4. Article 35: impact assessments for high risk processing;
  5. Articles 37 to 39: data protection officers.

Because the controller must be able to prove compliance, records and assessments are legal duties in their own right, not optional paperwork.

Maximum fine = EUR 20 million or 4 per cent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher

Article 83(5): the ceiling for breach of the basic principles. The 4 per cent figure is the higher one once worldwide annual turnover exceeds EUR 500 million (because 4 per cent of 500 million is 20 million).

slides.title: How the DPDP Act handles the same ideas
slides.html:
The DPDP Act has no list of principles, but most GDPR principles reappear in its sections; it has no fairness principle and no legitimate interests basis.

GDPR ideaWhere the DPDP Act deals with it
Lawfulnesss. 4: a lawful purpose (anything not expressly forbidden by law), plus consent or a legitimate use
Transparencys. 5, Rule 3 and s. 6(3)
Purpose limitation and minimisations. 6(1): consent limited to the specified purpose and necessary data
Accuracys. 8(3): only where data are used for decisions or disclosed
Storage limitations. 8(7) and (8), with Rule 8
Securitys. 8(5), with Rule 6
Breach intimations. 8(6), with Rule 7
Accountabilityss. 8(1), 8(4) and 10
FairnessNo fairness principle
Legitimate interestsNo legitimate interests basis

slides.title: Key recitals for Chapter 4: principles and bases
slides.html:
Recitals 39 to 50 explain the principles, require a basis for every operation, frame legitimate interests, and set the rules for compatible further processing.

Recital 39
Summarises Article 5 (class slides 41, 49 and 51): processing must be lawful, fair and transparent; information must be accessible and clear about the controller, purposes, risks, safeguards and rights; purposes must be explicit, legitimate and fixed at collection; data must be adequate, relevant and limited, stored for a strict minimum and processed only if the purpose cannot reasonably be met otherwise; and controllers should set erasure or review deadlines, rectify or delete inaccurate data, and secure data and equipment against unauthorised access.
Recital 40
Requires consent or another basis laid down by law for every processing operation.
Recital 47
Frames legitimate interests around the data subject's reasonable expectations given her relationship with the controller (as a client or employee, for example). Her interests may override where further processing is unexpected; the basis is unavailable to public authorities in their tasks; fraud prevention is a legitimate interest; and direct marketing may be one.
Recital 50
Allows compatible further processing without a separate basis (class slide 47) and lists the compatibility factors. It permits further processing regardless of compatibility with consent or a proportionate law, while preserving information and the right to object. It treats archiving, research and statistics as compatible, and reporting possible crimes to authorities as a legitimate interest.

slides.title: Key recitals for Chapter 4: risk, security, breaches and fines
slides.html:
Recitals 74 to 150 tie accountability to risk, explain protection by design, set out breach notification and guide how fines are fixed.

Recital 74
Establishes the controller's responsibility and liability and its duty to demonstrate effective measures proportionate to risk (Articles 5(2) and 24).
Recital 75
Defines risk as physical, material or non material damage, such as discrimination, identity theft, fraud, financial or reputational harm, loss of professional secrecy, reversal of pseudonymisation and loss of control. Risky processing: special or criminal data, profiling, children's data and large scale processing.
Recital 78
Protection by design and by default: minimisation, early pseudonymisation, transparency, monitoring by data subjects and improved security, with producers and public tenders encouraged to build it in (Article 25).
Recital 83
Risk evaluation and mitigation such as encryption, considering the state of the art, cost and the nature of the data (Article 32).
Recital 85
Notification to the authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours unless risk is unlikely, with reasons for delay and information in phases (Article 33).
Recital 86
Communication to data subjects without undue delay where risk is high, describing the breach and mitigation, in cooperation with authorities (Article 34), unlike Rule 7's duty to tell every Data Principal.
Recital 150
Every supervisory authority has power to fine; amounts are fixed case by case by nature, gravity, duration, consequences and mitigation; "undertaking" bears its meaning under Articles 101 and 102 TFEU; and individuals' fines reflect income levels (Article 83). Compare DPDP s. 33(2).

slides.title: Exam guidance: Chapter 4
slides.html:
Every operation needs an Article 6 basis and must respect all seven principles, and the controller must be able to prove that it does.

Exam focus. Common mistakes to avoid:

  1. Do not treat consent as preferred.
  2. Do not give public authorities legitimate interests.
  3. Do not forget that the 72 hours run from awareness.
  4. Do not credit the DPDP Act with fairness or legitimate interests.

Model problem

A delivery app reuses customers' order histories for individual pricing.

  1. Reuse for a new purpose without consent or a law triggers the Article 6(4) compatibility assessment.
  2. There is a weak link between delivery and pricing, the use is unexpected, and the consequences are adverse.
  3. The new purpose is therefore incompatible, so fresh consent is needed.
  4. If pricing is automated, add an Article 22 analysis.

slides.title: What valid consent means
slides.html:
Consent is the most cited and most misused lawful basis: it must be a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication, shown by a statement or clear affirmative action.

This chapter covers Articles 4(11), 7 and 8, the forced consent enforcement record and DPDP s. 6. Class slide 43 shows how the pieces fit: the lawful basis in Article 6(1)(a) is explained by the definition in Article 4(11), the conditions in Article 7 and the rule for children in Article 8.

Article 4(11), GDPR. Consent is any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes, by a statement or clear affirmative action.

Freely given
Only where there is a genuine choice and the person can refuse or withdraw without detriment (Recitals 42 and 43).
Specific
Tied to defined purposes, with separate consent for separate purposes.
Informed
The data subject knows at least the controller's identity and the purposes (Recital 42).
Unambiguous
Given by a statement or a clear affirmative act.

Each element blocks one kind of fake consent: pressure (not free), a blanket "yes" (not specific), ignorance (not informed) and mere silence (not unambiguous). Recital 32 (class slide 45) draws the practical line.

Counts as consent

Ticking a box, choosing settings or other clear conduct.

Never consent

Silence, pre ticked boxes and inactivity.

Electronic requests must be clear, concise and not unnecessarily disruptive. Planet49 (Case C 673/17, 1 October 2019) applied the pre ticked box rule to cookies.†

Unverified (†). Planet49 rests on secondary knowledge not checked against the judgment (Appendix G).

Remember: Free, Specific, Informed, Unambiguous, and always an act. Silence is never a "yes".

slides.title: Article 7: the four conditions
slides.html:
Article 7 adds four conditions to the definition: the controller must prove consent, separate the request, allow easy withdrawal and not make a service conditional on unnecessary consent.

The definition says what consent is; Article 7 (class slide 44) says how a controller must handle it. Read each rule as closing a loophole.

  1. Proof, Article 7(1). The controller must be able to demonstrate consent. The party relying on consent carries the burden, so consent it cannot show is as good as none.
  2. A distinguishable request, Article 7(2). A consent request in a written declaration that also covers other matters must be clearly distinguishable, intelligible, easily accessible and in plain language, and any infringing part is not binding. This stops consent being buried in terms and conditions.
  3. Withdrawal, Article 7(3). Consent may be withdrawn at any time, without affecting earlier processing; the data subject must be told this beforehand; and withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent. A "yes" that cannot be undone was never free.
  4. Conditionality, Article 7(4). In assessing whether consent is free, utmost account is taken of whether a contract or service is made conditional on consent to processing that it does not need.

Article 7(4) is circled on the class slide because it targets "take it or leave it" designs, where the only way to get the service is to agree to extra processing.

slides.title: Children's consent: Article 8
slides.html:
Where consent is relied on for online services offered directly to children, the GDPR age is 16, which States may lower to 13; India sets 18 for all processing.

Article 8, GDPR. Where consent is relied on for information society services offered directly to a child, processing is lawful from the age of 16; below that age, a holder of parental responsibility must consent or authorise.

  1. Member States may lower the age, but not below 13.
  2. Controllers must make reasonable efforts to verify parental consent, using available technology.
  3. National contract law is unaffected: Article 8 decides when consent to processing is valid, not whether a child's contract binds.

Article 8 is narrow: it applies only where consent is the basis, and only to information society services aimed directly at children. The DPDP Act is stricter on every point.

PointGDPR, Article 8DPDP Act, s. 9
Who is a childUnder 16 (or a national age not below 13)Everyone under 18
Parental consentFor consent-based information society services offered directly to a childVerifiable parental consent for all processing
Tracking and adsNo ban in Article 8 (Recital 38 seeks specific protection)Tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children banned

Exam focus. Never apply the age of 16 in India. A problem with Indian and German users needs both answers: parental consent below 16 (or the German age) under Article 8, and verifiable parental consent for every user under 18 under s. 9.

slides.title: Forced consent: the enforcement record
slides.html:
Forcing users to accept processing wholesale with the terms of service was challenged in noyb's 2018 "forced consent" complaints, and regulators have since fined Google and Meta heavily.

Class slide 46 reproduces noyb's project page. In May 2018 noyb filed four "forced consent" complaints, arguing that users were forced to accept privacy policies and terms of service wholesale:

Filed inAgainst
FranceGoogle
AustriaFacebook
BelgiumInstagram
GermanyWhatsApp

The page records that the CNIL fined Google 50 million euros in January 2019, that the fine was appealed with a hearing still to be fixed, and that the Meta complaints went to the Irish Data Protection Commission as lead authority under the one stop shop, because the Meta companies' main EU establishment is in Ireland.

Current law update. The CNIL fined Google LLC 50 million euros on 21 January 2019 for lack of transparency, inadequate information and invalid consent to ad personalisation; the Conseil d'État dismissed the appeal on 19 June 2020 (no. 430810), holding the CNIL competent because Google LLC then had no EU main establishment, and that the consent was neither specific nor unambiguous. After EDPB binding decisions, the Irish DPC announced on 4 January 2023 fines on Meta Platforms Ireland of 210 million euros (Facebook) and 180 million euros (Instagram), and on 19 January 2023 a fine of 5.5 million euros on WhatsApp Ireland, rejecting reliance on contractual necessity for behavioural advertising. noyb's own table still listed those complaints as pending when last reviewed, so cite the regulators' decisions, not class slide 46.

Meta Platforms v Bundeskartellamt, Case C 252/21, CJEU, 4 July 2023†

Dominance does not in itself invalidate consent but is an important factor, and personalised advertising is not generally necessary for a social network contract.† EDPB Opinion 08/2024 then addressed "consent or pay" models of large platforms.†

slides.title: Consent under the DPDP Act: section 6
slides.html:
DPDP s. 6 demands consent that is free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, limited to necessary data, as easy to withdraw as to give, and provable by the fiduciary.

Processing under the DPDP Act rests on consent or a legitimate use (s. 4), with no legitimate interests basis. Section 6 writes the GDPR's ideas into the definition of consent itself, and the Act illustrates each rule.

  1. s. 6(1), the standard. Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action, for the specified purpose and limited to necessary data. A telemedicine app's consent covers telemedicine but not access to phone contacts.
  2. s. 6(2), invalid parts. Parts infringing the law are invalid: an insurance app's waiver of the right to complain to the Board fails, while the rest stands.
  3. s. 6(3), the request. Clear, plain language; availability in English or an Eighth Schedule language; and the contact details of a DPO or authorised person.
  4. ss. 6(4) to (6), withdrawal. Consent may be withdrawn as easily as it was given. The Data Principal bears the consequences, without affecting earlier processing: a shopping platform may refuse new orders but must complete paid ones. The fiduciary must, within a reasonable time, stop processing and make its processors stop: a telecom company must stop emailed bills.
  5. Sections 6(7) to (9). Provide for Consent Managers.
  6. s. 6(10), proof. The burden of proving notice and consent is on the fiduciary.
PointGDPRDPDP Act
Bundling"Utmost account" of conditionality (Article 7(4))"Unconditional": the rule stated more strongly
NecessityA factor in judging freedomBuilt into consent
ChildrenUnder 16, consent-based online services (Article 8)Under 18: broader protection (s. 9)

slides.title: Key recitals on consent
slides.html:
Five recitals explain consent: 32 on how it is given, 33 on research, 38 on children, 42 on proof and knowledge, and 43 on imbalance and conditional consent.

Recitals are not binding in themselves, but the Court of Justice reads the Articles through them and examiners expect them to be cited.

Recital 32 (class slide 45)
Requires a clear affirmative act: a written, electronic or oral statement, ticking a box, choosing settings. Excludes silence, pre ticked boxes and inactivity. Consent must cover all processing for the same purposes, and every purpose where there are several. Electronic requests must be clear, concise and non disruptive.
Recital 33
Allows consent to certain areas of scientific research in line with recognised ethical standards ("broad consent"), with the option of consenting to parts only.
Recital 38
Gives children specific protection, especially against marketing and profiling and in services offered directly to them, and dispenses with parental consent for preventive or counselling services, paralleling DPDP s. 9(3).
Recital 42
Requires demonstrable consent; awareness of its extent in declarations covering other matters; pre formulated declarations in plain language without unfair terms; knowledge of the controller and purposes; and a genuine free choice without detriment.
Recital 43
Denies validity where there is a clear imbalance, especially with public authorities, and presumes consent not free where separate consents are not allowed for different operations or a contract or service depends on unnecessary consent. It is the foundation of the forced consent cases and of Article 7(4).

Remember: 32 = how, 33 = research, 38 = children, 42 = proof and knowledge, 43 = power and bundling.

slides.title: Exam guidance: consent
slides.html:
In a consent problem, test every element and every Article 7 condition; bundling unnecessary processing into a service destroys the freedom of consent.

Exam focus. Valid consent is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, given by an affirmative act, provable, and as easy to withdraw as to give; bundling unnecessary processing destroys its freedom.

Four mistakes cost marks:

  1. Treating acceptance of terms as consent to everything.
  2. Treating withdrawal as retroactive: it does not affect earlier processing.
  3. Applying the age of 16 in India, where everyone under 18 is a child.
  4. Citing class slide 46 as showing a pending appeal: the Conseil d'État upheld the fine on 19 June 2020.

Worked problem

A social network makes ad personalisation a condition of sign up.

  1. Contract basis. Ad personalisation is not necessary for a social network contract, so Article 6(1)(b) is not available, as the Irish DPC's Meta decisions show.
  2. Consent. Sign up depends on consent to processing the service does not need, so consent is not free (Article 7(4), Recital 43).
  3. GDPR result. The design fails under GDPR Articles 6(1)(b) and 7(4) and Recital 43, as the Meta decisions show.
  4. DPDP result. It also fails under s. 6(1), where consent is the only route and must be unconditional.

slides.part: Chapter 6: Special Categories of Personal Data
slides.title: The special categories in Article 9(1)
slides.html:
Special categories are data whose misuse risks discrimination and serious harm, so Article 9(1) prohibits processing them unless an exception applies.

Most personal data can be processed on any Article 6 basis. A short list of categories gets a stronger rule: a general prohibition with exceptions. This chapter covers Article 9, Lindqvist, indirect revelation and the DPDP approach.

Article 9(1) (class slide 54) prohibits processing data revealing four aspects of identity and belonging, and four kinds of data about the body and intimate life:

Data revealing

Racial or ethnic origin; political opinions; religious or philosophical beliefs; trade union membership.

And

Genetic data; biometric data for unique identification; health data; data concerning sex life or sexual orientation.

Why a prohibition? Because their misuse risks discrimination and serious harm. For ordinary data the law regulates how processing happens; for these categories the harm of misuse, such as discrimination, can be severe and hard to undo, so the starting point is a ban.

What counts is what the data reveal, not what they are called, which is why indirect revelation matters (see below).

Remember: "Ravi Plays Rugby Until Getting Badly Hurt Somewhere": Racial or ethnic origin, Political opinions, Religious or philosophical beliefs, Union membership, Genetic, Biometric, Health, Sex life or orientation.

slides.part: Chapter 6: Special Categories of Personal Data
slides.title: The Article 9(2) exceptions
slides.html:
Article 9(2) lifts the prohibition in ten situations, but only in addition to an Article 6 basis: special category data always need two legal grounds.

Think of a double lock. Article 6 supplies the lawful basis that every processing needs; an Article 9(2) exception must also open the prohibition. Explicit consent is only one of the ten keys.

  1. Explicit consent, unless law forbids it.
  2. Employment, social security and social protection law.
  3. Vital interests where consent is impossible.
  4. Legitimate activities of not for profit bodies concerning members.
  5. Data manifestly made public by the data subject.
  6. Legal claims and courts acting judicially.
  7. Substantial public interest under law with safeguards.
  8. Preventive or occupational medicine and health or social care.
  9. Public health.
  10. Archiving, research or statistics.

Article 10, GDPR. Criminal conviction data are governed separately: processing needs official authority, or an authorising law with safeguards.

Exam focus. Do not treat explicit consent as the only exception. Name the Article 9(2) exception and the Article 6 basis separately.

slides.part: Chapter 6: Special Categories of Personal Data
slides.title: Lindqvist: health data on a web page
slides.html:
Lindqvist read "health data" broadly, denied the household exemption to internet publication, and held that uploading to an EU hosted web page is not a transfer abroad.

Criminal proceedings against Bodil Lindqvist, Case C 101/01, CJEU, 6 November 2003

Facts
A Swedish parish catechist created web pages describing herself and eighteen colleagues by name, job and hobbies, noting that one had injured her foot and was on half time medical leave, without consent. She was prosecuted.
Held
  1. Naming and identifying people on a web page is processing by automatic means.
  2. The injured foot reference is health data under Article 8(1) of the Directive, which covers all physical and mental aspects of health.
  3. The household exemption does not cover publication on the internet to an indefinite audience.
  4. Loading data onto an EU hosted web page accessible worldwide is not a transfer to a third country under Article 25 of the Directive.
Significance
The broad reading of health data, the limits of the household exemption and the meaning of "transfer" (Chapter 8).

The case was decided under Directive 95/46/EC, so its article numbers are the Directive's, but its three readings are still used under the GDPR. The transfer point is practical: if uploading counted, every page visible worldwide would be a transfer to every country.

Correction. Lindqvist was decided on 6 November 2003; class slide 54 and syllabus.md wrongly say 2004, and the slide spells it "Lindquist".

slides.part: Chapter 6: Special Categories of Personal Data
slides.title: Indirect revelation and the DPDP approach
slides.html:
What can be inferred matters more than the label, because ordinary data can reveal sensitive facts; India's DPDP Act, by contrast, has no sensitive category at all.

OT v Vyriausioji tarnybinės etikos komisija, Case C 184/20, CJEU, 1 August 2022†

Publishing the names of officials' spouses or partners could indirectly reveal sexual orientation and so engaged Article 9.†

So ask what the data could show: purchases may reveal health, and location may reveal religion.

The DPDP approach. The DPDP Act has no sensitive category. It gives extra protection only to children and persons with disability who have lawful guardians (s. 9), and lists "volume and sensitivity" as a factor for notifying Significant Data Fiduciaries (s. 10(1)(a)).

Until IT Act s. 43A is omitted on 13 May 2027, the SPDI Rules 2011 continue to define sensitive personal data or information, such as passwords, financial information, health conditions, sexual orientation, medical records and biometrics,† and both the 2018 draft and the 2019 Bill had sensitive categories.†

For the uniform approach

Simple and context sensitive.

Against it

It ignores the particular dangers of health, caste, religion and sexual orientation data in Indian society, and the Significant Data Fiduciary mechanism only partly fills the gap.

Unverified (†). OT, the SPDI Rules' list of sensitive data and the features of the 2018 draft and the 2019 Bill rest on secondary knowledge not checked against the primary texts (Appendix G).

slides.part: Chapter 6: Special Categories of Personal Data
slides.title: Recital 51 and exam guidance
slides.html:
Recital 51 explains why sensitive data get specific protection and when a photograph becomes biometric data; in exams, always pair an Article 9(2) exception with an Article 6 basis.

Recital 51.

  1. Particularly sensitive data get specific protection because of the significant risks involved.
  2. The term "racial origin" does not endorse theories of separate human races.
  3. Photographs are biometric data only when processed by specific technical means allowing unique identification or authentication: an ordinary staff photograph is not, but facial recognition processing is.
  4. Processing is barred except in specified cases, while the general principles still apply.
  5. Member States may adapt the rules for legal obligations and public tasks.
  6. Derogations must be explicit, for example explicit consent or the legitimate activities of foundations and associations.

Recital 75 also treats special category processing as a source of risk.

Exam focus. Special category data need an Article 9(2) exception plus an Article 6 basis, and health data and inferred data are read broadly. Date Lindqvist correctly to 6 November 2003, do not treat explicit consent as the only exception, and do not attribute a "sensitive data" concept to the DPDP Act.

Worked problem

A fitness app publishes users' names, heart rates and the hospitals where they had surgery. This is health data that users have not themselves made public, so the "manifestly made public" exception is unavailable. The app needs explicit consent and must minimise what it processes and publishes.

slides.title: The catalogue of rights and Article 12
slides.html:
Chapter III gives data subjects rights to know about and influence processing, and Article 12 sets how quickly, cheaply and safely controllers must respond.

This chapter explains each right, Google Spain, the right to explanation debate and the narrower DPDP rights. Class slide 55 lists eight rights:

  1. The right to know (information duties, Articles 13 and 14)
  2. Access (Article 15)
  3. Rectification (Article 16)
  4. Erasure (Article 17)
  5. Restriction (Article 18)
  6. Portability (Article 20)
  7. Objection (Article 21)
  8. Rights concerning automated decisions (Article 22)

syllabus.md notes that portability and automated decision rights are absent from the DPDP Act.

Article 12, GDPR: how rights are exercised.

  1. Controllers must facilitate the rights.
  2. They respond without undue delay and within one month, extendable by two months with notice.
  3. Action is free unless requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, when a reasonable fee or refusal is possible, with the burden on the controller.
  4. Identity may be verified where there is reasonable doubt.

Remember: "Kids Always Rewrite Exams, Rarely Passing Over Algebra": Know, Access, Rectify, Erase, Restrict, Port, Object, Automated decisions, in article order.

slides.title: The right to know, access and rectification
slides.html:
Transparency comes first: controllers must tell people about processing (Articles 13 and 14), and people can then check and correct it (Articles 15 and 16).

Where the data come fromWhen information is owed
From the data subject (Article 13)At collection
From elsewhere (Article 14)Within a reasonable period and at most one month

Either way, the controller must give:

  1. the controller's identity and contacts, and the DPO's contacts;
  2. the purposes and legal basis, including legitimate interests;
  3. the recipients, and any transfers and safeguards;
  4. the retention period;
  5. the rights, the right to withdraw consent and the right to complain;
  6. whether provision is statutory or contractual, and the consequences of not providing data;
  7. any automated decision making, with meaningful information about the logic involved and its consequences.

Access, Article 15. The data subject gets confirmation of processing, access, a copy and the information above. It is the gateway to the other rights: nobody can correct, erase or object to processing she does not know about.

Rectification, Article 16. Rectification of inaccurate data and completion of incomplete data, without undue delay. It is how the data subject enforces the accuracy principle.

slides.title: Erasure: Article 17
slides.html:
Article 17 requires erasure without undue delay on six grounds, obliges a controller that published data to alert others, and yields to expression and other public interests.

Erasure is the strongest remedy, so the GDPR states exactly when it is due and when it gives way.

When erasure is due, Article 17(1). Without undue delay, where:

  1. the data are no longer necessary;
  2. consent is withdrawn without another basis;
  3. a successful objection is made;
  4. processing is unlawful;
  5. a legal obligation requires it; or
  6. the data were collected from a child for information society services.

Data made public, Article 17(2). A controller that made data public must take reasonable steps to tell other controllers to erase links and copies. Without this duty, erasure online would achieve little, because copies spread.

When the right yields, Article 17(3).

Expression

Freedom of expression

Law

Legal obligations and public tasks

Health

Public health

Knowledge

Archiving and research

Litigation

Legal claims

slides.title: Google Spain and the right to be forgotten
slides.html:
Google Spain held that a search engine controls its name search results and must, on request, delist outdated or irrelevant links: the origin of the right to be forgotten.

Google Spain SL and Google Inc. v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos and Mario Costeja González, Case C 131/12, CJEU (Grand Chamber), 13 May 2014

Facts
A search of Mr Costeja González's name showed 1998 newspaper notices of an auction to recover his social security debts, long since resolved.
Held
  1. A search engine processes personal data by finding, indexing, storing and displaying it, and is the controller of that processing.
  2. The processing was in the context of Google Spain's advertising activities, so EU law applied.
  3. On request, the operator must remove links to third party pages from name search results, even lawfully published ones, where the information is inadequate, irrelevant or no longer relevant, or excessive in the light of the time elapsed.
Reasoning
A name search produces a structured profile that would otherwise be hard to assemble, so the interference with Charter Articles 7 and 8 is serious. As a rule those rights override the operator's economic interest and the public's interest in access, unless the person's role in public life justifies a preponderant public interest.
Significance
The origin of the right to be forgotten now in Article 17; the newspaper's archive itself was untouched.

Google v CNIL, Case C 507/17, CJEU, 24 September 2019†

EU law requires delisting on EU versions of the search engine, not worldwide, though national authorities may order wider delisting after balancing.†

India. The DPDP Act gives a right to erasure (s. 12(3)) but no right to be forgotten, and does not apply to data the Data Principal made public (s. 3(c)(ii)).

slides.title: Restriction and portability
slides.html:
Restriction freezes data without deleting them; portability lets people take the data they provided to another controller. The DPDP Act has neither right.

Restriction, Article 18. Restriction means keeping data but marking them so that they are not otherwise used: a pause button for moments when deletion would be premature. It applies:

  1. while accuracy is contested;
  2. where processing is unlawful but the data subject prefers restriction to erasure;
  3. where the controller no longer needs the data but she needs them for legal claims; and
  4. while an objection is being assessed.
