slides.title: Practice questions: Part I
slides.html:
1. HealthPal, a Pune symptom checker app used in India and, through a German version priced in euros, in Germany, embeds a social plugin and an advertising pixel, makes personalised advertising a condition of its free plan, lets users aged 13 and above register, and is hacked. Advise HealthPal under the GDPR and the DPDP Act.
  2. Distinguish privacy, confidentiality, data protection and data security. Why is data protection a fundamental right in its own name in the EU?
  3. India proposes a programme of bulk interception of communications. Using Puttaswamy and Big Brother Watch v United Kingdom, explain what safeguards it would need.
  4. A Bengaluru firm sells German language courses priced in euros and tracks visitors from the EU. Does the GDPR apply, and what must the firm do? Contrast Section 3 of the DPDP Act.
  5. An Indian retailer targeting French customers embeds a social plugin and an advertising pixel on its website. Who controls what, and what arrangement is needed?
  6. A delivery app reuses customers' order histories to set individual prices. Is this further processing lawful under the GDPR?
  7. Explain the conditions for valid consent under Articles 4(11), 7 and 8 of the GDPR. Would a social network that makes ad personalisation a condition of sign up comply? Compare Section 6 of the DPDP Act.
  8. A fitness app publishes users' names, heart rates and the hospitals where they had surgery. Advise the app under Article 9 of the GDPR, and note the Indian position.
  9. Critically discuss the right to erasure and the right to be forgotten, with reference to Google Spain.
  10. An Indian lender automatically rejects credit applications from people in Germany. What does Article 22 of the GDPR require, and is there a "right to explanation"?
  11. A German hospital wants to send patient billing data to an Indian billing processor. Advise on Chapter V of the GDPR and the Indian position.
  12. Trace EU and US data transfers from Safe Harbour to the Data Privacy Framework. How secure is the present framework?

slides.title: Answer plans: questions 1 and 2
slides.html:
Question 1 is the integrated HealthPal problem: take it issue by issue, giving the GDPR and the DPDP answer for each.

Q1. HealthPal (GDPR and DPDP)

  1. Scope. GDPR for German users (Article 3(2)(a): a German version priced in euros); DPDP Act for Indian users (s. 3(a)), with duties from 13 May 2027.
  2. Health data. Symptom data need explicit consent (Article 9(2)(a)).
  3. Consent. Conditioning the free plan on advertising fails Article 7(4) and Recital 43; advertising is not contractually necessary (the Meta decisions); and the unconditional, necessity limited consent of s. 6(1) is not met.
  4. Plugin and pixel. HealthPal is a joint controller for collection and transmission (Fashion ID).
  5. Children. Under 16, or the German age, parental consent (Article 8); under the DPDP Act every user under 18 needs verifiable parental consent and cannot be tracked or targeted (s. 9).
  6. Breach. Authority within 72 hours, high risk users promptly (Articles 33 and 34); the Board and every affected user, with a 72 hour report (Rule 7); until 13 May 2027, compensation for wrongful loss under IT Act s. 43A, health data being sensitive under the SPDI Rules.
  7. Conclude. The model fails on consent and children under both laws: GDPR fines, DPDP penalties of up to 250 crore rupees once in force, and s. 43A claims meanwhile.

Q2. Privacy, confidentiality, data protection and security

  1. Privacy is broadest, including informational privacy (Article 21, Puttaswamy; Charter Article 7; Article 8 ECHR); confidentiality protects relationships of trust and usually ends once information is public.
  2. Data protection regulates fair and lawful handling at every stage, secret or not; data security is one component (GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32; DPDP s. 8(5) with Rule 6).
  3. Show the gap: a perfectly secure organisation can still breach data protection law by collecting too much, and public information remains regulated by the GDPR.
  4. The fundamental right: Charter Article 8, Article 16 TFEU and Recital 1, limited only under Charter Article 52(1), which is why Schrems I and II tested adequacy against the Charter.
  5. Conclude: Article 8 ECHR (private life) is not Article 8 of the Charter (data protection).

slides.title: Answer plans: questions 3 to 5
slides.html:
Scope and controllership questions are answered in a fixed sequence: who is processing, whether the GDPR reaches them, and who controls which stage.

Q3. Bulk interception in India

  1. The State is often the most intrusive processor (class slide 4); the Indian test is Puttaswamy: legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
  2. Use Big Brother Watch (Grand Chamber, 25 May 2021) persuasively: bulk interception is not unlawful in itself, but intrusion grows at each stage (interception, filtering, selection by selectors, examination by analysts).
  3. List the end to end safeguards: necessity and proportionality at every stage, independent authorisation at the outset, supervision and independent review afterwards, and protection of journalistic sources.
  4. Use the UK failings as a checklist: no independent authorisation, selector categories left out of warrants, weak protection of journalistic material.
  5. Conclude by linking to the critique of DPDP s. 17(2)(a), citing the Grand Chamber judgment as final.

Q4. Bengaluru language courses

  1. Personal data and processing: yes, by automated means; no Article 2(2) exclusion applies.
  2. No EU establishment, so Article 3(1) does not apply.
  3. Article 3(2)(a): German language courses priced in euros show an intention to offer services to people in the Union (Recital 23); mere accessibility would not be enough.
  4. Article 3(2)(b): tracking EU visitors is monitoring (Recital 24).
  5. Consequence: the firm must appoint an EU representative (Article 27).
  6. Contrast: the DPDP Act reaches foreign firms only through offering goods or services in India (s. 3) and has no monitoring limb.

Q5. Indian retailer with a plugin and pixel

  1. Scope: targeting French customers brings the retailer within Article 3(2).
  2. Personal data: the plugin sends the IP address and browser details as the page loads (Breyer; Recital 30).
  3. Controllership is functional (Article 4(7)); Fashion ID makes the retailer a joint controller only for collection and transmission, not the platform's later processing.
  4. Each joint controller needs its own legitimate interest; where consent is needed, the website operator must obtain it and inform visitors for its share.
  5. Conclude: an Article 26 arrangement allocating responsibilities transparently. The DPDP Act has no equivalent and is silent on sharing liability.

slides.title: Answer plans: questions 6 to 8
slides.html:
Principles, consent and special category questions turn on applying a test in order: compatibility factors, consent conditions, then the Article 9 double lock.

Q6. Delivery app pricing

  1. Identify the principle: purpose limitation, Article 5(1)(b).
  2. With no consent or law, apply the Article 6(4) compatibility factors: link between purposes, context and relationship, nature of the data, possible consequences, safeguards.
  3. Apply: a weak link, an unexpected use and adverse consequences.
  4. Conclude: the further processing is incompatible, so it needs its own basis, here fresh consent; add Article 22 analysis if pricing is automated.

Q7. Valid consent and the social network

  1. Define consent under Article 4(11): freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, by a statement or clear affirmative action; Recital 32 excludes silence, pre ticked boxes and inactivity.
  2. Set out Article 7: proof (7(1)), a distinguishable request (7(2)), easy withdrawal (7(3)) and conditionality (7(4)); then Article 8 for children.
  3. Apply: ad personalisation is not necessary for the contract, so Article 6(1)(b) fails, and making sign up conditional on it fails Article 7(4) and Recital 43.
  4. Cite the enforcement record: the CNIL fine upheld by the Conseil d'État (19 June 2020) and the Irish DPC's Meta decisions (January 2023).
  5. Compare DPDP s. 6(1): consent must be unconditional and limited to necessary data, consent is the only route here, and the fiduciary bears the burden of proof (s. 6(10)).
  6. Conclude: the design fails under both laws.

Q8. Fitness app and health data

  1. Classify: heart rates and surgery are health data, read broadly (Lindqvist, 6 November 2003: all physical and mental aspects of health).
  2. State the double lock: the Article 9(1) prohibition needs an Article 9(2) exception plus an Article 6 basis.
  3. Exclude "manifestly made public": users have not themselves published the data.
  4. Conclude under the GDPR: the app needs explicit consent and must minimise what it publishes.
  5. India: the DPDP Act has no sensitive category; until 13 May 2027 the SPDI Rules treat health conditions and medical records as sensitive.†

slides.title: Answer plans: questions 9 and 10
slides.html:
Rights essays are built on the Article, then the leading case, then the limits and the Indian comparison, ending with a view on balance.

Q9. Erasure and the right to be forgotten

  1. Set out Article 17(1): the six grounds for erasure without undue delay.
  2. Add Article 17(2) and Recital 66: a publishing controller must tell other controllers to erase links and copies.
  3. State the limits in Article 17(3) (expression, legal obligations and public tasks, public health, archiving and research, legal claims), with Recitals 65 and 153.
  4. Brief Google Spain (13 May 2014): the search engine is a controller and must delist inadequate, irrelevant or excessive links from name searches.
  5. Explain the reasoning: a name search builds a structured profile, so Charter Articles 7 and 8 override as a rule, unless a role in public life justifies access.
  6. Note the limits: the newspaper archive was untouched, and under Google v CNIL EU law requires delisting on EU versions, not worldwide, though national authorities may order wider delisting after balancing.†
  7. Compare India: a right to erasure (s. 12(3)) but no right to be forgotten, and no application to data the Data Principal made public (s. 3(c)(ii)).

Q10. Automated credit refusal and explanation

  1. Scope: offering credit to people in Germany falls within Article 3(2)(a).
  2. Article 22(1): a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, such as automatic refusal of online credit (Recital 71).
  3. Exceptions: contract, law or explicit consent; a token human sign off does not take the decision outside Article 22.
  4. Safeguards under Article 22(3): human intervention, a chance to express a view and to contest.
  5. Explanation: Articles 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g) and 15(1)(h) require meaningful information about the logic involved; only Recital 71 mentions an explanation; set out the academic debate.†
  6. Case law: SCHUFA (credit scores) and Dun & Bradstreet Austria (the procedure and principles actually applied).†
  7. Conclude: even under the contract exception, the lender must give human review, a chance to contest and meaningful information about the procedure and principles actually applied; the DPDP Act has no counterpart.

slides.title: Answer plans: questions 11 and 12
slides.html:
Transfer questions follow Chapter V's order: is there a transfer, is there adequacy, which safeguards apply and do they work in the destination's law.

Q11. German hospital and Indian processor

  1. Identify a transfer to a third country, so Chapter V applies (Article 44).
  2. Adequacy: India has no EU adequacy decision.†
  3. Safeguards: use the controller to processor clauses (Decision (EU) 2021/914).
  4. Carry out an impact assessment of Indian government access (Schrems II) and add encryption as a supplementary measure.
  5. The Indian firm is a processor, so sign an Article 28 contract covering the health data, for which the hospital also needs an Article 9(2) exception. Article 49 derogations are read narrowly and do not suit regular transfers (Recital 111: "occasional").
  6. Conclude on the Indian side: the processor is largely exempt under s. 17(1)(d).

Q12. From Safe Harbour to the Data Privacy Framework

  1. Explain why transfers are regulated (Article 44, Recital 101) and the adequacy standard of essential equivalence (Article 45, Recital 104).
  2. Schrems I (6 October 2015): Safe Harbour invalid for generalised access to content and the absence of a remedy.
  3. Schrems II (16 July 2020), also called DPC v Facebook Ireland: Privacy Shield invalid (FISA Section 702, Executive Order 12333, the Ombudsperson); clauses valid but checked case by case.
  4. The aftermath: modular clauses (Decision (EU) 2021/914), transfer impact assessments and the 1.2 billion euro Meta fine (22 May 2023).
  5. The Data Privacy Framework (10 July 2023), with a Data Protection Review Court,† upheld in Latombe v Commission (3 September 2025); appeal C 703/25 P pending.
  6. Conclude: the framework stands but transfers to countries with broad surveillance laws remain fragile; contrast the DPDP negative list.

slides.part: Chapter 9: Constitutional Basis and Legislative History
slides.title: Puttaswamy: privacy becomes a fundamental right
slides.html:
The DPDP Act stands on Puttaswamy (2017): nine judges held privacy, including informational privacy, a fundamental right that only a lawful, proportionate intrusion can limit.

Part II covers the DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025 (Module 6), built from syllabus.md and the Gazette texts of the Act and the Rules. Most operative provisions commence only on 13 May 2027, so each slide states the status of what it discusses. This chapter explains Puttaswamy and the six year legislative path to the Act.

Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 (nine judges, 24 August 2017)

Background
In the Aadhaar challenge the Union denied that privacy was a fundamental right, relying on M.P. Sharma (eight judges, 1954) and Kharak Singh (six judges, 1962). To reconsider those larger Benches, a nine judge Bench was constituted.
Held
Unanimously, privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of life and personal liberty under Article 21 and of the freedoms in Part III. M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh were overruled to that extent.
Reasoning
Privacy includes bodily privacy, privacy of choice and informational privacy, and data aggregation threatens informational privacy acutely. The plurality called for a robust data protection regime, noting the expert committee then at work, and required any intrusion to pass three tests.
  1. Legality: the intrusion must rest on a law.
  2. Legitimate aim: it must pursue a legitimate State aim.
  3. Proportionality: the means must be proportionate to the object.

Remember: L-A-P: a Law, a legitimate Aim, Proportionality. Every DPDP provision that lets privacy yield is tested against these three.

slides.part: Chapter 9: Constitutional Basis and Legislative History
slides.title: Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) and the yardstick for the Act
slides.html:
The 2018 Aadhaar judgment applied the 2017 proportionality test: it upheld Aadhaar in substance but struck down private authentication under Aadhaar Act s. 57.

Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India (Aadhaar) (2019) 1 SCC 1 (five judges, 26 September 2018)

Later treatment of the 2017 ruling: Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) applied proportionality, upheld Aadhaar in substance, and struck down Aadhaar Act s. 57 to the extent that it let private entities demand authentication under contract.

Keep the two judgments apart, because examiners do: the 2017 judgment recognised privacy, while the 2018 judgment upheld Aadhaar with limits.

Use in DPDP answers: Puttaswamy is the yardstick for DPDP ss. 17(2)(a), 7(b) and (c) and 44(3). Each of these lets privacy give way to another interest, so each must be measured against legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.

ProvisionWhat it allowsTaught in
s. 17(2)(a)The whole Act disapplied for notified State instrumentalitiesChapter 13
s. 7(b) and (c)State processing without consent for benefits and State functionsChapter 11
s. 44(3)RTI Act s. 8(1)(j) rewritten to exempt "information which relates to personal information"Chapter 13

slides.part: Chapter 9: Constitutional Basis and Legislative History
slides.title: The Srikrishna Committee and the 2018 draft
slides.html:
The Srikrishna Committee's 2018 draft Bill coined "Data Fiduciary" and "Data Principal" and followed the GDPR closely; the 2023 Act later abandoned much of that model.

Weeks before Puttaswamy was decided, the government set up an expert committee. Its draft is the first step on the path to the Act, so learn its dates and features.

  1. 31 July 2017: the committee under Justice B.N. Srikrishna is constituted.
  2. 27 July 2018: it reports, in A Free and Fair Digital Economy: Protecting Privacy, Empowering Indians, with the draft Personal Data Protection Bill, 2018.

The draft introduced the terms Data Fiduciary and Data Principal and followed the GDPR closely, with:

  1. an independent Data Protection Authority;
  2. sensitive data;
  3. portability;
  4. a right to be forgotten; and
  5. turnover based penalties.†

Caveat. A dagger (†) marks a statement resting on secondary knowledge, not checked against the primary text: here, the features of the 2018 draft and the 2019 Bill. Separately, "primarily modeled on GDPR", as syllabus.md puts it, is a common characterisation rather than an authoritative finding; no authoritative source using those words was located.

slides.part: Chapter 9: Constitutional Basis and Legislative History
slides.title: The 2019 Bill and the Joint Parliamentary Committee
slides.html:
The 2019 Bill went to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, which reported on 16 December 2021 and proposed one Data Protection Bill for personal and non personal data.

  1. 11 December 2019: the Personal Data Protection Bill, 2019 is introduced and referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC).
  2. 16 December 2021: the JPC report is presented after 78 sittings. It recommends a single Data Protection Bill, 2021 governing personal and non personal data.

Correction to syllabus.md. The JPC was chaired by Meenakshi Lekhi only until she joined the Council of Ministers on 7 July 2021; P.P. Chaudhary chaired it thereafter, including when its report was presented on 16 December 2021.

Why the JPC matters in an answer: its idea of one law for all data did not survive. The 2023 Act leaves non personal data unregulated, which is one of the departures an examiner expects you to list. And because syllabus.md names only Lekhi, naming both chairs shows the examiner you know the corrected position.

slides.part: Chapter 9: Constitutional Basis and Legislative History
slides.title: From withdrawal to the 2023 Act and the 2025 Rules
slides.html:
After the 2019 Bill was withdrawn in August 2022, a short new draft became the DPDP Act, 2023 within a year; the Rules followed on 13 November 2025.

  1. 3 August 2022: the 2019 Bill is withdrawn.
  2. 18 November 2022: a short draft DPDP Bill is published.
  3. 3 August 2023: the DPDP Bill, 2023 is introduced.
  4. 7 August 2023: passed by the Lok Sabha; 9 August 2023: passed by the Rajya Sabha.
  5. 11 August 2023: assent, as Act No. 22 of 2023.
  6. 13 November 2025: the Act partly commences and the Rules are notified.

Notice the speed: two failed bills took five years, while the final Act passed both Houses within a week of introduction. Its brevity is part of the story told on the next slide.

Law update. The Act was checked against the Gazette text of 11 August 2023, which is current except for the 2026 Removal of Difficulties Order and phased commencement (Chapter 13). The Rules were checked against G.S.R. 846(E) of 13 November 2025; the corrigenda (G.S.R. 892(E), 11 December 2025) were not seen.

slides.part: Chapter 9: Constitutional Basis and Legislative History
slides.title: What the 2023 Act dropped
slides.html:
The enacted Act is shorter and more permissive than the drafts: it relies on consent and executive rule making and drops most GDPR-style features.

Feature2018 draft, 2019 Bill, JPCDPDP Act, 2023
EnforcerIndependent Data Protection Authority (a regulator)Adjudicatory Board
Sensitive data, portability, right to be forgottenIncluded†Dropped, along with objection
PenaltiesTurnover based†Turnover penalties dropped: fixed caps
Non personal dataJPC: one Bill for personal and non personal dataLeft unregulated
Cross border dataLocalisation proposalsNegative list for transfers

The pattern to remember: a shorter, more permissive law that relies on consent and executive rule making. That is why critics ask whether it retreats from the GDPR model, and why Puttaswamy is the standard for testing the answer.

Exam focus. Puttaswamy makes informational privacy a fundamental right with a test of legality, legitimate aim and proportionality, and the DPDP Act is Parliament's response after two failed bills. Name both JPC chairs, do not treat the 2018 or 2019 texts as law, and remember that the 2017 judgment recognised privacy while the 2018 judgment upheld Aadhaar with limits. An answer on whether the 2023 Act retreats from the GDPR model should list the specific departures and test them against Puttaswamy.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Preamble, Scope and Key Definitions
slides.title: The long title: a balancing law
slides.html:
The long title frames the Act as a law about the manner of processing that balances the right to protect personal data against the need to process it lawfully.

This chapter covers the long title, the application rules in s. 3 and the definitions in s. 2. Start with the long title, because it explains the shape of everything that follows.

Long title. The Act provides for processing digital personal data "in a manner that recognises both the right of individuals to protect their personal data and the need to process such personal data for lawful purposes".

It is framed as a law about the manner of processing, not a ban on processing: it balances an individual right against a legitimate need to process.

It explains the design

The balance explains the Act's broad legitimate uses, its State exemptions and its duties for Data Principals.

It supports two readings

A protective purposive reading (the right) and weight for genuine processing needs (the need). Use whichever side the problem calls for.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Preamble, Scope and Key Definitions
slides.title: Where the Act applies: section 3
slides.html:
Section 3 covers digital personal data processed in India, and processing abroad connected with offering goods or services in India, minus two exclusions.

ClauseRuleConsequence
s. 3(a)Digital personal data processed in India, whether collected digitally or collected physically and digitised laterUndigitised paper records fall outside
s. 3(b)Processing outside India connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in IndiaForeign entities are caught only this way, with no monitoring limb
s. 3(c)Excludes personal or domestic processing, and data made public by the Data Principal or by a person legally obliged to publish itScraped public profiles leave the Act, which matters for training AI models

Read the three clauses together: (a) is territorial, (b) is the only extraterritorial hook, and (c) narrows both. A foreign business that merely watches Indians online, without offering them anything, is therefore outside.

Status: s. 3 commences on 13 May 2027.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Preamble, Scope and Key Definitions
slides.title: The actors: who is who in section 2
slides.html:
Know six actors: the Data Principal whose data it is, the Data Fiduciary who decides, the Processor who acts for it, and three special roles.

The definitions have been in force since 13 November 2025 and were confirmed against the Gazette text. Learn the clause letters as well: examiners penalise misstated ones.

Data Principal (s. 2(j))
The individual to whom data relate, including a child's parents or lawful guardian and the lawful guardian of a person with disability.
Data Fiduciary (s. 2(i))
Determines the purpose and means of processing, alone or with others.
Data Processor (s. 2(k))
Processes on a fiduciary's behalf.
Significant Data Fiduciary (s. 2(z))
A fiduciary notified under s. 10.
Data Protection Officer (s. 2(l))
Appointed by a Significant Data Fiduciary under s. 10(2)(a).
Consent Manager (s. 2(g))
A person registered with the Board, acting as a single point of contact through which a Data Principal can give, manage, review and withdraw consent on an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.

Why parents count as Data Principals: a child cannot consent for herself, so the Act gives the parent or guardian the Data Principal's position, which is what makes verifiable parental consent (s. 9) work.

Remember: the actors run g, i, j, k, l: Consent Manager (g), Fiduciary (i), Principal (j), Processor (k), DPO (l); the Significant Data Fiduciary sits at (z).

slides.part: Chapter 10: Preamble, Scope and Key Definitions
slides.title: The data terms in section 2
slides.html:
The Act regulates only digital personal data about an identifiable individual, and defines breach and processing widely enough to catch a misdirected email.

Data (s. 2(h))
A representation of information, facts, concepts, opinions or instructions suitable for processing.
Personal data (s. 2(t))
Any data about an individual identifiable by or in relation to it.
Digital personal data (s. 2(n))
Personal data in digital form.
Personal data breach (s. 2(u))
Any unauthorised processing or accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access that compromises confidentiality, integrity or availability.
Processing (s. 2(x))
A wholly or partly automated operation on digital personal data, from collection to erasure.
Specified purpose (s. 2(za))
The purpose stated in the notice.
Child (s. 2(f))
An individual under eighteen.
Person (s. 2(s))
Includes the State, defined in s. 2(zb) by reference to Article 12.

Two consequences of the "person" definition: the State is a fiduciary, subject to the exemptions in s. 17; and the Act uses "she" and "her" for every individual (s. 2(y)).

slides.part: Chapter 10: Preamble, Scope and Key Definitions
slides.title: DPDP terms in GDPR language, and exam traps
slides.html:
Most DPDP terms have GDPR counterparts, but India departs: joint fiduciaries without allocation rules, a Board, two lawful grounds and distinctive new actors.

DPDP ActGDPR
Data PrincipalData subject
Data FiduciaryController
Data ProcessorProcessor
Joint fiduciaries exist, without allocation rulesJoint controllers
The BoardSupervisory authority
Consent and legitimate usesThe six bases
Consent Managers and Significant Data FiduciariesNone: these are distinctive

Exam focus. The Act covers digital personal data processed in India, and processing abroad connected with offering goods or services in India, excluding personal or domestic use and data made public by the Data Principal or under a legal obligation. Do not apply it to undigitised paper, claim a monitoring limb, or misstate the clause letters (2(g), 2(i), 2(j), 2(k), 2(l), 2(t), 2(z)).

slides.title: Two gateways: section 4
slides.html:
A fiduciary may process personal data only for a lawful purpose and through one of two gateways: consent or a legitimate use. There is no legitimate interests ground.

Chapter II of the Act sets the duties of Data Fiduciaries (ss. 4 to 10 with the Rules), almost all commencing on 13 May 2027. Section 4 is the door to all of them.

s. 4. Processing is permitted only in accordance with the Act and for a lawful purpose, either with consent or for certain legitimate uses. A lawful purpose is any purpose not expressly forbidden by law.

  1. Is the purpose lawful, that is, not expressly forbidden? Almost always yes.
  2. Is there valid consent (s. 6), after notice (s. 5)? If not, go on.
  3. Does a legitimate use in s. 7 apply? If not, the processing is unlawful.

Why the contest is at steps 2 and 3: because "lawful purpose" is defined so permissively, the real protection lies in the consent and legitimate use rules. And because there are only two gateways, there is no general legitimate interests ground to fall back on, unlike the GDPR's six bases.

Remember: Chapter II in order, ss. 4 to 10: "Good Notice Comes Lawfully; Guard Children Specially" = Grounds, Notice, Consent, Legitimate uses, General obligations, Children, Significant fiduciaries.

slides.title: Notice before consent: section 5 and Rule 3
slides.html:
Every consent request must come with, or after, a stand alone notice telling the Data Principal what is collected, why, and how to withdraw, complain and reach the Board.

s. 5(1). Every request for consent must be accompanied or preceded by a notice stating:

  1. the personal data and purpose;
  2. how to withdraw consent and seek grievance redressal; and
  3. how to complain to the Board.

The Act's illustration is a bank's video based customer identification: the bank's request for her data must be accompanied or preceded by a notice describing the data and the purpose.

  1. Old consents (s. 5(2)). For consents given before commencement, notice must be given as soon as reasonably practicable, and processing may continue until withdrawal.
  2. Language (s. 5(3)). The notice must be available in English or any Eighth Schedule language.

Rule 3 sets the standard. The notice must:

  1. be understandable independently of other information;
  2. give a fair, plain account enabling specific and informed consent, including an itemised description of the data and the specified purpose with the goods, services or uses enabled; and
  3. give the link and means to withdraw consent as easily as it was given, exercise rights and complain to the Board.

Status: s. 5 and Rule 3 commence on 13 May 2027.

slides.title: Valid consent: section 6
slides.html:
Consent counts only if it is free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, affirmative and limited to necessary data, and the fiduciary must prove it.

As Chapter 5 explains in detail alongside the GDPR, s. 6 sets the following rules:

  1. Quality. Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, affirmative and limited to necessary data.
  2. Severance. Infringing parts are invalid; the rest stands.
  3. Form. Requests must be clear and plain.
  4. Withdrawal. It must be as easy as consent; the consequences are borne by the Data Principal; and processing must cease within a reasonable time.
  5. Consent Managers may be used.
  6. Proof. The fiduciary bears the burden of proof.

Why "unconditional" and "necessary" do the heavy lifting: together they stop a fiduciary from making a service conditional on consent to processing the service does not need. Because the burden of proof is on the fiduciary, it must keep records of every notice and consent.

Status: s. 6(1) to (8) and (10) commence on 13 May 2027; s. 6(9), on registering Consent Managers, commences earlier, on 13 November 2026.

Remember: F-S-I-U-U-A-N: Free, Specific, Informed, Unconditional, Unambiguous, Affirmative, Necessary data only.

slides.title: Legitimate uses I: voluntary provision and the State
slides.html:
Section 7 lists nine situations where processing needs no consent; the first five cover voluntary provision, State benefits and functions, and legal duties.

ClauseProcessing without consent is allowed…Illustration
s. 7(a)for the specified purpose for which the Data Principal voluntarily provided data, without objectingA pharmacy receipt sent to a number given for that purpose; a property broker who must stop once told help is no longer needed
s. 7(b)for the State to provide prescribed subsidies, benefits, services, certificates, licences or permits, where she previously consented or the data is in a notified database, under Rule 5 standardsMaternity benefit data used for other benefits
s. 7(c)for State functions under law, or in the interest of sovereignty, integrity or security–
s. 7(d)to fulfil a legal obligation to disclose to the State–
s. 7(e)to comply with Indian judgments or orders, or foreign judgments on contractual or civil claims–

Why s. 7(a) is special: it works like deemed consent. That is why the access and correction rights in ss. 11 and 12 apply to it just as they apply to consent (Chapter 12). It also ends with the purpose, which is why the broker must stop.

slides.title: Legitimate uses II: emergencies, employment and the critique
slides.html:
The last four legitimate uses cover emergencies and employment; the State clauses (b) and (c) are the ones most open to constitutional challenge.

ClauseProcessing without consent is allowed…
s. 7(f)for medical emergencies threatening life or health
s. 7(g)for treatment or health services during an epidemic or other public health threat
s. 7(h)for safety or assistance during a disaster or breakdown of public order
s. 7(i)for employment, or to protect the employer from loss or liability (espionage, trade secrets, confidentiality), or to provide benefits sought by employees

Exam focus. Clauses (b) and (c) are the most open to challenge, because they allow broad State processing without express necessity or proportionality. They must be read subject to Puttaswamy: legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.

Remember: s. 7 runs 1-4-3-1: one voluntary use (a), four State and legal uses (b) to (e), three emergencies (f) to (h), one employment use (i).

slides.title: General obligations and security: s. 8(1) to (5)
slides.html:
The fiduciary answers for all processing done by it or for it, and must keep data accurate and protected by at least the Rule 6 safeguards.

  1. Responsibility (s. 8(1)). It is responsible for all processing by it or its processors, regardless of contract.
  2. Processors (s. 8(2)). It may use processors only under a valid contract.
  3. Accuracy (s. 8(3)). It must ensure completeness, accuracy and consistency where data are used for decisions about the Data Principal or disclosed to another fiduciary.
  4. Measures (s. 8(4)). It must adopt technical and organisational measures.

Security (s. 8(5), Rule 6): reasonable safeguards, at minimum:

  1. encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokens;
  2. access controls;
  3. logging, monitoring and review to detect and investigate unauthorised access;
  4. continuity measures such as backups;
  5. retention of logs and data for one year unless law requires otherwise;
  6. security clauses in processor contracts; and
  7. organisational measures.

Why s. 8(5) is the duty to watch: failing to take reasonable security safeguards carries the highest penalty in the Schedule, up to 250 crore rupees. Responsibility "regardless of contract" means a fiduciary cannot shift that risk to its processor.

Remember: s. 8 in order: "Responsible People Always Measure Security, Breaches, Erasure, Contacts, Grievances".

slides.title: Breach intimation: s. 8(6) and Rule 7
slides.html:
On becoming aware of any breach, the fiduciary must tell every affected Data Principal and the Board without delay, then file a detailed report within 72 hours.

Breach (s. 8(6), Rule 7): there is no seriousness threshold. Every personal data breach, as defined in s. 2(u), triggers these steps.

  1. Tell each affected Data Principal, without delay, concisely and plainly, through her account or registered contact: the nature, extent and timing; the likely consequences; the mitigation; the protective steps she can take; and a contact.
  2. Tell the Board, without delay: a description, with the nature, extent, timing, location and likely impact.
  3. Within 72 hours, or a longer period allowed on written request, send the Board a detailed report: facts and causes, mitigation, findings about the person responsible, remedial measures, and the intimations given.
  4. The Board may then direct urgent measures, inquire and penalise (s. 27(1)(a)).

slides.title: Erasure, retention, contact and grievances: s. 8(7) to (10)
slides.html:
Data must be erased once consent is withdrawn or the purpose is spent, unless law requires retention; large platforms also face a three year erasure rule.

Erasure (s. 8(7) and (8), Rule 8): data must be erased, and processors made to erase, when consent is withdrawn or the purpose is no longer served, unless law requires retention.

Third Schedule classRegistered users in India
Electronic commerce entitiesAt least two crore
Social media intermediariesAt least two crore
Online gaming intermediariesAt least fifty lakh

These platforms must erase data three years after the user's last approach or exercise of rights, or after the Rules commenced, whichever is latest, except for account access and virtual tokens, with at least 48 hours' warning. In the other direction, every fiduciary must keep personal data, traffic data and logs for at least one year for the Seventh Schedule purposes (Rule 8(3)).

Contact and grievances: the DPO's or a responsible person's contact details must be published prominently and included in responses (s. 8(9), Rule 9); and an effective grievance mechanism must answer within a published period of at most ninety days (s. 8(10), Rule 14(3)).

slides.title: Children and persons with disability: s. 9, Rules 10 to 12
slides.html:
For anyone under eighteen, processing needs verifiable parental consent, must not harm her wellbeing, and may never involve tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising.

  1. s. 9(1): verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian is required before processing any personal data of a child, or of a person with disability who has a lawful guardian.
  2. s. 9(2): processing likely to harm a child's wellbeing is barred.
  3. s. 9(3): tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children are prohibited.
RuleWhat it requires
Rule 10Due diligence that the person claiming to be the parent is an identifiable adult, using reliable identity and age details already held, details voluntarily provided, or a virtual token issued by an entity entrusted by law or government
Rule 11Verification that a guardian was appointed by a court, designated authority or local level committee
Rule 12, Fourth ScheduleExempts classes such as clinical and mental health establishments and healthcare professionals (for health services), allied healthcare professionals, and educational institutions (for limited educational and safety monitoring), subject to conditions

And s. 9(5) allows an age threshold to be notified for verifiably safe processing.

Current law update: Removal of Difficulties Order, 2026. S.O. 5458(E), made under s. 43(1) on 5 October 2026 and in force from 6 October 2026, amends s. 9(1) to read "any personal data of a child or of a person with disability", making clear that verifiable consent is needed for both, and clarifies that the periodic audit in s. 10(2)(c)(ii) is a data audit. The supplied 2023 text does not show these changes, the Gazette text was not seen, and s. 43 permits such orders only within three years of commencement.

slides.title: Significant Data Fiduciaries: s. 10 and Rule 13
slides.html:
The government can notify high risk fiduciaries as significant; they must add an India based DPO, an independent auditor, and annual assessments, audits and algorithm checks.

Who (s. 10(1)). The government may notify fiduciaries as significant considering the volume and sensitivity of data, risk to Data Principals' rights, sovereignty and integrity, electoral democracy, State security and public order.

What (s. 10(2)). They must:

  1. appoint an India based DPO who is responsible to the board (the fiduciary's own governing board) and serves as grievance contact;
  2. appoint an independent data auditor; and
  3. carry out periodic impact assessments, audits and other prescribed measures.

Rule 13 adds:

  1. an impact assessment and audit every twelve months, with a report of significant observations to the Board;
  2. due diligence that algorithmic software does not endanger Data Principals' rights; and
  3. compliance with any committee specified restriction keeping data and traffic data in India.

Why the algorithmic duty matters: it is the closest Indian law comes to regulating automated decisions, because the Act gives individuals no Article 22 style right (Chapter 12). Breach of s. 10 obligations can cost up to 150 crore rupees.

slides.title: Compliance checklist for 13 May 2027
slides.html:
To be ready for 13 May 2027, a fiduciary must turn every Chapter II duty into a working process, from consent flows to breach plans and grievance handling.

  1. Map every purpose to consent or a s. 7 use.
  2. Redesign stand alone, itemised, multilingual notices.
  3. Build unbundled consent flows with easy withdrawal.
  4. Insert security clauses in processor contracts.
  5. Implement encryption or masking, access control, logging, backups and one year retention.
  6. Prepare a breach plan meeting the "without delay" and 72 hour duties.
  7. Adopt retention schedules, including the three year rule and 48 hour warning for large platforms.
  8. Publish contact details and a grievance process that answers within ninety days.
  9. Implement verifiable parental consent and stop tracking and targeted advertising of under eighteens.
  10. If notified as significant: appoint an India based DPO and auditor, carry out annual assessments and audits, and verify its algorithms.

Each step is a provision you have already met: ss. 4 to 7 (steps 1 to 3), s. 8 with Rules 6 to 9 and 14 (steps 4 to 8), s. 9 (step 9) and s. 10 (step 10). Learning the checklist is therefore a quick way to revise the whole chapter.

slides.title: Applying Chapter II: a breach at an education platform
slides.html:
A fiduciary needs a lawful purpose and consent or a legitimate use, must give notice, and stays responsible for security, breach intimation, accuracy, erasure and grievances.

On top of that core, children and Significant Data Fiduciaries carry added duties. A single problem can engage several of them at once.

Exam focus. Do not invent legitimate interests, limit breach intimation to serious breaches, set the child's age at sixteen, or forget the 13 May 2027 start.

slides.part: Chapter 12: Rights and Duties of Data Principals
slides.title: Right to access information: section 11
slides.html:
Chapter III gives four rights and five duties; the first right, access, yields only a summary, and only where she consented or voluntarily provided data.

Chapter III of the Act gives four rights (access, correction and erasure, grievance redressal, nomination) and imposes five duties. This chapter also covers Consent Managers and the rights the Act omits. Sections 11 to 15 commence on 13 May 2027.

s. 11(1). From a fiduciary to which she gave consent (including deemed consent under s. 7(a)), a Data Principal may obtain:

  1. a summary of the personal data and processing activities;
  2. the identities of all fiduciaries and processors with whom data were shared, with a description of what was shared; and
  3. other prescribed information.

Exception (s. 11(2)). The recipients and further information need not be disclosed for sharing with fiduciaries authorised by law, on written request, for preventing, detecting or investigating offences or cyber incidents or for prosecution.

The right is narrower than GDPR access: a summary rather than a copy, and only for consent and voluntary provision. If the fiduciary relies on any other legitimate use, there is no access right at all.

Remember: the four rights, ss. 11 to 14: A-C-G-N, "A Citizen Gets Nominated" = Access, Correction and erasure, Grievance, Nomination.

slides.part: Chapter 12: Rights and Duties of Data Principals
slides.title: Right to correction and erasure: section 12
slides.html:
For consent based and s. 7(a) processing, she can have data corrected, completed, updated and erased, but erasure yields to the specified purpose and legal compliance.

  1. s. 12(1): she may obtain correction, completion, updating and erasure in accordance with law.
  2. s. 12(2): the fiduciary must correct inaccurate or misleading data and complete and update data.
  3. s. 12(3): it must erase on request, unless retention is necessary for the specified purpose or for legal compliance.

The State is treated differently. Under s. 17(4), s. 12(3) does not apply to the State, and s. 12(2) applies only where a decision affecting her is made. So she cannot make a State body erase her data on request, and can make it correct data only where the data feed a decision about her.

This right is the individual's side of the fiduciary's own erasure duty in s. 8(7): one is triggered by her request, the other by withdrawal of consent or the end of the purpose.

slides.part: Chapter 12: Rights and Duties of Data Principals
slides.title: Grievance redressal and nomination: ss. 13 and 14
slides.html:
She must first complain to the fiduciary or Consent Manager, which must answer within at most ninety days, and she may nominate someone to act on her death or incapacity.

Grievance redressal (s. 13). She is entitled to readily available grievance redressal from a fiduciary or Consent Manager, and a response within the prescribed period, at most ninety days under Rule 14(3). She must exhaust this remedy before approaching the Board.

Why this matters: it reverses the GDPR, where a data subject may complain directly to a supervisory authority. Skipping the internal step is a common exam error.

Nomination (s. 14). She may nominate an individual to exercise her rights on her death or incapacity. Incapacity means inability to exercise them because of unsoundness of mind or infirmity of body.

The GDPR, by contrast, leaves the deceased to national law (Recital 27), so nomination is one of the DPDP Act's distinctive features.

slides.part: Chapter 12: Rights and Duties of Data Principals
slides.title: The five duties of Data Principals: section 15
slides.html:
Unusually, the Act places five duties on Data Principals themselves, backed by a penalty of up to 10,000 rupees.

  1. Comply with applicable laws.
  2. Do not impersonate another person when providing data.
  3. Do not suppress material information when providing data for State documents, unique identifiers, proof of identity or address.
  4. Do not file false or frivolous grievances or complaints.
  5. Furnish only verifiably authentic information when seeking correction or erasure.

Sanction. Breach can attract a penalty of up to 10,000 rupees (Schedule, item 5).

ViewArgument about the duty not to complain frivolously
CriticsIt deters genuine complaints
SupportersIt protects the Board and the integrity of State identity records

The duties fit the long title's balance: the Act protects the individual's right, but it also asks her not to abuse the system that protects it. The GDPR imposes no such duties.

Remember: LISFA, in statutory order: Laws, Impersonation, Suppression, Frivolous complaints, Authentic information.

slides.part: Chapter 12: Rights and Duties of Data Principals
slides.title: Consent Managers: s. 2(g), s. 6(8) and (9), Rule 4
slides.html:
A Consent Manager is a Board registered Indian company that acts for the Data Principal as one interoperable consent platform; its registration provisions operate from 13 November 2026.

A Consent Manager (s. 2(g)) is a Board registered single point of contact on an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform. It is accountable to and acts for the Data Principal (s. 6(8)), not the fiduciary, and must be registered on prescribed conditions (s. 6(9)).

Rule 4 and Part A of the First Schedule require it to be an Indian company with:

  1. adequate technical, operational and financial capacity;
  2. sound finances and management;
  3. a net worth of at least two crore rupees;
  4. adequate business prospects and capital;
  5. directors and managers of integrity;
  6. constitutional documents securing its obligations, amendable only with the Board's approval; and
  7. operations in Data Principals' interests.

Part B sets its continuing obligations. Rule 4, s. 6(9) and s. 27(1)(d) commence on 13 November 2026.

The GDPR has no equivalent.

Unverified comparison. The model resembles the RBI's account aggregator framework.†

slides.part: Chapter 12: Rights and Duties of Data Principals
slides.title: Rights the DPDP Act omits
slides.html:
The Act omits portability, objection, restriction and automated decision rights, so a person refused credit or a job by an algorithm has no right to human review.

The Act omits portability and automated decision rights, as syllabus.md notes, and also objection and restriction, although the 2018 draft and the 2019 Bill contained portability and a right to be forgotten.†

Consequences. A person refused credit or a job by an algorithm has no right to human review, to contest or to an explanation. She has only:

  1. the accuracy duty in s. 8(3);
  2. the summary access right (s. 11); and
  3. the grievance route (s. 13).

The absence of portability weakens competition, because users cannot easily take their data to a rival service.

DPDP Act has, GDPR lacksGDPR has, DPDP Act lacks
Nomination (s. 14)Portability
Compulsory internal grievances (s. 13)Objection
Duties of Data Principals (s. 15)Restriction
Consent ManagersArticle 22 protection

slides.part: Chapter 12: Rights and Duties of Data Principals
slides.title: Applying Chapter III: rejected by an algorithm
slides.html:
Data Principals get a summary, correction and erasure, grievance redressal (exhausted first) and nomination; they owe s. 15 duties and lack four GDPR rights.

Her route under the DPDP Act runs in a fixed order, so set it out step by step:

  1. Raise a grievance with the card issuer, which must answer within at most ninety days (s. 13, Rule 14(3)).
  2. Only then complain to the Board, which can inquire and penalise but not compensate (Chapter 13).
  3. Appeal against the Board's order lies to the TDSAT within sixty days (s. 29).

Exam focus. Do not describe access as a copy, skip the internal grievance step, or treat Consent Managers as operating before 13 November 2026.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Transfers outside India: a negative list (s. 16)
slides.html:
Transfers abroad are free unless the government restricts them to notified countries: a negative list, preserved stricter laws, and two Rules adding conditions.

This chapter covers transfers, exemptions, the Board, penalties, commencement, s. 44 and the litigation, and the interim role of s. 43A.

  1. s. 16(1): the government may restrict transfers to notified countries or territories; anywhere else, transfer is free.
  2. s. 16(2): stricter transfer laws remain applicable.
  3. Rule 15 adds conditions on making data available to foreign States or entities under their control.
  4. Rule 13(4) allows committee specified data of Significant Data Fiduciaries to be kept in India.

Status: all of these commence on 13 May 2027.

Chapter 8 compares the GDPR, which takes the opposite approach. GDPR transfers are barred unless a route applies, with an impact assessment; DPDP transfers are allowed unless restricted, with no impact assessment, and localisation comes only through sectoral rules or Rule 13(4).

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Partial exemption: s. 17(1)
slides.html:
For six listed purposes, most fiduciary duties, all Data Principal rights and the transfer rule fall away, but responsibility and security safeguards still apply.

Partial exemption (s. 17(1)): Chapter II (except s. 8(1) and (5)), Chapter III and s. 16 do not apply to processing:

  1. necessary to enforce legal rights or claims;
  2. by courts, tribunals and regulators performing judicial, quasi judicial, regulatory or supervisory functions;
  3. for preventing, detecting, investigating or prosecuting offences (s. 17(1)(c));
  4. in India, of non residents' data under contracts with foreign persons (s. 17(1)(d));
  5. for approved mergers, demergers and arrangements; and
  6. for ascertaining a loan defaulter's financial position.

What survives: the overarching responsibility and security safeguards still apply. So an investigating agency or a lender must still keep the data secure, even though the Data Principal cannot demand access or erasure.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Total exemption and the other powers: s. 17(2) to (5)
slides.html:
Section 17(2) removes the whole Act for notified State agencies and qualifying research, and further powers let the government exempt startups and the State.

Total exemption (s. 17(2)): the whole Act does not apply to:

  1. s. 17(2)(a): processing by State instrumentalities notified in the interests of sovereignty and integrity, security, foreign relations, public order or preventing incitement; or
  2. s. 17(2)(b): research, archiving and statistics that take no decision about a specific Data Principal and meet Rule 16 and Second Schedule standards.

Other powers:

ProvisionPower
s. 17(3)Notified fiduciaries, including startups, may be exempted from ss. 5, 8(3), 8(7), 10 and 11
s. 17(4)For the State, ss. 8(7) and 12(3) do not apply, and s. 12(2) applies only where decisions affect the Data Principal
s. 17(5)Within five years of commencement, the government may disapply any provision for notified fiduciaries for a period

Compare the two tiers: a partial exemption still leaves security in place, but a total exemption leaves nothing, which is why s. 17(2)(a) draws the strongest criticism.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Why s. 17(2)(a) is under challenge
slides.html:
Section 17(2)(a) exempts agencies by executive notification, without the safeguards that Big Brother Watch requires and Puttaswamy arguably requires, and it is under challenge.

Section 17(2)(a) exempts agencies by executive notification, without any:

  1. statutory necessity;
  2. proportionality;
  3. independent authorisation; or
  4. oversight.

These are exactly the safeguards required by Big Brother Watch and arguably by Puttaswamy, and the provision is under challenge in Venkatesh Nayak (later in this chapter).

Big Brother Watch and Others v United Kingdom, ECtHR, Apps. 58170/13, 62322/14, 24960/15; Chamber 13 Sept 2018; Grand Chamber 25 May 2021

The Grand Chamber demands end to end safeguards for surveillance (Chapter 1). In a s. 17(2)(a) answer it supplies the comparative standard: necessity, proportionality, independent authorisation and oversight.

How to structure the argument, using the Puttaswamy test:

  1. Legality: the exemption is in a statute, but which agency is exempt is left to executive notification.
  2. Legitimate aim: sovereignty, security, foreign relations and public order are legitimate aims.
  3. Proportionality: nothing in the clause requires necessity, independent authorisation or oversight; this is its weak point.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: The Data Protection Board: establishment and functions
slides.html:
The Board is an independent, digital, adjudicatory body: it acts on breach intimations, complaints and references, rather than regulating like a GDPR authority.

Establishment: the Board is a body corporate established by notification (s. 18) with a Chairperson and notified Members (s. 19). It was established by G.S.R. 844(E) from 13 November 2025, G.S.R. 845(E) reportedly providing four Members,† and it must act independently and, as far as practicable, as a digital office (s. 28(1)).

Functions (s. 27):

  1. On breach intimation, it may direct urgent remedial measures and inquire and penalise.
  2. It acts on Data Principals' complaints, government references and court directions against fiduciaries and Consent Managers.
  3. It acts on breaches of Consent Manager registration.
  4. It acts on references about intermediaries defying blocking directions.
  5. It may issue, modify or withdraw directions after a hearing.

Function 1 is s. 27(1)(a), met on the breach slide. Function 3 is s. 27(1)(d), which commences early, on 13 November 2026, alongside the Consent Manager rules; the rest of s. 27 starts on 13 May 2027.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Board procedure, appeals and alternatives: ss. 28 to 32
slides.html:
The Board filters complaints, follows natural justice with civil court powers, and its orders go on appeal to the TDSAT within sixty days.

Procedure (s. 28):

  1. It decides whether there are sufficient grounds to proceed, recording reasons for closing a matter.
  2. It follows natural justice.
  3. It has civil court powers to summon, take evidence and inspect.
  4. It may issue interim orders.
  5. It must not seize equipment in a way that disrupts daily functioning.

Appeals and alternatives:

  1. Appeal to the TDSAT within sixty days, to be decided within six months if possible (s. 29).
  2. Orders are executable as civil decrees (s. 30).

Mediation (s. 31)

The Board may direct mediation.

Voluntary undertaking (s. 32)

The Board may accept a voluntary undertaking, which bars proceedings unless breached.

The TDSAT's role comes from s. 44(1), already in force. Mediation and undertakings let a matter end without a penalty, which suits a body that adjudicates rather than regulates.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Penalties: s. 33, s. 34 and the Schedule
slides.html:
The Board fines only significant breaches, after a hearing, within fixed caps; the highest is 250 crore rupees for unreasonable security, and the money goes to the State.

Penalties (s. 33): imposed for significant breaches after a hearing, considering:

  1. nature, gravity and duration;
  2. the type of data;
  3. repetition;
  4. gain made or loss avoided;
  5. mitigation and its timeliness;
  6. proportionality and deterrence; and
  7. likely impact.

Penalties are credited to the Consolidated Fund (s. 34).

Schedule maxima:

BreachMaximum
Failing to take reasonable security safeguards (s. 8(5))250 crore rupees
Failing to intimate a breach (s. 8(6))200 crore rupees
Children's obligations (s. 9)200 crore rupees
Significant Data Fiduciary obligations (s. 10)150 crore rupees
Data Principals' duties (s. 15)10,000 rupees
Breach of a voluntary undertakingUp to the original amount
Any other breach50 crore rupees

Remember: 250, 200, 200, 150, 50 = Security, Intimation, Children, Significant, the rest. The caps are fixed, never linked to turnover.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Blocking, overriding effect, and no compensation
slides.html:
Repeat offenders can be blocked, the Act prevails over conflicting laws and civil courts are barred, yet the Act gives the victim of a breach no compensation.

Other provisions:

ProvisionRule
s. 37After penalties in two or more instances and a Board reference advising it, the government may, after a hearing, direct blocking of public access to the fiduciary's services in India
s. 38The Act is additional to other laws but prevails in a conflict
s. 39Civil courts are barred
s. 43Difficulty removal orders may be made within three years

The compensation gap follows from three provisions read together:

  1. The Board penalises (s. 33).
  2. Penalties go to the State, not the victim (s. 34), and the Act provides no compensation.
  3. From 13 May 2027 IT Act s. 43A is omitted (s. 44(2)), so a victim of negligent leakage must rely on tort or contract.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Commencement in three phases
slides.html:
The Act and Rules commence in three phases: 13 November 2025 (definitions and Board), 13 November 2026 (Consent Managers) and 13 May 2027 (everything operative).

  1. Phase one (13 November 2025): G.S.R. 843(E) brought into force ss. 1(2), 2, 18 to 26, 35, 38 to 43, 44(1) and 44(3): definitions, the Board, good faith protection, consistency, jurisdiction, rule making, removal of difficulties, and the TRAI and RTI amendments. Rule 1 of the supplied Rules brought Rules 1, 2 and 17 to 21 into force (definitions and the Board).
  2. Phase two (13 November 2026): ss. 6(9) and 27(1)(d) and Rule 4 (Consent Managers).
  3. Phase three (13 May 2027): ss. 3 to 5, 6(1) to (8) and (10), 7 to 17, the rest of s. 27, ss. 28 to 34, 36, 37 and 44(2), and Rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23.

So fiduciaries' duties, rights, transfers, exemptions, inquiries, penalties, appeals, blocking and the omission of s. 43A all start on 13 May 2027. Until then only the phase one and two provisions operate: definitions, the Board's machinery, the general provisions, the RTI and TRAI amendments and, from 13 November 2026, Consent Managers.

Law update. A reported 2026 proposal to shorten the transition was not notified.†

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Section 44 and the pending litigation
slides.html:
Section 44 amends three statutes: the TDSAT becomes the appellate tribunal, IT Act s. 43A goes from 13 May 2027, and the RTI privacy exemption is rewritten.

ProvisionChangeStatus
s. 44(1)Makes the TDSAT the appellate tribunal, by amending s. 14 of the TRAI Act, 1997In force
s. 44(2)Omits IT Act s. 43A, adds the DPDP Act to the proviso to IT Act s. 81, and omits s. 87(2)(ob)From 13 May 2027
s. 44(3)Substitutes RTI Act s. 8(1)(j) so that it exempts "information which relates to personal information"In force since 13 November 2025

Why s. 44(3) is contested: it removes the old qualifications about public activity, unwarranted invasion of privacy and the larger public interest, although the general override in RTI s. 8(2) survives.

Under judicial consideration. Venkatesh Nayak v Union of India, W.P.(C) No. 177 of 2026, with connected petitions by journalists and publishers, challenges ss. 17(1)(c), 17(2), 33(1), 36 and 44(3) and Rules 17 and 23(2). On 16 February 2026 Surya Kant CJI and Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul M. Pancholi JJ issued notice, declined an interim stay and referred the matter to a larger Bench. No Board appointments appear on the official record reviewed; in October 2026 the Kerala High Court, in C R Neelakandan v Union of India (WP(PIL) No. 15 of 2026), recorded the Union's statement that the Board was constituted but not yet functional and would be made functional within eight weeks.† Reports of earlier appointments are unsupported.

slides.part: Chapter 13: Transfers, Exemptions, the Board, Penalties and Implementation
slides.title: Section 43A until 13 May 2027, and exam guidance
slides.html:
Until 13 May 2027, IT Act s. 43A lets a person harmed by negligent security of sensitive data claim compensation; afterwards the Board penalises without compensating.

IT Act ss. 43A and 46; SPDI Rules 2011. Until 13 May 2027, a body corporate negligent in maintaining reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data, which causes wrongful loss or gain, must compensate the person affected through the adjudicating officer.

PointUntil 13 May 2027From 13 May 2027
LawIT Act s. 43A with the SPDI RulesDPDP Act; s. 43A omitted by s. 44(2)
ForumAdjudicating officer (s. 46)Data Protection Board
OutcomeCompensation to the person affectedPenalty to the State; the victim relies on tort or contract

Exam focus. Transfers are free unless restricted; s. 17 grants wide partial and total exemptions; the Board adjudicates and fines up to fixed caps, with appeals to the TDSAT; and most of the Act starts on 13 May 2027. Do not call the Act fully in force, credit the Board with power to award compensation, link penalties to turnover, or claim that s. 44(3) is stayed. Analytical questions test s. 17(2)(a) against Puttaswamy and the criticism that the Act punishes but does not compensate.

slides.title: Module 6 in ten points
slides.html:
The notes' own final revision list for Module 6: ten facts that carry most DPDP answers.

  1. Puttaswamy (2017) sets legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
  2. The JPC was chaired by Meenakshi Lekhi and then P.P. Chaudhary (report of 16 December 2021).
  3. The key definitions are in s. 2(g), (i), (j), (k), (l), (t) and (z).
  4. Processing needs consent or a legitimate use.
  5. Every breach is intimated, with a 72 hour report.
  6. Children are under 18.
  7. The 2026 Order amended ss. 9(1) and 10(2)(c)(ii).
  8. Commencement runs 13 November 2025, 13 November 2026 and 13 May 2027.
  9. Transfers follow a negative list.
  10. s. 43A survives until 13 May 2027.

Add the three big criticisms to every essay answer: the State clauses s. 7(b) and (c) and the s. 17(2)(a) exemption lack necessity and proportionality; the Act omits portability, objection, restriction and automated decision rights; and it punishes but does not compensate.

slides.title: Part II practice questions
slides.html:
1. (Problem 1, Modules 5 and 6) HealthPal, a Pune symptom checker app used in India and, through a German version priced in euros, in Germany, embeds a social plugin and an advertising pixel, makes personalised advertising a condition of its free plan, lets users aged 13 and above register, and is hacked. Advise HealthPal on its position under the GDPR and the DPDP Act.
  2. (Problem 3, Modules 6 and 7) A ransomware group abroad encrypts a city water utility's systems, threatens to leak customer data and declares that it wants to show that the State cannot protect its people; water supply fails for two days. Discuss the group's liability and the utility's obligations under the DPDP Act.
  3. "The DPDP Act, 2023 retreats from the GDPR model." Trace the path from Puttaswamy to the 2023 Act, list the specific departures, and test them against Puttaswamy.
  4. Explain the application of the DPDP Act under s. 3. Does it apply to a Singapore firm that scrapes Indian engineers' public profiles to sell analytics to US companies?
  5. When may a Data Fiduciary process personal data without consent? Discuss s. 4 and the legitimate uses in s. 7, and identify the clauses most open to challenge.
  6. An education platform's student data are breached. What must the platform do under the DPDP Act and the Rules, and what penalties does it face?
  7. A person is rejected by an automated card scoring system. What can she do under the DPDP Act, which rights does the Act omit, and how would the GDPR differ?
  8. Write a short note on Consent Managers under the DPDP Act and Rules.
  9. Critically examine the exemptions in s. 17 of the DPDP Act, especially s. 17(2)(a), in the light of Puttaswamy.
  10. "The DPDP Act punishes but does not compensate." Discuss with reference to the Data Protection Board, the penalty schedule and IT Act s. 43A.
  11. Is the DPDP Act in force? Explain the phased commencement of the Act and the Rules, and the interim position.

slides.title: Answer plans: the two integrated problems
slides.html:
Problem answers score when each law is applied in turn: scope, lawful ground, children, breach and remedies, then a clear conclusion.

Q1. HealthPal under the GDPR and the DPDP Act

  1. Scope: the GDPR applies to German users (Article 3(2)(a)); the DPDP Act to Indian users (s. 3(a)), with duties from 13 May 2027.
  2. Health data: symptom data are health data needing explicit consent (Article 9(2)(a)).
  3. Forced consent: conditioning the free plan on advertising consent fails Article 7(4) and Recital 43, and advertising is not contractually necessary (the Meta decisions); nor is the unconditional, necessity limited consent of s. 6(1) met.
  4. Joint control: embedding the plugin and pixel makes HealthPal a joint controller for collection and transmission (Fashion ID).
  5. Children: users under 16, or the German age, need parental consent (Article 8); under the DPDP Act every user under 18 needs verifiable parental consent and cannot be tracked or targeted (s. 9).
  6. Breach: notify the authority within 72 hours and promptly inform users at high risk (Articles 33 and 34); intimate the Board and every affected user, with a 72 hour report (Rule 7).
  7. Meanwhile: until 13 May 2027, users suffering wrongful loss may claim compensation under IT Act s. 43A, health data being sensitive under the SPDI Rules.
  8. Conclude: the model fails on consent and children under both laws: GDPR fines, DPDP penalties of up to 250 crore rupees once in force, and s. 43A claims meanwhile.

Q2. Ransomware at a city water utility

  1. Cyber terrorism: a contaminant and unauthorised access that disrupt essential services, with a declared intent to strike terror, satisfy IT Act s. 66F(1)(A).
  2. Reach: s. 75 gives the Act reach; s. 70 applies if the systems are protected; UAPA s. 15 and BNS s. 113 overlap.†
  3. Fallback: if intent cannot be proved, ss. 43 and 66 and BNS extortion apply.
  4. The utility: from 13 May 2027 it must intimate the Board and its customers (s. 8(6), Rule 7), and risks penalties if its safeguards were unreasonable.
  5. Conclude: a prosecution for cyber terrorism, punishable with up to life, plus regulatory exposure for the utility.

slides.title: Answer plans: history and scope
slides.html:
For essay questions, lay the foundation first, set out the provisions in the Act's order, apply them, and finish with the notes' critique.

Q3. Does the DPDP Act retreat from the GDPR model?

  1. Foundation: Puttaswamy (2017): informational privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21; any intrusion needs legality, a legitimate aim and proportionality; the plurality called for a robust data protection regime.
  2. History: the Srikrishna Committee and the draft PDP Bill, 2018, which followed the GDPR closely; the 2019 Bill and the JPC (Lekhi, then P.P. Chaudhary; report of 16 December 2021); withdrawal in 2022; Act No. 22 of 2023. Do not treat the 2018 or 2019 texts as law.
  3. Departures: sensitive data, portability, the right to be forgotten, objection and turnover penalties dropped; an adjudicatory Board instead of a regulator; non personal data left unregulated; a negative list instead of localisation.
  4. Test against Puttaswamy: s. 7(b) and (c) and s. 17(2)(a) lack express necessity and proportionality (Big Brother Watch safeguards); s. 44(3) rewrites the RTI exemption.
  5. Balance: the long title weighs right against need; the Act also has distinctive features, such as Consent Managers, nomination and protection of everyone under 18.
  6. Conclude: a shorter, more permissive law relying on consent and executive rule making, whose key provisions are before a larger Bench in Venkatesh Nayak.

Q4. Application under s. 3 and the Singapore scraper

  1. Long title and definitions: digital personal data (s. 2(n)), personal data (s. 2(t)), processing (s. 2(x)).
  2. s. 3(a): processing in India of data collected digitally or digitised later; undigitised paper falls outside.
  3. s. 3(b): processing abroad connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India; no monitoring limb.
  4. s. 3(c): personal or domestic processing, and data made public by the Data Principal or under a legal obligation (the blogger illustration).
  5. Apply: the firm offers nothing in India, so s. 3(b) does not reach it, and s. 3(c)(ii) excludes the public profiles; it is probably outside the Act, unlike under GDPR Article 3(2)(b).
  6. Conclude with status: s. 3 commences on 13 May 2027.

slides.title: Answer plans: lawful grounds and a breach
slides.html:
Applied questions reward a fixed sequence: state the gateway or duty, list each element with its provision, then state the exposure.

Q5. Processing without consent

  1. s. 4: a lawful purpose (anything not expressly forbidden) plus consent or a legitimate use; only two gateways, so no legitimate interests ground.
  2. s. 7, in order: (a) voluntary provision, with the pharmacy and broker illustrations; (b) State benefits under Rule 5 (maternity benefit data); (c) State functions; (d) legal obligations; (e) judgments; (f) to (h) emergencies; (i) employment.
  3. Critique: (b) and (c) allow broad State processing without express necessity or proportionality, so read them subject to Puttaswamy.
  4. Conclude: a legitimate use replaces consent, not the fiduciary's s. 8 duties; the provisions commence on 13 May 2027.

Q6. Breach at an education platform

  1. Define: a personal data breach (s. 2(u)) covers any unauthorised processing or accidental disclosure or loss of access; there is no seriousness threshold.
  2. Who must be told: students are children (under eighteen, s. 2(f)), so parents are Data Principals (s. 2(j)).
  3. Intimation: each parent and the Board without delay, with the Rule 7 contents; a detailed report within 72 hours (s. 8(6)).
  4. Safeguards: test the platform against s. 8(5) and Rule 6 (encryption, access control, logging, backups, one year logs).
  5. Children: verifiable parental consent (s. 9(1), Rule 10); no tracking or targeted advertising (s. 9(3)).
  6. Board and penalties: urgent measures, inquiry and penalty (s. 27(1)(a), s. 33): up to 250 crore rupees (safeguards), 200 crore (intimation) and 200 crore (children).
  7. Conclude: these duties apply from 13 May 2027, and the Board penalises but does not compensate.

slides.title: Answer plans: rights and Consent Managers
slides.html:
Rights questions score when you list what she has, what she lacks and how the GDPR differs, citing the provision for each.

Q7. Rejected by an automated card scoring system

  1. Rights: a summary and the recipients (s. 11, only for consent and s. 7(a) processing); correction and erasure (s. 12); grievance redressal, exhausted first, within ninety days (s. 13, Rule 14(3)); nomination (s. 14).
  2. Fiduciary duty: accuracy where data are used for decisions (s. 8(3)); if the issuer is significant, Rule 13 algorithmic due diligence.
  3. Omissions: no human review, contest or explanation; no portability, objection, restriction or Article 22 protection.
  4. GDPR contrast: she would have Article 22 rights and a direct complaint to a supervisory authority.
  5. Conclude: summary, correction and redress only; do not describe access as a copy.

Q8. Consent Managers

  1. Define: s. 2(g): a Board registered single point of contact to give, manage, review and withdraw consent on an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.
  2. Role: accountable to and acts for the Data Principal (s. 6(8)); registered on prescribed conditions (s. 6(9)).
  3. Conditions: Rule 4 and First Schedule Part A: Indian company, capacity, sound finances, net worth of at least two crore rupees, directors of integrity, protected constitutional documents; Part B continuing obligations.
  4. Oversight: grievances (s. 13) and Board action on breaches of registration (s. 27(1)(d)).
  5. Status and comparison: from 13 November 2026; resembles the RBI's account aggregator framework†; the GDPR has no equivalent.

slides.title: Answer plans: exemptions, enforcement and commencement
slides.html:
Critical questions need the provision, the constitutional test and the current litigation, ending in a clear position.

Q9. The s. 17 exemptions and Puttaswamy

  1. Context: the State is a fiduciary (s. 2(s), s. 2(zb), Article 12).
  2. Partial (s. 17(1)): six grounds; Chapter II (except s. 8(1) and (5)), Chapter III and s. 16 disapplied; responsibility and security survive.
  3. Total (s. 17(2)): (a) notified State instrumentalities; (b) research, archiving and statistics meeting Rule 16 standards.
  4. Other powers: s. 17(3) startups; s. 17(4) the State; s. 17(5) five year power.
  5. Test: s. 17(2)(a) exempts by executive notification without statutory necessity, proportionality, independent authorisation or oversight, the safeguards required by Big Brother Watch and arguably by Puttaswamy.
  6. Conclude: challenged in Venkatesh Nayak (notice, no interim stay, larger Bench), so it remains operative unless stayed.

Q10. Punishes but does not compensate

  1. The Board: established by notification (ss. 18, 19); adjudicates intimations, complaints and references (s. 27) with civil court powers (s. 28).
  2. Penalties: s. 33 factors; Schedule maxima from 250 crore rupees down to 10,000 rupees; fixed caps, not turnover.
  3. No compensation: penalties go to the State, credited to the Consolidated Fund (s. 34), and the Act provides no compensation.
  4. Interim: IT Act s. 43A compensation through the adjudicating officer until s. 44(2) omits it on 13 May 2027; then only tort or contract.
  5. Conclude: appeals (s. 29), mediation (s. 31) and undertakings (s. 32) do not fill the gap, which grounds the criticism.

Q11. Phased commencement

  1. Enactment: assent 11 August 2023; Rules by G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025.
  2. Phases: 13 November 2025 (definitions, Board, ss. 44(1) and 44(3)); 13 November 2026 (Consent Managers); 13 May 2027 (duties, rights, exemptions, penalties, omission of s. 43A).
  3. Caveats: s. 43A meanwhile; the 2026 Removal of Difficulties Order; the unnotified proposal to shorten the transition.†
  4. Conclude: only partly in force; never call it fully in force.

slides.title: What Part III covers
slides.html:
Part III studies how the IT Act, 2000 deals with computer misuse on two tracks: civil contraventions under s. 43 and criminal offences under ss. 65 to 67B.

Part III follows CyberCrimes.pdf, the class presentation for Module 7. It runs from the foundational classes (L1 and L2, self study) to the civil contraventions in s. 43 and the offences in ss. 65 to 67B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, with s. 66F (cyber terrorism) as the class focus (L3).

This chapter lays the foundation for everything after it. It explains why cybercrime defeats ordinary criminal law, how it is defined and classified, what the Budapest Convention does, the two tracks of the IT Act, and the definitions and technology used later.

  1. Chapter 14: concepts, the two tracks, s. 2(1) definitions and a technical primer.
  2. Chapter 15: civil liability under ss. 43 and 43A, and how claims are adjudicated.
  3. Chapter 16: the offences in ss. 65, 66 and 66B, and when the general criminal law also applies.
  4. Chapter 17: identity theft, personation and privacy violation under ss. 66C, 66D and 66E.

Law update. No IT Act bare text was supplied for these notes, so read India Code before quoting a section. Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) have replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act, and the IPC references on the class slides are updated in these notes.

slides.title: Five features that make cybercrime different
slides.html:
Cybercrime is different because of five features: scale, accessibility, anonymity, portability and transferability, and a global, transboundary nature.

Class slide 2 lists these five features. Each one explains why rules built for crime in the physical world struggle online, so use them to open any answer on why special cyber laws exist.

Scale

One person can attack millions of targets cheaply.

Accessibility

Cheap tools and tutorials remove the skill barrier.

Anonymity
