IPC ss. 354C and 354D (class slide 26)Voyeurism and stalkingBNS ss. 77 and 78
IPC s. 292 (class slides 35 and 36)ObscenityBNS s. 294
IPC s. 419 (class slide 27)Cheating by personationBNS s. 319
IPC s. 120B (class slide 30)Criminal conspiracyBNS s. 61
Terrorist act, formerly defined only in UAPA s. 15TerrorismAlso defined in BNS s. 113

Two consequences follow. The Sharat Babu and Full Bench comparison is now made against the BNS, and BNS s. 111 includes cyber crimes in organised crime, which can be used against fraud syndicates.†

Unverified (†). Every BNS section number in this table rests on secondary knowledge (Appendix G). The IPC was repealed from 1 July 2024, so never cite an IPC section without its BNS equivalent.

slides.part: Chapter 20: Procedure, Jurisdiction and the General Criminal Law
slides.title: Proving cyber offences
slides.html:
Cyber prosecutions stand or fall on electronic records, so the BSA s. 63 certificate, forensic imaging and a recorded chain of custody all matter.

This is background. Prosecutions rest on electronic records such as logs, emails, chats, device images, CCTV and provider records.

BSA s. 63. Secondary electronic evidence requires a certificate under s. 63, formerly Evidence Act s. 65B.

Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020) 7 SCC 1, SC† (background)

Held the s. 65B certificate mandatory.†

  1. Forensic imaging and hash values show that evidence has not been altered. (Hashing is a one way function that turns data into a fixed length value, which is why any change to the data shows.)
  2. A recorded chain of custody shows who handled the evidence.
  3. Admissibility, authenticity and weight remain distinct questions: evidence can be admitted yet still be doubted or given little weight.

Exam focus. In a problem, add one line on proof: which electronic records exist, the s. 63 BSA certificate for secondary evidence, and how integrity is shown (hash values, chain of custody).

slides.part: Chapter 20: Procedure, Jurisdiction and the General Criminal Law
slides.title: Exam guidance: procedure
slides.html:
Three years is the line: three years and above is cognizable, three years is bailable, and compounding is narrow and barred for offences against women and children.

Exam focus. Offences punishable with three years and above are cognizable and those with three years bailable (s. 77B); compounding is limited and barred for offences against women and children (s. 77A); Inspectors investigate (s. 78); and s. 75 reaches conduct abroad involving Indian computers.

Common mistakes to avoid:

  1. calling s. 66E or a first s. 67 offence non bailable;
  2. compounding s. 66E committed against a woman; and
  3. citing IPC sections without their BNS equivalents.

slides.title: Chapter 14: why cybercrime law exists
slides.html:
Cybercrime law exists because offences built around tangible property and documents could not capture computer misuse; the IT Act answers with two tracks.

  1. Five features (class slide 2): scale, accessibility, anonymity, portability and transferability, and a global, transboundary nature.
  2. R v Gold (HL, 1988)†: gaining access to Prestel by a trick was not making a false instrument; Lord Brandon's "Procrustean attempt"; making it a crime was for Parliament.
  3. Responses: a US computer fraud law (1984), expanded in 1986 as the CFAA; the UK Computer Misuse Act (class slide 3 says 1991; usually cited as 1990†); India's IT Act, 2000 and the IT (Amendment) Act, 2008, in force from 27 October 2009, which added most offences in ss. 66A to 67C.
  4. "Cybercrime" is undefined. Classify by the computer's role: target, tool or incidental (an evidence question).
  5. Budapest Convention: four categories (confidentiality, integrity and availability offences; computer related forgery and fraud; content related offences; copyright). The slide says 64 parties (check the count); India is not a party.†
  6. The NCRB 2017 figures (a 77 per cent rise over 2016) are dated: cite the latest Crime in India.
ContraventionsOffences
WhereChapter IX: s. 43(a) to (j), ss. 43A, 44, 45Chapter XI: ss. 65 to 74, with ss. 75 to 78
Mental elementNone, except s. 43(j)Intention, knowledge, dishonesty or fraud
Decided byAdjudicating officer, or civil court above the limit (s. 46)Criminal courts (s. 77B)
Investigated byController or authorised officer (s. 28)Officer not below Inspector (s. 78)
OutcomeCompensation or penalties; compoundable (s. 63)Imprisonment, fine or both; compoundable only within s. 77A

slides.title: Chapter 14: definitions and techniques
slides.html:
Know the key s. 2(1) definitions and map each attack technique to its provisions, because problem questions are built from these techniques.

Definitions (s. 2(1); clause letters to be checked against India Code†): access (a) includes instructing or communicating with a computer's resources, so sending instructions counts; computer (i); computer network (j); computer resource (k): a computer, communication device, system, network, data, database or software; computer system (l); data (o); electronic record (t); information (v).

TechniqueProvisions engaged
Hackings. 43(a) and s. 66
Malware (virus, worm, ransomware)s. 43(c), (d) and (i), s. 66, and s. 66F with terrorist intent
Denial of services. 43(e) and (f) and s. 66
Phishing and vishingss. 66C and 66D
SIM swappingss. 43, 66C and 66D
Skimmingss. 43(b) and 66C, and s. 66B for stolen devices
Image abusess. 66E, 67 and 67A

Authentication confirms who a user is; authorisation decides what she may do. Many "unauthorised access" disputes are really about authorisation. Cybersecurity protects systems, while cybercrime punishes misuse.

slides.title: Chapter 15: the ten clauses of section 43
slides.html:
Section 43 imposes uncapped civil compensation for ten acts done without the owner's permission, with no mental element except under clause (j).

ClauseAct done without permission
(a)Accessing or securing access (since 2008, any computer resource)
(b)Downloading, copying or extracting data: employee data theft
(c)Introducing a computer contaminant or virus
(d)Damaging: destroy, alter, delete, add, modify or rearrange
(e)Disrupting a system
(f)Denying access to authorised persons (denial of service)
(g)Assisting another to gain access, such as by sharing passwords
(h)Charging services used by one person to another's account
(i)Destroying, deleting or altering information or diminishing its value (2008)
(j)Stealing, concealing, destroying or altering source code with intent to damage (2008): the only "premeditated" clause
  1. Liability is uncapped since 2008 (previously one crore rupees).
  2. Unauthorised access: DPP v Bignell (1997)†: authorised users misusing data are not unauthorised; Allison (HL, 1999)†: access is unauthorised if the person is not entitled to control access of that kind and lacks consent. Both are persuasive only.

slides.title: Chapter 15: adjudication, section 43A and the problems
slides.html:
Claims up to five crore rupees go to the adjudicating officer, then the TDSAT and the High Court; s. 43A survives only until 13 May 2027.

  1. Adjudicating officer (s. 46) for claims up to five crore rupees; considers gain, loss and repetition (s. 47). Larger claims go to civil courts.
  2. Appeal to the TDSAT (s. 57, since the Finance Act, 2017), then the High Court on fact or law (s. 62).
  3. s. 61 bars civil courts within the officer's competence; the Controller may investigate (s. 28); contraventions may be compounded (s. 63).

Section 43A: a body corporate handling sensitive personal data that is negligent in reasonable security practices, causing wrongful loss or gain, must compensate. The SPDI Rules 2011 define sensitive data.†

Current law update. DPDP s. 44(2)(a) omits s. 43A from 13 May 2027. Until then, s. 43A and the SPDI Rules govern private sector data security; afterwards the Board penalises without compensating. Section 43 is unaffected.

  1. Problem I (Ram and Sharpie): sharing credentials is s. 43(g); using them to alter a story is s. 43(a), (d) and (i); dishonesty adds s. 66. No s. 66F without terrorist intent.
  2. Problem II (Ajay): copying is s. 43(b) whatever his intent; s. 43(j) and s. 66 need intent; s. 65 unlikely (code not required by law to be kept).
  3. Aaron Swartz: the better view reserves criminal liability for genuine dishonesty or fraud, leaving contractual breaches to the civil track.

slides.title: Chapter 16: sections 65, 66, 66B and the general law
slides.html:
Section 65 needs source code the law requires to be kept, s. 66 is a s. 43 act plus dishonesty or fraud, and s. 66B covers stolen devices.

SectionCore rulePunishment
s. 65Knowingly or intentionally concealing, destroying or altering source code required by law to be keptThree years or two lakh rupees or both
s. 66Any s. 43 act done dishonestly or fraudulentlyThree years or five lakh rupees or both
s. 66BDishonestly receiving or retaining a stolen computer resource or deviceThree years or one lakh rupees or both
  1. Syed Asifuddin (AP HC, 29 July 2005): ESN and SID codes are computer source code, so altering an ESN attracts s. 65.
  2. "Dishonestly" and "fraudulently": IPC ss. 24 and 25, now BNS ss. 2(7) and 2(9)†. Receiving stolen property: IPC s. 411, now BNS s. 317†.

Special law or general law, in three steps:

  1. Sharat Babu (2017): where s. 67 applies, IPC s. 292 cannot be invoked for the same act.
  2. Gagan Harsh Sharma (Bom HC, 2018): IPC charges quashed where the IT Act covered the conduct.
  3. Full Bench (Awadhesh Kumar Parasnath Pathak reference): the general law survives where it has an extra ingredient, such as deception in cheating.

Current position. In the Bombay High Court, compare ingredients; Sharat Babu governs where both provisions cover the same conduct. The question is unsettled nationally and must now be answered against the BNS.

slides.title: Chapter 17: sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.html:
Section 66C punishes using another's credential, s. 66D cheating by personation, and s. 66E gender-neutral image-based privacy violation.

SectionCore rulePunishment
s. 66CFraudulently or dishonestly using another's electronic signature, password or unique identification featureThree years and one lakh rupees
s. 66DCheating by personation by means of a communication device or computer resourceThree years and one lakh rupees
s. 66EIntentionally or knowingly capturing, publishing or transmitting an image of a private area without consent, in circumstances violating privacyThree years or two lakh rupees or both
  1. A fake bank caller who obtains a transfer commits s. 66D; if she then logs in with a captured one time password, also s. 66C. Cheating by personation in the general law is now BNS s. 319†.
  2. s. 66E is gender neutral with no minimum sentence; voyeurism (IPC s. 354C, now BNS s. 77†) protects women, covers watching private acts and has a one year minimum. Stalking (IPC s. 354D) is now BNS s. 78†. They are usually charged together.
  3. s. 66E is not compoundable against a woman or child (s. 77A).
  4. NASSCOM v Ajay Sood (Delhi HC, 2005)†: phishing as passing off, the paradigm of s. 66D personation.

Current law update: digital arrest. Not a statutory offence. The Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance on 17 October 2025, directed the CBI to investigate on 1 December 2025, urged a standalone offence on 29 July 2026, and on 4 August 2026 asked the RBI for an SOP on mule accounts. Prosecutions use s. 66D (and s. 66C) with the BNS.†

slides.title: Chapters 18 and 19: cyber terrorism and content
slides.html:
Section 66F needs terrorist intent (Limb A) or espionage-type access (Limb B) and carries life; ss. 67 to 67B rise in severity from obscenity to child abuse material.

  1. s. 66F Limb (A): terrorist intent + deny access, penetrate or access, or contaminant + actual or likely serious harm. Limb (B): knowing unauthorised access to restricted information with reason to believe in its misuse. Up to life, including conspiracy (s. 66F(2)).
  2. Anees Ansari (Mumbai sessions court, reported 2022): life under s. 66F for research and planning; no appellate s. 66F judgment located.
  3. UAPA s. 15 and BNS s. 113 overlap†; Limb (B) is open to a Shreya Singhal style overbreadth critique.
s. 67s. 67As. 67B
MaterialLascivious, prurient or depravingSexually explicit act or conductChildren (under 18): wide range of acts, including browsing and downloading
First conviction3 years and ₹5 lakh5 years and ₹10 lakh5 years and ₹10 lakh
Repeat5 years and ₹10 lakh7 years and ₹10 lakh7 years and ₹10 lakh
  1. Aveek Sarkar (2014): community standards replace Hicklin. Apoorva Arora (2024): profanity is not obscenity. Imran Khan (2025): a like is not publication.
  2. Just Rights for Children Alliance (2024): downloading and keeping CSEAM can be an offence. Sharat Babu (2017): s. 67 excludes IPC s. 292 for the same act.

slides.title: Chapter 20: procedure in one view
slides.html:
Three years is the dividing line for bail, compounding is narrow, Inspectors investigate, and s. 75 reaches conduct abroad.

ProvisionsBail (s. 77B)Compounding (s. 77A)
ss. 65, 66, 66B, 66C, 66DBailableCompoundable
s. 66E; s. 67 (first conviction)BailableOnly if the victim is not a woman or child
s. 67 (repeat); ss. 67A, 67BNon bailableNot compoundable
s. 66FNon bailableNot compoundable
s. 43CivilCompoundable under s. 63
  1. s. 78: officer not below Inspector (lowered from Deputy Superintendent in 2008). s. 80†: search of public places and arrest without warrant. s. 75: conduct abroad involving computers in India.
  2. s. 85: persons in charge of a company deemed guilty unless they prove lack of knowledge or due diligence; Aneeta Hada (2012)†: arraign the company.
  3. s. 79: intermediary safe harbour; "actual knowledge" means a court order or government notification (Shreya Singhal). s. 81: overriding effect, the basis of Sharat Babu.
  4. New codes: BNS, BNSS and BSA since 1 July 2024; secondary electronic evidence needs a BSA s. 63 certificate (formerly s. 65B; Arjun Panditrao Khotkar†).

Remember: Three years: cognizable, bailable, and usually compoundable. Above three years: non bailable and never compoundable.

slides.title: Practice questions: Part III
slides.html:
1. Why could traditional criminal law not deal with computer misuse? Explain with reference to R v Gold, and distinguish contraventions from offences under the IT Act.
  2. An employee changes a server password before resigning and locks everyone out. Discuss his liability under the IT Act.
  3. "Sections 43 and 66 cover the same conduct." Explain, and state when IPC or BNS charges may be added to IT Act charges for the same facts.
  4. A repair shop buys suspected stolen phones and changes their identifiers. Discuss the liability of the shop.
  5. A fake CBI officer keeps a retiree on a video call and extracts her savings. Discuss the offences, the investigation and the reporting of the case.
  6. Distinguish s. 66E of the IT Act from the offence of voyeurism in the general criminal law.
  7. Ransomware deployed from abroad cuts power to several districts, with a declared aim of showing the State's helplessness. Is this cyber terrorism?
  8. Critically evaluate Limb (B) of s. 66F of the IT Act.
  9. Trace the development of the test for obscenity from Hicklin to Apoorva Arora, and explain its relevance to s. 67.
  10. A man shares a former partner's intimate videos in a group chat; one member reposts them and another merely likes the post. Discuss the liability of each.
  11. Does downloading and keeping child sexual abuse material on a phone, without sharing it, amount to an offence?
  12. Explain the rules on cognizability, bail and compounding of IT Act offences, and the effect of the new criminal codes.
  13. Problem 2 (Module 7): On leaving a software company, Riya copies its proprietary code, logs into the company's cloud account with her manager's password and deletes client files, and later sends a colleague's intimate photographs to a group chat. Advise.
  14. Problem 3: A ransomware group abroad encrypts a city water utility's systems, threatens to leak customer data and declares that it wants to show that the State cannot protect its people; water supply fails for two days. Advise on the liability of the group and the position of the utility.

slides.title: Plans 1 and 2: foundations and section 43
slides.html:
Open each answer with the rule, apply it clause by clause, and close by naming the forum or the offence that results.

Q1. Traditional criminal law, R v Gold, and the two tracks

  1. Define the problem: "cybercrime" is undefined; class slide 2's five features (scale, accessibility, anonymity, portability, transboundary nature) explain why ordinary law struggles.
  2. Use R v Gold (HL, 1988)†: access to Prestel by a trick charged as making a false instrument under the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981; acquittal upheld as a "Procrustean attempt"; the gap was for Parliament.
  3. State the responses: the US law of 1984 (CFAA, 1986), the UK Computer Misuse Act (1990†), and India's IT Act, 2000 and 2008 Amendment.
  4. Classify by the computer's role: target, tool, incidental.
  5. Contrast the tracks using class slide 7: mental element, forum, investigator, remedy and compounding.
  6. Conclude: the IT Act answers Gold with a civil and a criminal track; never confuse s. 43 with s. 66.

Q2. The employee who changes the server password

  1. Rule: s. 43 makes a person liable who acts "without permission of the owner or any other person who is in charge"; identify the owner.
  2. Apply: changing the password is damage by alteration (s. 43(d)); locking everyone out denies access to authorised persons (s. 43(f)); it alters information and diminishes its utility (s. 43(i)). Compare class slide 10's placement cell example.
  3. No mental element is needed for these clauses; compensation is uncapped.
  4. If done dishonestly or fraudulently, s. 66 applies: three years or five lakh rupees or both; cognizable, bailable, compoundable.
  5. Forum: claims up to five crore rupees to the adjudicating officer (s. 46, factors in s. 47), then the TDSAT and the High Court.

slides.title: Plans 3 and 4: special law and stolen devices
slides.html:
When the IT Act and the general law overlap, compare ingredients before adding any BNS charge, and prove every element of each IT Act offence.

Q3. Sections 43 and 66, and adding IPC or BNS charges

  1. Rule: s. 66 punishes any s. 43 act done dishonestly or fraudulently (class slide 14); define both terms (IPC ss. 24, 25, now BNS ss. 2(7), 2(9)†).
  2. Contrast consequences: civil compensation versus a cognizable, bailable offence.
  3. Step one: Sharat Babu (2017): s. 67 with s. 81 is a special scheme excluding IPC s. 292 for the same act.
  4. Step two: Gagan Harsh Sharma (Bom HC, 2018): IPC ss. 408 and 420 quashed because the IT Act covered the conduct.
  5. Step three: the Full Bench: the general law survives where it has an extra ingredient, such as deception in cheating.
  6. Conclude with the current position: compare ingredients; unsettled nationally; answer against the BNS.

Q4. The repair shop and the stolen phones

  1. s. 66B: dishonestly receiving or retaining stolen devices, knowing or having reason to believe them stolen; three years or one lakh rupees or both (IPC s. 411, now BNS s. 317†).
  2. s. 65: changing identifiers alters source code on the Syed Asifuddin reasoning (ESN and SID are source code), but only if the codes must be maintained by law.
  3. ss. 43 and 66: altering data without permission, and dishonestly.
  4. Any BNS charge depends on a comparison of ingredients (the Full Bench test).
  5. Conclude: s. 66B, s. 65 (if the legal requirement is met) and ss. 43 and 66; all bailable and compoundable.

slides.title: Plans 5 and 6: digital arrest and section 66E
slides.html:
Name every provision engaged for each actor, prove its ingredients, then deal with procedure, investigation and reporting.

Q5. The fake CBI officer (digital arrest)

  1. Identify the pattern: class slide 22's digital arrest scam (impersonated officials, forged orders, threats of arrest, days on a video call).
  2. s. 66D: cheating by personation through a communication device; s. 66C if her credentials were used.
  3. Add BNS forgery and extortion (and cheating and personation of public servants).
  4. Note that "digital arrest" is not a statutory offence; cite In Re: Victims of Digital Arrest Related to Forged Documents (cognisance 17 October 2025; CBI to investigate, 1 December 2025; directions of 29 July and 4 August 2026).
  5. Investigation by an officer not below Inspector (s. 78), possibly the CBI; report at once on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

Q6. Section 66E and voyeurism

  1. Define s. 66E and its Explanation: transmit, capture, private area, publishes, circumstances violating privacy; three years or two lakh rupees or both.
  2. Define voyeurism: IPC s. 354C (Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013; now BNS s. 77†): one to three years with fine, three to seven on repetition; consent to capture is not consent to dissemination.
  3. Contrast: gender neutral v protects women; images of private areas v watching private acts; no minimum v one year minimum.
  4. Compounding: s. 66E is not compoundable against a woman or child (s. 77A).
  5. Illustrate: the Goa trial room camera (2015) and the Kerala burqa case (2023), both charged under the IPC and s. 66E; the two are usually charged together.

slides.title: Plans 7 and 8: cyber terrorism
slides.html:
Cyber terrorism answers go element by element, and an evaluation answer contrasts the overbroad Limb (B) with the safeguarded Limb (A).

Q7. Ransomware from abroad that cuts power

  1. State Limb (A): terrorist intent, a specified cyber act and actual or likely serious harm.
  2. Act: ransomware is a contaminant introduced through unauthorised access. Harm: power cuts disrupt essential services. Intent: the declared aim of showing the State's helplessness.
  3. Note "likely to cause" and conspiracy (s. 66F(2)); s. 70 if the grid is a protected system.
  4. Reach under s. 75; trial depends on extradition and international cooperation.
  5. Procedure: cognizable, non bailable, not compoundable; Inspector investigates. Note the UAPA s. 15 and BNS s. 113 overlap†.
  6. Conclude: Limb (A), up to life; without proof of intent, ss. 43, 66 and 70 and BNS extortion.

Q8. Critical evaluation of Limb (B)

  1. State Limb (B) and its elements; no terrorist intent, so in substance espionage.
  2. Identify the problem: a possible life sentence for "any restricted information" usable in relation to decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation or incitement, grounds borrowed from Article 19(2).
  3. Show overbreadth: read literally, it could catch a researcher or journalist who exceeds authorised access.
  4. Use Shreya Singhal (2015) 5 SCC 1: s. 66A fell for vagueness and overbreadth; no challenge to Limb (B) was located.
  5. Contrast Limb (A), which requires terrorist intent and serious harm and is far more defensible.
  6. Conclude: Limb (B) invites a Shreya Singhal style challenge.

slides.title: Plans 9 and 10: obscenity
slides.html:
Trace the obscenity tests in order, then separate each actor, because sharing, reposting and liking are treated differently.

Q9. From Hicklin to Apoorva Arora

  1. Hicklin (1868)†: the most vulnerable reader; the Obscene Publications Act 1959: the average reasonable person.
  2. Miller (1973)†: the three part community standards test.
  3. Ranjit Udeshi (1965)†: modified Hicklin, preponderating social purpose; s. 292 upheld under Article 19(2).
  4. Bobby Art (1996)†: context; Ajay Goswami (2007)†: contemporary mores and national standards.
  5. Aveek Sarkar (2014): community standards replace Hicklin; Apoorva Arora (2024): profanity is not obscenity.
  6. Relevance: s. 67 mirrors s. 292(1) (now BNS s. 294†), so this law governs electronic obscenity; Sharat Babu excludes s. 292 for the same act.

Q10. The shared, reposted and liked videos

  1. The sharer: s. 66E (publishing or transmitting an image of a private area without consent) and s. 67A (sexually explicit act).
  2. The reposter: reposting is transmission (the 2023 Allahabad decision†), so ss. 66E and 67A as well.
  3. The member who likes: neither publishing nor transmitting (Imran Khan, 2025).
  4. Procedure: s. 67A is non bailable; s. 66E is bailable but not compoundable because the victim is a woman (s. 77A).
  5. IPC s. 292 (BNS s. 294†) cannot be added for the same material (Sharat Babu).

slides.title: Plans 11 and 12: CSEAM and procedure
slides.html:
Possession questions turn on s. 67B and POCSO s. 15; procedure questions turn on the three-year line in ss. 77A and 77B.

Q11. Downloading and keeping CSEAM

  1. s. 67B(b): creating, collecting, seeking, browsing and downloading are covered; publication is not required.
  2. POCSO s. 15 (substituted 2019): storing without deleting or reporting with intent to share (fine of at least ₹5,000), for transmission (up to three years) or for commercial purposes (three to five years).
  3. Just Rights for Children Alliance (2024): the Madras High Court reversed; storage without deletion or reporting can itself indicate the required intention.
  4. Use the term CSEAM, as the Court directed.
  5. Procedure: s. 67B is non bailable and not compoundable; five years and ten lakh rupees, seven on repetition.

Q12. Cognizability, bail, compounding and the new codes

  1. s. 77B: three years and above cognizable; three years bailable; list the bailable and non bailable offences.
  2. s. 77A: compounding only up to three years; barred for repeat convictions, socio economic offences and offences against women and children; list the results.
  3. Investigation and reach: s. 78 (Inspector), s. 80† (search and arrest), s. 75 (conduct abroad).
  4. Companies: s. 85, with Aneeta Hada†.
  5. New codes: BNS, BNSS and BSA since 1 July 2024; BNS equivalents of IPC sections†; the BSA s. 63 certificate.
  6. Conclude: IT Act offences are unchanged, but every general law reference must be updated.

slides.title: Plans 13 and 14: the integrated Module 7 problems
slides.html:
Integrated problems reward a disciplined order: take each act, name the contravention, add the offence, then state remedies and procedure.

Q13. Problem 2: Riya

  1. Copying the code: s. 43(b), and s. 66 if dishonest; s. 65 only if the code must be kept by law.
  2. Using the manager's password: s. 43(a) access and s. 66C identity theft.
  3. Deleting client files: s. 43(d) and (i), and s. 66 if dishonest.
  4. Sending the photographs: s. 66E and, if explicit, s. 67A (non bailable); s. 66E cannot be compounded because the victim is a woman.
  5. Remedies: the company claims compensation before the adjudicating officer (or a civil court above five crore rupees).
  6. Prosecution under ss. 66, 66C, 66E and 67A, with BNS charges only where they add an ingredient (the Full Bench test).

Q14. Problem 3: the water utility

  1. Limb (A): a contaminant and unauthorised access that disrupt essential services, with a declared intent to strike terror, satisfy s. 66F(1)(A).
  2. Reach: s. 75 over the group abroad; s. 70 if the systems are protected.
  3. Overlap: UAPA s. 15 and BNS s. 113†.
  4. Fallback: if intent cannot be proved, ss. 43 and 66 and BNS extortion.
  5. The utility: from 13 May 2027 it must intimate the Board and its customers (s. 8(6), Rule 7) and risks penalties if its safeguards were unreasonable.
  6. Conclude: a prosecution for cyber terrorism, punishable with up to life, together with regulatory exposure for the utility.

slides.title: Problem 1: HealthPal, scope and consent
slides.html:
Problem 1 tests scope, sensitive data, bundled consent and joint control under both the GDPR and the DPDP Act on a single app; take each law in turn.

Problem 1 (Modules 5 and 6). HealthPal, a Pune symptom checker app used in India and, through a German version priced in euros, in Germany, embeds a social plugin and an advertising pixel, makes personalised advertising a condition of its free plan, lets users aged 13 and above register, and is hacked.

  1. Scope. The GDPR applies to German users under Article 3(2)(a) (the euro-priced German version shows targeting), and the DPDP Act to Indian users under s. 3(a), with duties from 13 May 2027.
  2. Sensitive data. Symptom data are health data needing explicit consent (Article 9(2)(a)).
  3. Bundled consent. Conditioning the free plan on advertising consent fails Article 7(4) and Recital 43, and advertising is not contractually necessary, as the Meta decisions show.
  4. Joint control. Embedding the plugin and pixel makes HealthPal a joint controller for collection and transmission (Fashion ID).
  5. DPDP consent. The DPDP Act's unconditional, necessity limited consent (s. 6(1)) is not met either.

Exam focus. Answer integrated problems issue by issue, giving the GDPR rule and the DPDP rule for each, rather than writing two separate essays.

slides.title: Problem 1: children, breach and the result
slides.html:
HealthPal also fails on children and must report its breach under both laws, so it faces GDPR fines, DPDP penalties and s. 43A claims.

IssueGDPRDPDP Act
ChildrenUsers under 16, or the German age, need parental consent (Article 8)Every user under 18 needs verifiable parental consent and cannot be tracked or targeted (s. 9)
BreachNotify the authority within 72 hours and promptly inform users at high risk (Articles 33 and 34)Intimate the Board and every affected user, with a 72 hour report (Rule 7)
Compensation nowNot addressed in the notes' answerUntil 13 May 2027, users suffering wrongful loss may claim under IT Act s. 43A; health data are sensitive under the SPDI Rules
ExposureGDPR finesPenalties of up to ₹250 crore (250 crore rupees) once in force

Result. The business model fails on consent and children under both laws, exposing HealthPal to GDPR fines, DPDP penalties of up to 250 crore rupees once in force, and s. 43A claims meanwhile.

Notice why the problem mixes three regimes: the DPDP duties start only on 13 May 2027, and until then s. 43A fills the gap for compensation.

Exam focus. Always date the DPDP Act in an answer: most duties apply from 13 May 2027, and s. 43A survives until then.

slides.title: Problem 2: Riya leaves with the code
slides.html:
Problem 2 has four acts; map each to a s. 43 clause and, with dishonesty or another ingredient, to an offence.

Problem 2 (Module 7). On leaving a software company, Riya copies its proprietary code, logs into the company's cloud account with her manager's password and deletes client files, and later sends a colleague's intimate photographs to a group chat.

ActContraventionOffence
Copies the codes. 43(b)s. 66 if dishonest; s. 65 only if the code must be kept by law
Uses the manager's passwords. 43(a) accesss. 66C identity theft
Deletes client filess. 43(d) and (i)s. 66 if dishonest
Sends the intimate photographsNot applicables. 66E and, if explicit, s. 67A (non bailable); s. 66E cannot be compounded because the victim is a woman

Remedies and prosecution. The company may claim compensation before the adjudicating officer (or a civil court above five crore rupees), and Riya may be prosecuted under ss. 66, 66C, 66E and 67A, with BNS charges only where they add an ingredient (the Full Bench test).

Remember: C-L-D-S, Riya's four acts in order: Copy (s. 43(b)), Login (s. 66C), Delete (s. 43(d), (i)), Send (ss. 66E, 67A).

slides.title: Problem 3: ransomware on a water utility
slides.html:
Problem 3 combines cyber terrorism with data protection: the attackers face s. 66F, and the utility faces DPDP breach duties from 13 May 2027.

Problem 3 (Modules 6 and 7). A ransomware group abroad encrypts a city water utility's systems, threatens to leak customer data and declares that it wants to show that the State cannot protect its people; water supply fails for two days.

  1. Limb (A). A contaminant and unauthorised access that disrupt essential services, with a declared intent to strike terror, satisfy s. 66F(1)(A).
  2. Reach. s. 75 gives the Act reach over the group abroad.
  3. Protected systems. s. 70 applies if the systems are protected.
  4. Overlap. UAPA s. 15 and BNS s. 113 overlap.†
  5. Fallback. If intent cannot be proved, ss. 43 and 66 and BNS extortion apply.
  6. The utility. From 13 May 2027 it must intimate the Board and its customers (s. 8(6), Rule 7) and risks penalties if its safeguards were unreasonable.

Result. A prosecution for cyber terrorism, punishable with up to life, together with regulatory exposure for the utility.

Unverified (†). The UAPA and BNS overlap rests on secondary knowledge (Appendix G). Mention it, but build the answer on the text of s. 66F.

slides.title: Final revision: Module 5 (GDPR)
slides.html:
Module 5 in one view: a fundamental right, scope, personal data, principles and bases, consent, sensitive data, delisting, automated decisions and transfers.

  1. Charter Article 8 and TFEU Article 16 make data protection a fundamental right.
  2. Big Brother Watch (Grand Chamber, 2021) demands end to end safeguards.
  3. Scope turns on Articles 2 and 3 (Jehovah's Witnesses, Google Spain).
  4. Breyer, Nowak and EDPS v SRB define personal data.
  5. Fashion ID limits joint control.
  6. Article 5 sets seven principles and Article 6 six bases.
  7. Consent follows Articles 4(11), 7 and 8 (the CNIL's Google fine was upheld on 19 June 2020).
  8. Lindqvist was decided on 6 November 2003.
  9. Google Spain created delisting.
  10. Article 22 governs automated decisions.
  11. Schrems II is DPC v Facebook Ireland (16 July 2020).
  12. The most cited recitals are 22, 23, 26, 32, 39, 43, 47, 50, 71, 85 and 104.

slides.title: Final revision: Module 6 (DPDP Act)
slides.html:
Module 6 in one view: the constitutional basis, the legislative history, the key definitions, consent and legitimate uses, breaches, children, commencement and transfers.

  1. Puttaswamy (2017) sets legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
  2. The JPC was chaired by Meenakshi Lekhi and then P.P. Chaudhary (report of 16 December 2021).
  3. The key definitions are in s. 2(g), (i), (j), (k), (l), (t) and (z).
  4. Processing needs consent or a legitimate use.
  5. Every breach is intimated, with a 72 hour report.
  6. Children are under 18.
  7. The 2026 Order amended ss. 9(1) and 10(2)(c)(ii).
  8. Transfers follow a negative list.
  9. s. 43A survives until 13 May 2027.

Commencement runs in three stages:

  1. 13 November 2025
  2. 13 November 2026
  3. 13 May 2027

slides.title: Final revision: Module 7 (cyber crimes)
slides.html:
Module 7 in one view: s. 43 and its criminal form, the offences from s. 65 to s. 67B with their leading cases, and the procedure that governs them.

  1. s. 43 imposes uncapped civil liability and s. 66 is its criminal form.
  2. s. 65 needs source code required by law (Syed Asifuddin, 2005).
  3. ss. 66C and 66D cover identity theft and personation, including digital arrest frauds now under CBI investigation.
  4. s. 66E protects every gender.
  5. s. 66F needs terrorist intent and carries life (Anees Ansari, 2022).
  6. Apoorva Arora, Imran Khan, Just Rights for Children Alliance and Sharat Babu state the current law on ss. 67 to 67B.
  7. Procedure follows ss. 75, 77A, 77B and 78, read with the BNS, BNSS and BSA.

Exam focus. These seven lines are a ready made conclusion for any Module 7 essay: they name the rule, the case and the procedure for each provision.

slides.title: Corrections 1 to 5: the syllabus
slides.html:
Appendix F lists every point where the syllabus, a class slide or a supplied text differs from the verified position at 7 November 2026; always cite the correct position.

Each item names its source as the notes do: syllabus.md, or a numbered slide in the lecturer's decks GDPR.pdf and CyberCrimes.pdf. So "GDPR.pdf slide 54" means class slide 54 of the GDPR deck.

1. syllabus.md; GDPR.pdf slide 54. What it says: Bodil Lindqvist (CJEU, 2004); spelt "Lindquist" on the slide. Correct position: Decided 6 November 2003, Case C 101/01; spelt Lindqvist. Discussed in: 6.3.

2. syllabus.md, Landmark Cases. What it says: Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland listed apart from Schrems I and II. Correct position: It is Schrems II (Case C 311/18, 16 July 2020). Discussed in: 8.4.

3. syllabus.md, Module 6. What it says: JPC "chaired by Meenakshi Lekhi". Correct position: Lekhi until July 2021; P.P. Chaudhary thereafter, including at presentation of the report on 16 December 2021. Discussed in: 9.3.

4. syllabus.md, Module 5. What it says: "Jehovah's Witnesses v Finland". Correct position: Informal name; formally Tietosuojavaltuutettu, Case C 25/17, a preliminary reference. Discussed in: 2.4.

5. syllabus.md, Module 6. What it says: 2018 draft "primarily modeled on GDPR". Correct position: A common characterisation; no authoritative source using those words was located. Discussed in: 9.3.

slides.title: Corrections 6 to 10: GDPR slides and early cybercrime slides
slides.html:
Three GDPR slides are out of date or incomplete, and two early cybercrime slides need a date correction and a caution about changing figures.

6. GDPR.pdf slide 4. What it says: Big Brother Watch (2018). Correct position: The Grand Chamber judgment of 25 May 2021 is final. Discussed in: 1.4.

7. GDPR.pdf slide 24. What it says: Pseudonymised data are subject to the GDPR. Correct position: Correct for the key holder; for a recipient without the key, see EDPS v SRB (2025). Discussed in: 3.5.

8. GDPR.pdf slide 46. What it says: Google's appeal pending; Meta complaints under investigation. Correct position: Fine upheld by the Conseil d'État, 19 June 2020; Irish DPC decisions January 2023. Discussed in: 5.5.

9. CyberCrimes.pdf slide 3. What it says: UK Computer Misuse Act 1991. Correct position: Usually cited as the Computer Misuse Act 1990†. Discussed in: 14.3.

10. CyberCrimes.pdf slide 5. What it says: 64 parties to the Budapest Convention. Correct position: The figure changes; check the current count. Discussed in: 14.5.

Exam focus. Items 6 and 8 are classic traps: cite Big Brother Watch as the Grand Chamber judgment of 25 May 2021, and the CNIL's Google fine as upheld on 19 June 2020.

slides.title: Corrections 11 to 15: the cybercrime slides
slides.html:
Five cybercrime slides need updating: dated statistics, repealed IPC sections, a wrong case date, later digital arrest orders, and a quashed FIR.

11. CyberCrimes.pdf slide 6. What it says: NCRB 2017 statistics. Correct position: Dated; use the latest NCRB report. Discussed in: 14.6.

12. CyberCrimes.pdf slides 14, 19, 26, 36. What it says: IPC ss. 24, 25, 411, 354C, 354D, 292. Correct position: IPC repealed from 1 July 2024; BNS equivalents in section 20.6†. Discussed in: 20.6.

13. CyberCrimes.pdf slide 18. What it says: Syed Asifuddin (2006). Correct position: Decided 29 July 2005; 2005 Cri LJ 4314 (also 2006 (1) ALD (Cri) 96). Discussed in: 16.2.

14. CyberCrimes.pdf slide 22. What it says: Suo motu cognisance of digital arrest scams. Correct position: Later orders: CBI investigation (1 December 2025); further directions (29 July and 4 August 2026). Discussed in: 17.5.

15. CyberCrimes.pdf slide 43. What it says: College Romance: interim protection. Correct position: Supreme Court quashed the FIR on 19 March 2024 (2024 INSC 223). Discussed in: 19.3.

slides.title: Corrections 16 to 19: research, bare text and case law
slides.html:
The last four corrections concern a s. 66F conviction, an amended DPDP text, the omission of s. 66A, and a qualified Bombay High Court ruling.

16. Earlier research for these notes. What it says: No Section 66F case found. Correct position: Class slide 30 reports a 2022 Mumbai sessions court conviction. Discussed in: 18.5.

17. dpdp_act.pdf. What it says: Original text of ss. 9(1) and 10(2)(c)(ii). Correct position: Amended by S.O. 5458(E) from 6 October 2026. Discussed in: 11.7.

18. IT Act (general). What it says: Section 66A. Correct position: Struck down in Shreya Singhal (2015) and formally omitted from 30 November 2023. Discussed in: Appendix D.

19. Gagan Harsh Sharma (2018). What it says: IPC charges cannot run with IT Act charges. Correct position: Qualified by a Bombay High Court Full Bench: compare ingredients. Discussed in: 16.5.

Items 16, 18 and 19 change Module 7 answers directly: use Anees Ansari only as a press reported trial court example, never cite s. 66A as live law, and always run the Full Bench ingredient comparison before adding a BNS charge.

slides.title: What the dagger means: data protection items
slides.html:
A dagger (†) marks a statement resting on standard secondary knowledge that was not checked against the primary text; Appendix G lists these items in groups.

Items marked with a dagger (†) rest on standard secondary knowledge and were not checked against the primary text for these notes. Treat them as reliable background, but verify before quoting.

EU materials.

  1. The source of the slide examples (EDPB Guidelines 3/2018); the OECD's eight principles; the Law Enforcement Directive.
  2. Planet49; Meta Platforms v Bundeskartellamt; EDPB Opinion 08/2024; Article 82(4); the standing holding in Fashion ID; Wirtschaftsakademie; OT; Google v CNIL; SCHUFA; Dun & Bradstreet Austria.
  3. Article 86 of the AI Act; the academic debate on a right to explanation; EDPB Recommendations 01/2020; Executive Order 14086.
  4. The absence of an adequacy decision for India; and the statement that no comprehensive United States federal privacy law had been enacted.

Indian data protection materials.

  1. Features of the 2018 draft and the 2019 Bill (sensitive data, portability, right to be forgotten, turnover penalties).
  2. The SPDI Rules' list of sensitive data and the ISO 27001 standard; the RBI direction of April 2018; the composition notified by G.S.R. 845(E).
  3. C R Neelakandan; the reported proposal to shorten the eighteen month period; and the account aggregator comparison.

slides.html:

Cybercrime materials. These were not checked against the primary text:

Exam focus. When you rely on a † item, say so briefly (for example, "the BNS equivalent is reportedly s. 317") and anchor the answer on a verified authority or on the text of the section.

slides.title: Practice questions: Part IV
slides.html:
1. Problem 1 (Modules 5 and 6): HealthPal, a Pune symptom checker app used in India and, through a German version priced in euros, in Germany, embeds a social plugin and an advertising pixel, makes personalised advertising a condition of its free plan, lets users aged 13 and above register, and is hacked. slides.title: Plans 1 and 2: HealthPal and the Module 5 and 6 corrections
slides.html:
For HealthPal, run each issue through both laws; for the corrections, give the source, the error and the correct position.

Q1. Problem 1: HealthPal

  1. Scope: GDPR for German users (Article 3(2)(a)); DPDP Act for Indian users (s. 3(a)), with duties from 13 May 2027.
  2. Health data: explicit consent under Article 9(2)(a).
  3. Bundled consent: fails Article 7(4) and Recital 43; advertising is not contractually necessary (the Meta decisions); DPDP s. 6(1) is not met.
  4. Joint control: the plugin and pixel make HealthPal a joint controller for collection and transmission (Fashion ID).
  5. Children: Article 8 (under 16, or the German age) and DPDP s. 9 (under 18; verifiable parental consent; no tracking or targeting).
  6. Breach: Articles 33 and 34 (72 hours; inform high risk users) and Rule 7 (Board and every affected user; 72 hour report); s. 43A claims until 13 May 2027 (health data are sensitive under the SPDI Rules).
  7. Conclude: the model fails on consent and children under both laws; GDPR fines, DPDP penalties up to 250 crore rupees once in force, s. 43A claims meanwhile.

Q2. Corrections to syllabus.md and the GDPR slides

  1. Explain that Appendix F records every difference from the verified position at 7 November 2026.
  2. Syllabus: Lindqvist (6 November 2003, not 2004); DPC v Facebook Ireland is Schrems II; the JPC chairs (Lekhi, then P.P. Chaudhary); Tietosuojavaltuutettu is the formal name of Jehovah's Witnesses; "primarily modeled on GDPR" is unsourced.
  3. GDPR slides: Big Brother Watch Grand Chamber (25 May 2021); pseudonymised data and EDPS v SRB (2025); the CNIL fine upheld (19 June 2020) and the Irish DPC decisions (January 2023).
  4. Bare text: ss. 9(1) and 10(2)(c)(ii) amended by S.O. 5458(E) from 6 October 2026.
  5. Conclude: cite the corrected position and, where relevant, the later authority.

slides.title: Plans 3 to 5: Module 7 corrections, the dagger, and the one-line rules
slides.html:
Show the examiner that you know which classroom statements have changed, which rest on secondary sources, and what the current rule is for each provision.

Q3. Module 7 corrections and their effect

  1. Dates: the Computer Misuse Act is usually cited as 1990†; Syed Asifuddin was decided on 29 July 2005.
  2. Figures: the Budapest party count changes; the NCRB 2017 statistics are dated.
  3. Repealed law: IPC sections on the slides become BNS sections (section 20.6†); s. 66A is struck down and omitted from 30 November 2023.
  4. Later developments: digital arrest orders (1 December 2025; 29 July and 4 August 2026); College Romance FIR quashed (19 March 2024).
  5. Case law: a 2022 s. 66F sessions court conviction exists; Gagan Harsh Sharma is qualified by the Full Bench ingredient test.
  6. Conclude: each correction changes what you cite, and the last two change the analysis itself.

Q4. The dagger (†)

  1. Define: a statement resting on standard secondary knowledge, not checked against the primary text (Appendix G).
  2. Give the groups: EU materials, Indian data protection materials, cybercrime materials, items not reviewed at all, and items likely to change soon.
  3. Cybercrime examples: R v Gold, Bignell, Allison, the trial court reports, s. 70 punishment, s. 80 wording, the UAPA and BNS overlap, every BNS number.
  4. Use: flag the item, verify the primary source (India Code for the IT Act), and anchor the answer on verified authority or the section's text.

Q5. Module 7 in one-line rules

  1. s. 43: uncapped civil liability; s. 66: its criminal form.
  2. s. 65: source code required by law (Syed Asifuddin).
  3. ss. 66C and 66D: identity theft and personation, including digital arrest frauds; s. 66E: protects every gender.
  4. s. 66F: terrorist intent, up to life (Anees Ansari, 2022).
  5. ss. 67 to 67B: Apoorva Arora, Imran Khan, Just Rights for Children Alliance, Sharat Babu.
  6. Procedure: ss. 75, 77A, 77B and 78, read with the BNS, BNSS and BSA.

quiz.concept: Security is only part of data protection
quiz.q: A cloud company protects customer records with state-of-the-art encryption and has never suffered a breach. But it collects far more data than its service needs and later reuses the data for unrelated profiling. Can it still be in breach of data protection law?
quiz.ok: Yes, because security is only one part of data protection, which also limits collection and use.
no: Yes, but only if its encryption falls short of the security standard that the GDPR requires.
No, because data protection law is breached only when data escape the controller's systems.
No, because strong encryption and a clean breach record satisfy its data protection duties.
quiz.why: Data security means the technical and organisational measures that keep data confidential, intact and available. It is one component of data protection, which governs fair and lawful handling at every stage, so over-collection breaches minimisation and unrelated reuse breaches purpose limitation even if nothing leaks. The option blaming weak encryption reaches 'yes' for the wrong reason: the problem is excessive and repurposed processing, not security.

quiz.q: A marketing firm copies the names and opinions in a newspaper's public reader comments into a profiling database. It argues that because the information is already public, no duty of confidence exists, so EU data protection law has nothing to say. What is the flaw in this argument?
quiz.ok: It merges confidentiality with data protection, which regulates personal data even when they are public.
no: There is none; once information is public, it falls outside both the law of confidence and the GDPR alike.
It ignores that public data become confidential again once they are copied into a private database.
It overlooks that the GDPR protects public information only where it reveals special category data.
quiz.why: Confidentiality protects information shared in relationships of trust and usually ends once the information becomes public. Data protection is a separate regime governing every stage of processing, whether or not the data are secret, so public information remains regulated by the GDPR. The view that public data fall outside is closer to the Indian position, because the DPDP Act excludes data the Data Principal herself made public.

quiz.concept: Sectoral model turns on the holder
quiz.q: A US hospital's patient records and a US fitness app's heart-rate logs reveal similar health information, yet only the hospital's records are covered by the US health privacy statute. What feature of the regulatory model explains the difference?
quiz.ok: Under a sectoral model, coverage turns on who holds the data, not on what they reveal.
no: The US follows an omnibus model, which reaches health data only when held by medical providers.
Under a sectoral model, coverage depends on whether the person consented to the collection.
Under a sectoral model, coverage turns on how much harm a disclosure could cause the person.
quiz.why: The United States follows a sectoral approach: separate statutes govern separate industries and some areas are left unregulated. HIPAA covers health plans, clearinghouses, providers transacting electronically and their business associates, so coverage depends on who holds the data, and a health app outside those categories may escape it. The EU's omnibus GDPR applies one baseline to all sectors, public and private, so the same data would be covered whoever held them.

quiz.concept: Why a regulation replaced the Directive
quiz.q: The principles of Directive 95/46/EC were considered sound. Why, then, did the EU replace it with a regulation rather than a new directive?
quiz.ok: The Directive's national implementation caused fragmentation; a directly applicable regulation harmonises the rules.
no: A directive could not bind private companies, so a regulation was needed to reach businesses in the private sector.
The Court had invalidated the Directive's principles, so a new set of principles had to be written.
A regulation lets each Member State choose its own enforcement method while sharing common principles.
quiz.why: A directive leaves form and method to national law, and Recital 9 records that the Directive, though sound in principle, produced fragmented implementation and legal uncertainty that obstructed data flows and distorted competition. A regulation is directly applicable, so Article 1 aims to harmonise and to strengthen and unify protection. The problem was uneven implementation, not the principles themselves. Authority: Recital 9; Article 1.

quiz.q: A data subject argues that because data protection is a fundamental right under the Charter, it must always prevail over a journalist's freedom of expression. How does the GDPR's own framework answer this?
quiz.ok: The right is not absolute; it must be balanced against other fundamental rights in line with proportionality.
no: The right is absolute because it is a Charter right, so expression yields wherever personal data appear.
Expression prevails, because data protection is a statutory right created by the GDPR rather than a fundamental one.
The right yields only to rights named in the Articles, because recitals cannot be used to interpret them.
quiz.why: Recital 4 states that processing should serve mankind and that the right to data protection is not absolute: it must be balanced against other fundamental rights, such as freedom of expression, in accordance with proportionality. Data protection is a fundamental right in its own name (Charter Article 8, TFEU Article 16), so the 'statutory right only' view is wrong, but fundamental status does not make it absolute. Recitals cannot override an Article, yet the Court relies on them to interpret the Articles. Authority: Recital 4; Charter Article 52(1).

quiz.concept: Protection and free flow of data
quiz.q: A trade negotiator claims that international data protection instruments have only ever aimed to slow down commerce. How does the background to the OECD Guidelines of 1980 answer this?
quiz.ok: They aimed both to protect individuals and to stop divergent national laws obstructing transborder data flows.
no: They were a binding treaty that required members to put privacy ahead of trade in every case.
They confined data protection to the public sector so that private commerce could grow unregulated.
They aimed mainly to give security agencies a common standard for sharing intelligence abroad.
quiz.why: The Preface to the OECD Guidelines shows a double motive: protecting people against unlawful storage, inaccurate data and unauthorised disclosure, while preventing divergent national laws from obstructing the transborder flows on which banking and insurance depend. Convention 108's preamble likewise seeks to reconcile privacy with the free flow of information, a tension that runs through every later instrument. The Guidelines are not binding, and they cover both the public and the private sectors.

quiz.concept: Charter right as a standard of review
quiz.q: A student asks how the Court of Justice could strike down a Commission decision on international data transfers simply by reference to the Charter of Fundamental Rights. What is the best explanation?
quiz.ok: Data protection is a fundamental right in its own name under the binding Charter.
no: Data protection is a Treaty objective, so the Court reviews such decisions for procedural error.
The Charter binds the Commission only after a Member State has incorporated it into its national law.
The Court applied Article 8 ECHR, which binds Union institutions directly as part of the GDPR itself.
quiz.why: Article 8 of the Charter protects personal data as a right distinct from private life in Article 7, and the Treaty of Lisbon made the Charter binding and introduced Article 16 TFEU. Any limitation must therefore satisfy Article 52(1): provided by law, respecting the essence of the right, necessary and proportionate. That is why adequacy decisions were measured against the Charter in Schrems I and II. Students often confuse Article 8 ECHR (private life) with Article 8 of the Charter (data protection).

quiz.concept: Structured paper notes are a filing system
quiz.q: Members of a religious community preaching door to door keep handwritten notes of the names, addresses and beliefs of the people they visit, organised by neighbourhood so they can find them again. The community argues that paper notes are outside the GDPR. Is it right?
quiz.ok: No. Manual records structured by criteria for easy retrieval form a filing system, whatever their physical form.
no: Yes. The GDPR is confined to processing by automated means, so handwritten notes kept on paper are excluded.
Yes. Notes taken during religious activity fall within the purely personal or household exemption.
No. A handwritten note that contains a name is within the GDPR, whether or not it is structured.
quiz.why: Article 2(1) covers automated processing and manual processing of data forming part of, or intended for, a filing system: a structured set of data accessible by specific criteria (Article 4(6)). Notes organised by area for retrieval meet that test, whatever their physical form, while unstructured notes would fall outside (Recital 15), so the 'every note' option goes too far. The household exemption does not cover preaching, which is directed outside the members' private sphere. Authority: the Jehovah's Witnesses case (Tietosuojavaltuutettu, Case C 25/17).

quiz.concept: Joint control does not need access
quiz.q: A religious community organises, coordinates and encourages its members' handwritten note taking about the people they visit door to door, but never sees the notes itself. It argues that it cannot be a controller of data it has never had access to. How should a court respond?
quiz.ok: It is a joint controller, because joint control rests on influence over processing, not on access.
no: It is a processor for its members, because it merely acted on their behalf by coordinating the preaching.
It is not a controller, because controllership requires physical possession of the personal data concerned.
It is the sole controller, and the members are only processors acting on the community's instructions.
quiz.why: Controllership is functional: whoever determines why and how data are processed, alone or jointly, is a controller. By organising, coordinating and encouraging the collection, the community took part in determining purposes and means, so it was a joint controller with its members even without access to the notes. The members still decided what to record in practice, so the community was not the sole controller. Authority: the Jehovah's Witnesses case (Case C 25/17).

quiz.concept: Household exemption does not shield platforms
quiz.q: A person uses a social network to share holiday photographs and family birthdays with a small circle of relatives. Who, if anyone, is within the GDPR for this activity?
quiz.ok: The user is exempt as household activity, but the social network providing the means remains covered.
no: Both are exempt, because the household exemption covers the activity and everyone who enables it.
Both are covered, because processing on an online platform falls outside the household exemption.
The user is covered as a controller, but the network is exempt because it merely hosts the content.
quiz.why: Article 2(2)(c) excludes purely personal or household activity, and Recital 18 includes social networking within such activity. The same recital states that controllers or processors that provide the means for such activity, such as social networks, remain covered. Publishing to an indefinite internet audience would be different, but sharing within a small family circle stays personal. Authority: Article 2(2)(c); Recital 18.

quiz.q: A French company runs a car-sharing app offered only in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, and none of its users is in the EU. The processing is carried out in the context of the company's activities in France. Does the GDPR apply?
quiz.ok: Yes. Processing in the context of an EU establishment is covered wherever the users are.
no: No. The GDPR protects only data subjects who are physically present in the Union at the time.
No. Article 3(1) applies only where the goods or services are offered to people in the Union.
Yes, because a French company must appoint an EU representative for its North African users.
quiz.why: Article 3(1) applies the GDPR to processing in the context of the activities of an EU establishment, regardless of where the processing occurs, and the location of data subjects is irrelevant under that limb. The test that looks at people 'in the Union' belongs to Article 3(2), which applies only to controllers outside the Union. An EU representative is required of non-EU controllers caught by Article 3(2), not of a French company. Forgetting that Article 3(1) applies even when every data subject is outside the Union is a common error.

quiz.concept: Indian firm targeting and monitoring EU
quiz.q: A Bengaluru start-up with no office in Europe sells German-language courses on its website, priced in euros with online ordering, and tracks EU visitors' browsing to predict what they will buy. What is its position under the GDPR?
quiz.ok: It is caught by both the offering and the monitoring limbs of Article 3(2) and normally needs an EU representative.
no: It is outside the GDPR, because it has no establishment in the Union and processes its customers' data on servers in India.
It is covered only for customers who are EU citizens, since the GDPR protects nationals of Member States.
It is covered under Article 3(1), because offering services to Europeans gives it an establishment there.
quiz.why: With no EU establishment, Article 3(1) cannot apply, but Article 3(2) reaches non-EU controllers that offer goods or services to people in the Union or monitor their behaviour there. An EU language and currency with the possibility of ordering show an intention to target (Recital 23), and tracking visitors to predict their preferences is monitoring (Recital 24). The test is location, not nationality, and such a controller must normally appoint an EU representative (Article 27).

quiz.q: A US news app is marketed only to the American market and priced only in dollars. An American tourist downloads and uses it while travelling in Italy. Does the GDPR apply to the app's processing of her data?
quiz.ok: No. Her presence in the Union is incidental, and the app does not envisage offering services to people there.
no: Yes. She is physically in the Union while the data are processed, and that presence is enough to trigger Article 3(2).
No. The GDPR protects only EU citizens, and she remains an American national throughout her trip.
Yes. An app that can be downloaded and used inside the Union is treated as targeting the Union.
quiz.why: Article 3(2) asks whether the controller apparently envisages offering goods or services to people in one or more Member States (Recital 23). An app aimed solely at the US market with dollar pricing shows no such intention, and mere accessibility is not targeting. The 'citizens only' option reaches the right answer for the wrong reason: the test turns on location, not nationality, but being in the Union is necessary rather than sufficient.

quiz.q: A bank in Taiwan with no EU establishment serves German citizens who live permanently in Taiwan. A German regulator says the GDPR applies because the customers are EU nationals. Is the bank outside the GDPR?
quiz.ok: Yes. Article 3(2) protects people who are in the Union, and nationality does not bring processing within it.
no: No. The GDPR follows EU citizens wherever they live, so their data are protected in Taiwan too.
No. Processing the data of EU nationals gives the bank an establishment in the Union for the purposes of Article 3(1).
Yes, because banks are governed by sector-specific financial law rather than by the GDPR.
quiz.why: Article 3(2) reaches non-EU controllers processing data of data subjects 'who are in the Union', so location, not nationality, is the trigger. The bank serves people in Taiwan, so it is outside the GDPR although its customers are German nationals. The GDPR is an omnibus law covering all sectors, so there is no general banking exclusion. Treating nationality as decisive is a common error.

quiz.concept: Processing in the context of establishment
quiz.q: A US parent company runs a search engine entirely from servers in America. Its Spanish subsidiary only sells the advertising space shown alongside search results. Why can the establishment rule bring the US company's search processing within EU law?
quiz.ok: The search processing is in the context of the subsidiary's activities, as the two are inextricably linked.
no: The subsidiary itself performs the search processing, so it is the controller of the results.
The complainants are resident in Spain, and the data subject's residence is the decisive test.
An EU subsidiary, whatever it does, makes its parent established in the Union for the group's activities.
quiz.why: Article 3(1) covers processing 'in the context of the activities' of an EU establishment, regardless of where the processing occurs, and the phrase is read broadly. In Google Spain the processing by Google Inc. in the United States was in the context of Google Spain's advertising sales because the two activities were inextricably linked. The link must exist; a subsidiary does not drag in every group activity, and residence is irrelevant under Article 3(1). Authority: Google Spain (Case C 131/12).

quiz.concept: DPDP Act has no monitoring limb
quiz.q: A Singapore firm with no business in India sells nothing to Indians but tracks Indian users' browsing to build profiles it sells to advertisers abroad. A similar firm outside the EU tracks people in the EU. Assuming both laws are in force, which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: The EU-tracking firm falls under the GDPR's monitoring limb; the India-tracking firm probably escapes.
no: Both are caught, because each law applies whenever its residents' data are processed anywhere in the world.
Neither is caught, because both laws reach foreign firms only when they offer goods or services.
The India-tracking firm is caught under the DPDP Act, but the GDPR would need an EU establishment.
quiz.why: GDPR Article 3(2)(b) reaches non-EU controllers that monitor the behaviour of people in the Union, including online tracking and profiling (Recital 24). DPDP s. 3(b) reaches processing outside India only where it is connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India, and the Act has no monitoring limb. Foreign entities that profile Indians without selling to them therefore escape the Act.

quiz.q: A clinic in Mumbai keeps patient registers on paper, never digitised and organised alphabetically. A clinic in Berlin keeps identical paper registers. Assuming both laws are in force, how do the DPDP Act and the GDPR treat these records?
quiz.ok: The Berlin registers are a GDPR filing system; the Mumbai registers stay outside the DPDP Act until digitised.
no: Both sets are outside their laws, because each law is confined to processing carried out by automated means.
Both sets are within their laws, because each law covers structured manual records kept in registers.
The Mumbai registers are covered once collected, while the Berlin registers need automated processing.
quiz.why: The GDPR covers manual processing of data forming part of a filing system, so an alphabetical register is inside it. The DPDP Act applies only to digital personal data: data collected digitally, or collected physically and digitised later (s. 3(a)). Undigitised paper records therefore fall outside the Indian Act, although they would come within it once digitised.

quiz.concept: Legal persons are not data subjects
quiz.q: A business marketing list contains the registered name and switchboard number of a limited company, and the name and personal mobile number of a sole trader. Which entries are personal data under the GDPR?
quiz.ok: The sole trader's entry may be; the company's details are not, because legal persons are not protected.
no: Both are personal data, because the GDPR protects companies and individuals whose contact details are recorded.
Neither is personal data, because business contact information falls outside the GDPR.
The company's entry is, because a registered name identifies it directly, but the sole trader's is not.
quiz.why: Personal data must relate to a natural person, a living human being, and Recital 14 excludes legal persons, so a company's name and contact details are not personal data. A sole trader is an individual, so data about her business may relate to her as a person. The 'business data are never personal' view ignores that the test is whether information relates to an identifiable natural person. Authority: Article 4(1); Recital 14.

quiz.concept: Dynamic IP addresses and legal means
quiz.q: A government website logs visitors' dynamic IP addresses to defend against cyber attacks. Only the internet service provider can link an address to a subscriber, but national law lets the operator, after an attack, turn to an authority that can obtain the subscriber's identity. Are the logged addresses personal data in the operator's hands?
quiz.ok: Yes, because the operator has legal means reasonably likely to be used to identify the user.
no: No, because the operator itself holds no information that links the address to a named person.
Yes, because an IP address is personal data in itself, whoever holds it and whatever the law says.
No, because a dynamic address changes at each connection and so cannot identify a person.
quiz.why: Identifiability is judged by all means reasonably likely to be used, by the controller or another person (Recital 26). Breyer held that a dynamic IP address is personal data for a website operator that has legal means to identify the user with additional information held by the provider. IP addresses are not always personal data: identification is not reasonably likely if prohibited by law or practically impossible because of disproportionate effort. Authority: Breyer (Case C 582/14).

quiz.concept: Opinions about a person are personal data
quiz.q: A candidate asks for his marked examination script, including the examiner's handwritten comments. The examining body says the comments are the examiner's opinions and not the candidate's personal data. How should this be resolved?
quiz.ok: The comments are the candidate's personal data because they evaluate him, and they are also the examiner's.
no: The comments are only the examiner's personal data, because they express the examiner's own views.
Neither the answers nor the comments are personal data, because they concern knowledge, not identity.
Only the candidate's answers are his personal data, because an examiner's opinions relate to the examiner, not to him.
quiz.why: Information 'relates to' a person by its content, purpose or effect. In Nowak the candidate's answers reflected his knowledge and competence, and the examiner's comments evaluated his individual performance and affected him, so both were his personal data. The same information can relate to several people, so the comments were also the examiner's personal data, which is why the 'examiner only' view is incomplete. Authority: Nowak (Case C 434/16).

quiz.q: A retailer replaces each customer's phone number with a hash before storing purchase histories, and keeps the original customer list in another system. It claims the purchase data are now anonymous and outside the GDPR. Why is the claim weak?
quiz.ok: A phone-number hash can be reversed by hashing every possible number, so customers stay identifiable.
no: Hashing is reversible with a key, just like encryption, so it does not remove identifiers.
Anonymous data remain within the GDPR, so even true anonymisation would not take the data outside it.
Purchase histories are special category data, which the GDPR treats as incapable of anonymisation.
quiz.why: Anonymous information that no longer relates to an identifiable person falls outside the GDPR (Recital 26), but only if re-identification is not reasonably likely. Hashing is one way, unlike encryption, which is reversible with a key; yet a hash of a phone number can be reversed by hashing every possible number, so hashing alone rarely anonymises. The retailer also keeps the original list, so the data remain personal data in its own hands.

quiz.q: A contract describes a cloud vendor as a mere 'processor' for a retailer. In practice the vendor decides to reuse the retailer's customer data to train its own recommendation service, which it sells to other clients. How is the vendor classified for that reuse?
quiz.ok: As a controller, because controllership turns on who actually decides the purposes and means.
no: As a processor, because the contract's description of the parties' roles is decisive in law.
As the retailer's agent, so that the retailer answers for the reuse under the GDPR.
As neither, because data used only to train software fall outside the GDPR's material scope.
quiz.why: Controllership is functional: whoever actually decides why and how data are processed is the controller (Article 4(7)), whatever a contract says. A processor acts only on the controller's documented instructions under an Article 28 contract, and a vendor that pursues its own purposes steps outside that role. A contractual label cannot override what the vendor actually does. Authority: Articles 4(7), 4(8) and 28.

quiz.concept: Joint control can be stage specific
quiz.q: An online clothes retailer embeds a social network's 'Like' button, which sends every visitor's IP address and browser details to the network as soon as the page loads. The network later uses the data for its own profiling. For which processing is the retailer a joint controller?
quiz.ok: Only the collection and transmission of the data, not the network's later processing of it.
no: All of it, including the network's later profiling, because the retailer enabled the data flow in the first place.
None, because the visitors did not click the button, so no processing of their data occurred.
None, because the network designed the plugin and decides how the plugin operates.
quiz.why: By embedding the plugin, the retailer decisively influenced the collection and transmission of visitors' data for its own commercial benefit, so it was a joint controller with the network for those operations. It had no influence over the network's later processing, so it is not responsible for that stage; joint control can be partial and stage specific. Data flow as soon as the page loads, without any click. Authority: Fashion ID (Case C 40/17).

quiz.q: An online retailer embeds a social network's 'Like' button, which transmits visitors' data to the network as soon as a page loads, and that processing requires consent. Who must obtain the consent and inform visitors for the collection and transmission stage?
quiz.ok: The website operator, for its own share of the processing, because it triggers the data flow.
no: Only the social network, because it is the party that ultimately receives and uses the data.
No one, because embedded plugins are already covered by the social network's own terms.
Both parties jointly, through one consent that the network collects for all its processing.
quiz.why: Fashion ID held that, where consent is needed, the website operator must obtain it and inform visitors for its share of the processing, the collection and transmission it triggers by embedding the plugin. Each joint controller also needs its own legitimate interest where that basis is relied on. Leaving everything to the network would ignore the operator's own role as joint controller for that stage. Authority: Fashion ID (Case C 40/17).

quiz.q: An Indian retailer embeds a third-party tracking tool, so that the retailer and the tool's provider together determine the purpose and means of collecting visitors' data. What does the DPDP Act require of them about allocating responsibilities, compared with the GDPR?
quiz.ok: Nothing specific; unlike Article 26, the Act has no rule requiring joint fiduciaries to allocate responsibilities.
no: A written arrangement allocating rights and information duties, with its essence made available to Data Principals.
Registration of the arrangement with the Board, which then fixes each party's share of the liability.
Nothing, because the Act does not recognise that fiduciaries can act jointly with other persons.
quiz.why: A Data Fiduciary is any person who determines purpose and means 'alone or in conjunction with other persons' (s. 2(i)), so joint fiduciaries exist. But there is no equivalent of GDPR Article 26, which requires joint controllers to allocate responsibilities and make the essence of the arrangement available to data subjects, so the Act is silent on how liability is shared in a Fashion ID situation. The 'no joint fiduciaries' option misreads the definition.

quiz.q: A city council must process residents' data to collect a local tax that the law requires it to levy. Its new compliance officer insists on asking every resident for consent first, because 'consent is the safest and preferred basis'. What is wrong with this advice?
quiz.ok: There is no hierarchy; a legal obligation or public task fits, and consent is not the default.
no: Nothing; consent is the preferred basis, and the other bases apply only where consent is refused.
Consent is right, but it must be explicit consent because tax data are a special category of data.
The council should rely on legitimate interests, which is the usual basis for public authorities.
quiz.why: Article 6(1) lists six bases with no hierarchy; consent is not the default, and the basis should be fixed before processing begins. A council collecting a tax it is required to levy can rely on a legal obligation or a public task with a basis in law. Legitimate interests is unavailable to public authorities performing their tasks, and consent given to a public authority is doubtful where there is a clear imbalance (Recital 43). Authority: Article 6(1); Recital 47.

quiz.q: An online grocer needs each customer's address to deliver orders. It also analyses purchase histories to build profiles for targeted promotions, and its terms say both are 'necessary for the contract'. How does Article 6(1)(b) apply?
quiz.ok: The address is objectively necessary for delivery; profiling for promotions is not, so it needs another basis.
no: Both are necessary, because the grocer is free to define in its terms what the contract requires.
Neither is necessary, because contractual necessity covers only steps taken before a contract exists.
Both are necessary once the customer accepts the terms, since acceptance makes both of them part of the bargain.
quiz.why: Contractual necessity covers processing necessary for a contract with the data subject, or for pre-contract steps at her request, and it is judged objectively rather than by what the controller writes into its terms. A grocery order cannot be delivered without an address, but it can be performed without promotional profiling. The profiling must rest on another basis, such as consent. Authority: Article 6(1)(b).

quiz.q: A private bank wants to analyse customers' transaction patterns to detect fraud, without asking for consent. Which analysis properly supports reliance on legitimate interests?
quiz.ok: Fraud prevention is a legitimate interest, if necessary and not overridden by customers' interests.
no: A business interest suffices, because legitimate interests needs no balancing once it is identified.
It is unavailable, because legitimate interests may be relied on only by public authorities.
It applies to banks as of right, because financial regulation makes fraud analysis a legal duty.
quiz.why: Article 6(1)(f) requires a legitimate interest, necessity and a balancing test in which the data subject's interests, especially a child's, may override. Recital 47 names fraud prevention as a legitimate interest and frames the balance around the data subject's reasonable expectations given her relationship with the controller. The basis is in fact unavailable to public authorities performing their tasks, the reverse of one option. Authority: Article 6(1)(f); Recital 47.

quiz.concept: Vital interests means life or death
quiz.q: A gym wants to rely on 'vital interests' to share members' attendance records with a health-insurance partner, arguing that regular exercise is vital to members' health. Is that basis available?
quiz.ok: No. Vital interests covers life-or-death situations, not the general promotion of good health.
no: Yes. Processing that benefits a person's health protects her vital interests under the GDPR.
Yes, provided that the members are told in advance and given a chance to object to the sharing.
