She files a complaint directly with the Data Protection Board without using the fiduciary's grievance mechanism, which must answer within a period of at most ninety days. What is the problem?
quiz.ok: She must first exhaust the fiduciary's grievance redressal before approaching the Board.
no: None, because like the GDPR the Act lets her complain directly to the Board.
She must first appeal to the TDSAT, which then refers the complaint on to the Board.
She must first ask a Consent Manager to approve her complaint before the Board can act.
quiz.why: Section 13 entitles her to readily available grievance redressal from the fiduciary or Consent Manager, with a response within the prescribed period (at most ninety days under Rule 14(3)), and requires her to exhaust that remedy before approaching the Board. This differs from the GDPR, which allows a direct complaint to a supervisory authority. The TDSAT hears appeals from the Board, not first complaints.

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. A Data Principal wants her daughter to be able to close her online accounts if she dies or becomes unable to act through serious illness. What does the DPDP Act allow, and how does the GDPR compare?
quiz.ok: She may nominate her daughter to exercise her rights; the GDPR leaves the deceased to national law.
no: Nothing, because data rights end at death under both laws and cannot be exercised by anyone.
Her daughter inherits the rights by law under both regimes, so no nomination is needed.
She may nominate only a lawyer, and the GDPR gives an identical right to nominate a representative.
quiz.why: Section 14 lets a Data Principal nominate an individual to exercise her rights on death or incapacity, meaning inability because of unsoundness of mind or infirmity of body; a nominee could seek erasure of a deceased person's accounts. The GDPR does not protect deceased persons and leaves them to Member States (Recital 27). Nomination is a feature the DPDP Act has and the GDPR lacks.

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. Which of the following acts by a Data Principal breaches a duty under s. 15 of the DPDP Act?
quiz.ok: Filing a complaint with the Board that she knows is false, to pressure a company.
no: Withdrawing her consent the day after giving it, without offering the fiduciary a reason.
Refusing a shopping app access to her contacts list, which the app does not need.
Asking a fiduciary more than once for a summary of the data it holds about her.
quiz.why: Section 15 requires a Data Principal to comply with applicable law, not to impersonate another person, not to suppress material information when providing data for State documents or identifiers, not to file false or frivolous grievances or complaints, and to furnish only verifiably authentic information when seeking correction or erasure. Withdrawing consent, refusing unnecessary data and exercising access are her rights, not breaches. Breach of a duty can attract a penalty of up to 10,000 rupees.

quiz.q: The DPDP Act's duty not to file false or frivolous complaints is backed by a penalty of up to 10,000 rupees. What is the critics' main concern, and what do supporters reply?
quiz.ok: It may deter genuine complaints; supporters say it protects the Board and identity records.
no: It lets fiduciaries fine complainants directly; supporters say fiduciaries need that power.
It makes an unsuccessful complaint a crime; supporters say this deters cybercrime in general.
It bars complaints about the State; supporters say State processing is exempt anyway.
quiz.why: Critics argue that the duty not to complain frivolously deters genuine complaints, while supporters say it protects the Board and the integrity of State identity records. The penalty is imposed by the Board, not by fiduciaries, and a complaint that merely fails is not the same as a false or frivolous one. Authority: s. 15; Schedule, item 5.

quiz.concept: Consent Managers act for the Data Principal
quiz.q: A technology company proposes to act as a Consent Manager while selling advertising based on the consents it handles. Why does this model sit uneasily with the Act?
quiz.ok: Consent Managers are accountable to, and act on behalf of, the Data Principal, not third parties.
no: Consent Managers must be State bodies, so a private company cannot perform that role.
Consent Managers may act only for fiduciaries, so they cannot deal with Data Principals.
Consent Managers copy a GDPR model, and the GDPR bans such conflicts of interest outright.
quiz.why: A Consent Manager is a single point of contact through which a Data Principal can give, manage, review and withdraw consent on an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform (s. 2(g)). It is accountable to and acts on behalf of the Data Principal (s. 6(8)), so a business model built on serving advertisers conflicts with that role. The GDPR has no equivalent of the Consent Manager, which is a distinctive feature of the Indian Act.

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. A person in India is refused a credit card by an automated scoring system and wants a human to review the decision, as an applicant in Germany could under the GDPR. What can she use under the DPDP Act?
quiz.ok: A right to a summary, correction and grievance redressal, but no right to human review.
no: A right to human review and to contest the decision, which the Act copies from Article 22 of the GDPR.
A right to object to the scoring, which the Act grants for processing done without consent.
A right to port her data to a rival bank, which obliges the first bank to reconsider.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act omits portability, objection, restriction and automated decision rights. A person rejected by an algorithm may seek a summary of her data and processing (s. 11), correction (s. 12) and grievance redressal (s. 13), and the fiduciary has an accuracy duty where data are used for decisions (s. 8(3)). Under the GDPR the same applicant would have Article 22 rights, including human intervention and the chance to contest.

quiz.q: Once s. 16 is in force, an Indian payments company wants to move data to a country that the government has not notified as restricted. A sectoral regulation, however, requires payment data to be stored only in India. What is the result?
quiz.ok: The sectoral rule still binds, because the DPDP Act preserves stricter laws on transfers.
no: The transfer is free, because the DPDP Act overrides sectoral rules on cross-border transfers.
The transfer needs a transfer impact assessment and the Board's approval beforehand.
The transfer is barred, because the Act forbids transfers outside India by default.
quiz.why: Section 16(1) lets the government restrict transfers to notified countries, a negative list under which transfers are otherwise free. But s. 16(2) preserves stricter transfer laws, so a sectoral localisation requirement continues to bind. The Act has no impact assessment requirement, and localisation arises only through sectoral rules or Rule 13(4). Authority: s. 16.

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. A bank processes a borrower's data to ascertain the financial position of a loan defaulter, which falls within the partial exemption in s. 17(1). Which obligations still apply to that processing?
quiz.ok: Its overarching responsibility for the processing and its duty to take reasonable security safeguards.
no: None, because the exemption takes the processing out of the Act.
The duties to give the borrower notice and to answer her requests for a data summary.
The duty to obtain the borrower's consent first, unless a court has specifically authorised the processing.
quiz.why: Under s. 17(1), Chapter II (except s. 8(1) and (5)), Chapter III and s. 16 do not apply to listed processing, including ascertaining a loan defaulter's financial position. The overarching responsibility in s. 8(1) and the security safeguards in s. 8(5) still apply, so the exemption is partial. Notice and access fall within the disapplied provisions, and total exemption from the whole Act is reserved for s. 17(2).

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. An Indian outsourcing firm processes, in India, the personal data of German residents under a contract with a German company. Why is the Indian firm largely outside the DPDP Act's main duties?
quiz.ok: Processing in India of non-residents' data under a foreign contract is partly exempt.
no: The Act applies only to the data of Indian citizens, wherever the processing takes place.
The GDPR applies instead, and the DPDP Act yields wherever a foreign law also applies.
Data of persons outside India are not personal data under the DPDP Act's definition.
quiz.why: Section 17(1)(d) disapplies most of Chapter II, Chapter III and s. 16 for processing in India of personal data of persons outside India under a contract with a person outside India, which protects the outsourcing industry. The overarching responsibility and security safeguards still apply. The German exporter must meanwhile satisfy GDPR Chapter V for the transfer. Authority: s. 17(1)(d).

quiz.q: Section 17(2)(a) lets the government exempt any notified State instrumentality from the whole DPDP Act in the interests of security or public order, without any stated necessity test, independent authorisation or oversight. Why is it vulnerable to challenge?
quiz.ok: It allows intrusion by mere notification, lacking the proportionality and safeguards Puttaswamy requires.
no: The Constitution forbids exempting State bodies from a data protection statute.
Only the Board, not the central government, may grant exemptions on security grounds.
Puttaswamy held that the State may process personal data only with each affected person's prior consent.
quiz.why: Section 17(2)(a) exempts agencies by executive notification without any statutory necessity, proportionality, independent authorisation or oversight. Puttaswamy requires legality, a legitimate aim and proportionality, and Big Brother Watch, persuasively, demands independent authorisation and oversight in surveillance regimes. The objection is not that exemptions are impossible but that this one lacks those safeguards.

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. A university uses a large dataset of patient records for statistical research that takes no decision about any individual, meeting the prescribed standards. A hospital uses the same data to decide which patients to drop from a care programme. Which processing is exempt under s. 17(2)(b)?
quiz.ok: Only the university's, as no decision is taken about any specific person.
no: Both, because processing health data for a public benefit is exempt from the Act.
Neither, because the research exemption applies only to processing carried out by State instrumentalities.
Only the hospital's, because care decisions are taken in the patient's own interest.
quiz.why: Section 17(2)(b) disapplies the whole Act for research, archiving and statistics that take no decision about a specific Data Principal and meet the Rule 16 and Second Schedule standards. Deciding which patients to drop is a decision about specific individuals, so the hospital remains fully bound. The exemption is not limited to State bodies. Authority: s. 17(2)(b); Rule 16.

quiz.concept: The Board penalises but does not compensate
quiz.q: After 13 May 2027, a customer whose data leaked through a company's negligent security asks the Data Protection Board to award her compensation for her losses. What can the Board do?
quiz.ok: Impose a penalty, credited to the Consolidated Fund, but it cannot award her compensation.
no: Award her compensation up to the Schedule maximum for the company's failure to take security safeguards.
Order the company to compensate her through the adjudicating officer under the IT Act.
Refer her claim to the TDSAT, which assesses compensation as a tribunal of first instance.
quiz.why: The Board penalises significant breaches after a hearing, and penalties are credited to the Consolidated Fund (s. 34); the Act provides no compensation. IT Act s. 43A, which let affected persons claim compensation through the adjudicating officer, is omitted from 13 May 2027 (s. 44(2)), so a victim of negligent leakage must then rely on tort or contract. Crediting the Board with power to award compensation is a common error.

quiz.concept: Interim compensation under the IT Act
quiz.q: In 2026, before the DPDP Act's duties and penalties have commenced, a company negligently fails to maintain reasonable security practices for customers' sensitive personal data, causing one customer wrongful loss. What remedy does she have?
quiz.ok: Compensation from the company for her loss, claimed through the adjudicating officer.
no: A penalty imposed by the Data Protection Board and paid over to her as compensation.
Nothing, because the IT Act's data protection rules were repealed in November 2025.
A complaint to the Board after she has exhausted the company's grievance mechanism.
quiz.why: Until 13 May 2027, a body corporate negligent in maintaining reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data, which causes wrongful loss or gain, must compensate the person affected through the adjudicating officer (IT Act ss. 43A and 46, with the SPDI Rules 2011). The DPDP duties and penalties start only on 13 May 2027, and even then the Board penalises without compensating. Section 43A is omitted from that date, not from November 2025.

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. A large company facing a Board penalty argues, by analogy with the GDPR, that any penalty must be fixed as a percentage of its worldwide turnover. How does the DPDP Act actually set penalties?
quiz.ok: Within fixed Schedule caps, weighing gravity, duration, gain, mitigation and proportionality.
no: As a percentage of worldwide turnover, following the GDPR's model for large undertakings.
At the full Schedule amount, leaving the Board no discretion to reduce it for mitigation.
By the TDSAT, with the Board recommending an amount after its inquiry.
quiz.why: Section 33 requires the Board to impose penalties for significant breaches after a hearing, considering nature, gravity and duration, the type of data, repetition, gain made or loss avoided, mitigation and its timeliness, proportionality and deterrence, and likely impact. The Schedule sets fixed maxima, such as 250 crore rupees for failing to take reasonable security safeguards, and penalties are not linked to turnover. The TDSAT hears appeals; it does not set penalties at first instance.

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. During a Board inquiry, a fiduciary offers a voluntary undertaking to fix its consent flows within a set time, and the Board accepts it. What is the effect?
quiz.ok: The Board's proceedings on those matters are barred, unless the undertaking is later breached.
no: The inquiry continues regardless, and the undertaking only reduces the eventual penalty by half.
The undertaking counts as a confession, so the Board must impose the maximum penalty.
The fiduciary becomes exempt from the Act for the period of the undertaking.
quiz.why: Section 32 lets the Board accept voluntary undertakings that bar proceedings unless breached, and breach of an undertaking can attract a penalty of up to the original amount. The Board may also direct mediation (s. 31). Both are alternatives to taking a matter through to a penalty.

quiz.q: Comparing India's Data Protection Board with an EU supervisory authority, which description of the Board's role best fits the DPDP Act?
quiz.ok: An adjudicatory body that acts on breaches and complaints, directs remedies and imposes capped penalties.
no: A rule-making regulator that issues the Rules and decides which fiduciaries are significant.
A compensation tribunal that awards damages to Data Principals who are harmed by breaches of the Act's provisions.
A licensing authority whose approval a fiduciary needs before it begins processing.
quiz.why: The Board inquires into breaches on intimation, complaints, government references and court directions, may direct urgent remedial measures, issue directions, accept undertakings, direct mediation and impose penalties up to fixed caps (ss. 27 to 34). Rule making and the notification of Significant Data Fiduciaries lie with the government, and the Board awards no compensation. Unlike a GDPR supervisory authority, it hears a Data Principal only after the fiduciary's own grievance process is exhausted.

quiz.q: Assume the Act and Rules are fully in force. An app has been penalised by the Board in two separate cases and keeps breaching the Act. The Board concludes that the app's services should no longer be available in India. Can the Board block the app itself?
quiz.ok: No. The Board may advise blocking; the government decides after hearing the app.
no: Yes. The Board may block an app it has penalised twice, without a further hearing.
No. Only a court can block an app's services, on a petition brought by the Board.
Yes, after the app's users have been notified and given a chance to object.
quiz.why: Under s. 37, after penalties in two or more instances and a Board reference advising it, the government may, after giving the fiduciary a hearing, direct blocking of public access to its services in India. The Board's role is to refer and advise; the blocking decision belongs to the government. The two-instance condition is met here.

quiz.concept: Classifying cybercrime by the computer's role
quiz.q: Police investigating a murder recover threatening messages from the victim's phone. A separate team investigates a ransomware attack that encrypted a hospital's servers. How does the "computer's role" classification treat these two matters?
quiz.ok: The phone is incidental, raising evidence questions; the hospital's servers are the target of the crime.
no: The phone is a tool of the murder, and the hospital's servers are merely incidental to the ransomware.
Both are tool cases, because a computer was used at some stage of each crime.
Both are target cases, because in each a computer system holds the key data.
quiz.why: The classification asks what the computer did in the crime. Where a device merely holds evidence of an ordinary crime it is incidental, and the questions it raises are about evidence, not substantive offences. Ransomware attacks the system itself, so the computer is the target, which usually needs cyber-specific offences such as ss. 43 and 66.

quiz.q: Hacking into a server needed new, cyber-specific offences, but harassment sent by email can be charged under existing criminal law. What best explains the difference?
quiz.ok: In hacking the computer is the target; in email harassment it is merely the tool for an existing crime.
no: In email harassment the computer is incidental, because it merely stores evidence of what the offender said.
Hacking is usually committed from abroad, while email harassment is usually committed by someone within India.
Email harassment involves no computer at all, because email is a communication service rather than a computer system.
quiz.why: The classification asks what role the computer plays in the crime. Where it is the target, as in hacking, malware or denial of service, the conduct usually needs cyber-specific offences such as ss. 43 and 66, because older offences were not built for it. Where it is a tool, it is used to commit a crime that already exists, such as harassment or fraud; a device is incidental only when it merely holds evidence of a crime committed by other means.

quiz.q: Before computer misuse laws existed, two people used another customer's password, obtained by a trick, to enter an online information service. They were prosecuted for making a false instrument under a forgery statute. Why did the prosecution fail?
quiz.ok: Access by a trick did not fit an offence built for documents, and creating new crimes was for the legislature.
no: The defendants held the customer's password, so their access was authorised and no wrong of any kind was done.
Forgery requires proof of a tangible loss of property, which the defendants did not cause because they merely read stored messages.
The forgery statute did apply, but the defendants were acquitted because the evidence against them was electronic.
quiz.why: The court refused to force the facts into a statute designed for false documents: dishonestly gaining access to a data bank by a trick was not then a crime, and making it one was for Parliament. The lesson is that offences built around tangible property and documents could not capture computer misuse. That gap is why dedicated laws such as the IT Act were needed.

quiz.q: A company proves that an outsider accessed its server without permission, but it cannot prove any intention, dishonesty or fraud. On which track of the IT Act can it proceed, and why?
quiz.ok: The civil track, because s. 43 contraventions need no mental element and lead to compensation.
no: The criminal track, because unauthorised access is an offence whatever the accused's state of mind.
Neither track, because both contraventions and offences require proof of a dishonest intention.
The criminal track, because the civil track is reserved for breaches of contractual terms.
quiz.why: Section 43 covers unauthorised access and interference without any mental element (except clause (j)), and leads to compensation. Offences such as s. 66 need intention, knowledge, dishonesty or fraud, which the company cannot prove. So the absence of a guilty mind closes the criminal track but leaves the civil one open.

quiz.q: An attacker never logs in to a target machine but sends it a stream of commands over the network, which the machine executes. The defence argues there was no "access" because the attacker never entered the system. How does the IT Act's definition answer this?
quiz.ok: Access includes instructing or communicating with a computer's resources, so sending commands is itself access.
no: Access means a successful login with credentials, so commands sent without logging in are not access.
Access requires physical contact with the device, so commands sent remotely fall outside the definition.
Access covers only reading stored data, so executing commands is interference rather than access.
quiz.why: The definition covers gaining entry into, instructing or communicating with the logical, arithmetical or memory function resources of a computer, system or network. Because instructing and communicating are included, a remote attacker who sends commands has "accessed" the machine even without a login. The definition is deliberately wider than entry.

quiz.q: A bank clerk logs in with her own valid credentials and then opens customer accounts she has no work reason to view. Which distinction best frames whether her access was "unauthorised"?
quiz.ok: Her authentication was valid; the dispute is about authorisation, meaning what she was permitted to do.
no: Her authentication failed, because a valid login cannot exist where the purpose of the access is improper.
Her authorisation was settled by the login itself, so only the question of authentication remains open.
Neither concept applies, because unauthorised access disputes arise where outsiders break in, not where insiders log in.
quiz.why: Authentication confirms who a user is; authorisation decides what she may do. The clerk proved her identity, so the real question is whether viewing these accounts was within what she was permitted to do. The notes observe that many "unauthorised access" disputes are really about authorisation, not authentication.

quiz.q: Under the Budapest Convention's grouping of offences, an attacker who floods a company's systems so that legitimate users cannot reach them commits which kind of offence?
quiz.ok: An offence against the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data and systems.
no: A computer-related forgery and fraud offence, because the company suffers a financial loss.
A content-related offence, because the traffic sent to the system is itself unlawful content.
A copyright offence, because the system's software is reproduced in the attacker's traffic.
quiz.why: The Convention's first category covers attacks on systems and data themselves, such as illegal access, interception and data interference, and flooding a system attacks its availability. Forgery and fraud involve deception for gain, and content offences concern material such as child pornography. This first category maps onto ss. 43 and 66 of the IT Act.

quiz.q: An employee copies a company's customer database and leaves the original untouched. Which feature of cybercrime best explains why traditional concepts such as theft struggle with this conduct?
quiz.ok: Portability and transferability, because data can be copied instantly without loss to the owner.
no: Anonymity, because the employee's identity is hidden behind proxies, encryption and false accounts.
Scale, because one person can copy millions of records quickly and at almost no cost.
Accessibility, because cheap tools and tutorials let anyone copy data without skill.
quiz.why: Theft assumes the owner is deprived of a thing, but data can be copied without loss, so the owner still has the original. The notes list portability and transferability as the feature that strains concepts such as theft. Anonymity, scale and accessibility are real features of cybercrime, but none explains why taking a copy of data does not look like theft.

quiz.concept: Why Budapest covers procedure and cooperation
quiz.q: The Budapest Convention does not stop at defining offences: it also covers criminal procedure and international cooperation. Which feature of cybercrime best explains why a treaty limited to defining offences would not be enough?
quiz.ok: Its transboundary nature, because offender, victim, servers and evidence are often in different countries.
no: Its accessibility, because cheap tools and tutorials let unskilled people commit offences in large numbers.
Its anonymity, because false identities and proxies make offenders impossible to identify under any procedure.
Its scale, because one person can attack millions of victims, too many for any national court to try.
quiz.why: Cybercrime is global and transboundary: the offender, the victim, the servers and the evidence may all be in different countries, which raises problems of jurisdiction and cooperation. Defining offences alike in every State does not by itself let one State gather evidence or reach an offender in another, so the Convention also covers procedure and international cooperation. Accessibility, anonymity and scale are real features of cybercrime, but none is mainly a cross-border problem.

quiz.concept: Copying a database: s. 43 or s. 66
quiz.q: Before resigning, a sales manager copies her employer's client database to a pen drive without permission. What decides whether this is only a civil contravention or also a criminal offence?
quiz.ok: Whether she acted dishonestly or fraudulently, since the copying is a s. 43 act either way.
no: Whether the data was copied to removable storage rather than sent out by email or uploaded online.
Whether the employer's loss exceeds the adjudicating officer's pecuniary limit.
Whether she was still an employee when the copying took place, rather than after leaving.
quiz.why: Copying data without permission is a s. 43(b) contravention whatever her motive, and the clause expressly covers removable storage. Section 66 punishes the same act when it is done dishonestly or fraudulently, so the mental element is the only thing that turns the civil wrong into a crime. The size of the claim affects the forum, not the track.

quiz.concept: Inadvertent copying: civil and criminal effect
quiz.q: A programmer downloads his employer's proprietary trading code before leaving, genuinely believing he was copying only open-source files. How does his honest mistake affect his liability?
quiz.ok: It does not defeat the civil claim for copying, but it negates the dishonesty that s. 66 requires.
no: It defeats both claims, because every clause of s. 43 requires an intention to cause damage.
It defeats neither claim, because s. 66, like s. 43, is made out by copying without the owner's permission.
It defeats the civil claim but not the criminal one, because compensation requires deliberate wrongdoing.
quiz.why: Section 43(b) imposes liability for copying without permission whatever the copier's intent, so inadvertence is no answer to the civil claim. Section 66 and s. 43(j) need dishonesty or an intent to damage, which a genuine mistake negates. The notes' second classroom problem reaches exactly this result.

quiz.q: A former web producer posts his old employer's server credentials in an online chat room and urges others to use them. He never logs in himself. Under s. 43, what is the best characterisation of his own conduct?
quiz.ok: Assisting another person to gain access in contravention of the Act, which s. 43 expressly covers.
no: No contravention, because s. 43 is engaged only by a person who personally logs in to or accesses the system.
Unauthorised access by him, because posting credentials is treated as a login by the poster.
Introducing a computer contaminant, because shared credentials operate like a virus on the server.
quiz.why: Clause (g) covers assisting any person to gain access in contravention of the Act, for example by sharing passwords, so the poster is liable even though he never logged in. If he aimed to cause his former employer wrongful loss, his conduct is dishonest and s. 66 applies too. The person who uses the credentials is separately liable for unauthorised access.

quiz.concept: Using leaked credentials to alter a story
quiz.q: A stranger uses credentials posted in a chat room to log in to a newspaper's server and rewrite a published story to harm the paper. No terrorist intent is shown. What is the best analysis of the stranger's liability?
quiz.ok: Access without permission and alteration of information under s. 43, and s. 66 if done dishonestly.
no: Cyber terrorism under s. 66F, because altering a news story threatens the information of the public.
Nothing beyond the poster's liability, because the person who shared the credentials is the one who made the access possible.
No liability, because he used valid credentials and so his access was with the owner's permission.
quiz.why: Logging in without the owner's permission is unauthorised access under s. 43(a), and rewriting the story alters information under clauses (d) and (i). Because his purpose was to harm the paper, the conduct is dishonest and s. 66 applies as well. Section 66F does not arise without terrorist intent, and valid credentials used without the owner's permission do not supply permission.

quiz.concept: Password change that locks everyone out
quiz.q: An employee who manages his company's server, angry at being passed over for promotion, changes the main server password the day before resigning. No one in the company can log in for a week. Which analysis fits best?
quiz.ok: Damaging the system, denying access and diminishing the information's value under s. 43, and s. 66 if dishonest.
no: A mere breach of his employment contract, because no data was copied, deleted or removed from the server.
Tampering with source code under s. 65 rather than s. 43, because a changed password alters the program that runs the server.
An offence under s. 66B, because by locking the server he retains it as a stolen computer resource.
quiz.why: The notes treat this exact pattern as contraventions under s. 43(d), (f) and (i): altering the system damages it, legitimate users are denied access, and the information loses its utility. If the act is dishonest, s. 66 also applies. Liability does not depend on any data being copied or removed.

quiz.q: A student changes the password of a placement cell's email account, which becomes unusable for days, and candidates miss job offers. Nothing is deleted. Why does this still count as "damage" under s. 43?
quiz.ok: Damage is defined to include altering, modifying or rearranging, not only destroying or deleting.
no: Damage is measured by the financial loss caused, so the missed job offers supply the damage.
Damage requires a computer contaminant, and a changed password is treated as a contaminant.
Damage requires physical harm to hardware, which the lost use of the account is deemed to be.
quiz.why: Explanation (iv) defines damage as destroying, altering, deleting, adding, modifying or rearranging a computer resource by any means. Changing the password alters the account, so it is damage even though nothing was deleted. The missed offers matter to the amount of compensation, not to whether there was damage.

quiz.concept: Denial of service without touching data
quiz.q: An attacker floods an online store's website with traffic so that customers cannot reach it for a day. No data is accessed, copied or deleted. The attacker argues that s. 43 is not engaged. Why is that wrong?
quiz.ok: Section 43 also covers disrupting a system and denying access to authorised persons, not only access or damage.
no: Section 43 treats any traffic sent to a website as unauthorised access, whatever the effect on users.
Section 43 treats lost sales as damage to data, so the store's loss of business supplies the damage.
Section 43 covers the attack only if malware was used, because flooding is otherwise lawful use.
quiz.why: Section 43 lists ten acts, including disrupting a system (an unexpected deviation from normal operation) and denying access to authorised persons, as in denial of service attacks. Flooding the site disrupts it and shuts out customers, so liability does not depend on touching data. If done dishonestly or fraudulently, the same conduct is a s. 66 offence.

quiz.concept: Only the source code clause needs intent
quiz.q: In a s. 43 claim, the defendant argues that compensation cannot be ordered because the claimant has not proved any intention on his part. When is that argument a good one?
quiz.ok: Only where the claim is for stealing, concealing, destroying or altering source code with intent to cause damage.
no: In every s. 43 claim, because compensation under the Act is payable only for intentional wrongdoing.
Only where the claim is for unauthorised access, because access must be deliberate to count as access.
Never, because no clause of s. 43 refers to the defendant's knowledge, intention or other state of mind.
quiz.why: Liability under s. 43 is civil and needs no mental element, with one exception: clause (j), the source code clause, requires intent to cause damage, which makes it the only "premeditated" contravention. So the argument fails for access, copying, contaminants or disruption, but succeeds against a source code claim where intent is not shown. Saying no clause mentions intent overlooks clause (j).

quiz.concept: Forum for a large compensation claim
quiz.q: A company wants ₹8 crore in compensation from a hacker under s. 43. Claims up to ₹5 crore go to the adjudicating officer. Where should this claim be filed?
quiz.ok: In a civil court, because the claim exceeds the adjudicating officer's pecuniary limit.
no: Before the adjudicating officer, because s. 43 claims of every size belong to that officer.
Before the Appellate Tribunal directly, because large claims bypass the adjudicating officer.
In a criminal court, because a claim above the limit converts the contravention into an offence.
quiz.why: The adjudicating officer decides claims up to ₹5 crore, and larger claims go to civil courts. The tribunal hears appeals from the officer, not original claims, and the size of a claim never changes the civil nature of a s. 43 contravention. Sending large claims to the officer is a listed examination error.

quiz.q: An adjudicating officer awards ₹40 lakh against a company under s. 43. The company believes the officer misread the facts. What route does its challenge take?
quiz.ok: An appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, now the TDSAT, and then to the High Court on fact or law.
no: A fresh suit in a civil court, which can reopen any matter that falls within the officer's competence.
A direct appeal to the Supreme Court, because the officer exercises the powers of a civil court in the matter.
A revision before the Controller, who supervises adjudicating officers and may set aside awards.
quiz.why: Appeals from the adjudicating officer lie to the Appellate Tribunal, now the TDSAT after the Finance Act, 2017, and then to the High Court on fact or law (s. 62). Section 61 bars civil courts from matters within the officer's competence, so a fresh suit is not available. The Controller's role is to investigate, not to hear appeals.

quiz.q: Two hackers each caused the same ₹10 lakh loss to a business. One made a large profit and had done the same thing twice before; the other made nothing and was a first-timer. Why might the adjudicating officer award different amounts?
quiz.ok: The officer must consider the gain or unfair advantage made, the loss caused and any repetition.
no: The officer must consider only the loss caused, so identical losses must produce identical awards.
The officer must consider only the defendant's means, so the richer hacker must always pay more.
The officer must consider only whether the act was dishonest, which turns the claim into s. 66.
quiz.why: Section 47 directs the adjudicating officer to consider the gain or unfair advantage made, the loss caused and any repetition. The first hacker's profit and repeated conduct therefore justify a higher award even though the losses are equal. Dishonesty matters to criminal liability under s. 66, not to the factors in s. 47.

quiz.q: In March 2026, while s. 43A was still in force, a hacker breaches an online lender's servers and leaks customers' sensitive personal data. The lender had implemented reasonable security practices. A customer who suffered loss sues the lender under s. 43A. What is the likely outcome?
quiz.ok: The claim against the lender fails, because s. 43A requires negligence in maintaining reasonable security practices.
no: The claim succeeds, because s. 43A makes the holder of sensitive data strictly liable for any leak.
The claim succeeds, because the hacker's offence under s. 66 is attributed to the body corporate.
The claim succeeds, because the customers never consented to their data being exposed to a hacker.
quiz.why: Section 43A makes a body corporate pay compensation only where it is negligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices and that negligence causes wrongful loss or gain. A lender with reasonable practices is not liable merely because it was attacked, while the hacker remains liable under ss. 43 and 66. Lack of consent to a leak does not turn s. 43A into strict liability.

quiz.q: A researcher uses a university network he is allowed to use, but downloads articles in bulk in breach of the database's terms of service. The Aaron Swartz prosecution raised the issue that Indian law faces here. What is that issue?
quiz.ok: Whether breaching contractual terms of use makes access "without permission" under ss. 43 and 66.
no: Whether downloading articles counts as copying data when the articles are sold to the public.
Whether a university can ever be a person in charge of a computer network under s. 43.
Whether s. 66F applies to bulk downloading that slows down a university's network.
quiz.why: The criticism of the US prosecution was that it let terms of service or codes of conduct define felonies. The Indian question is the same: does a breach of contract turn permitted access into access "without permission" under ss. 43 and 66? No settled Indian authority was located, so it remains a question for argument.

quiz.q: A company runs its website on servers it leases from a hosting firm that owns the hardware. The company's IT head, who is in charge of the network, lets an outside consultant log in to test its security. The hosting firm was never asked and says the access was "without permission" under s. 43. Is it right?
quiz.ok: No, because permission from the owner or any other person in charge of the system is enough.
no: Yes, because only the owner of the hardware can give permission for access to a computer system.
Yes, because permission given by an employee never counts unless the company's board has approved it.
No, because security testing by a consultant falls outside s. 43, whether or not anyone gave permission.
quiz.why: Section 43 applies only where an act is done "without permission of the owner or any other person who is in charge" of the computer, system or network. The IT head is a person in charge who permitted this access, so on the section's words it was not done without permission, and the hosting firm's ownership does not change that. That is why every unauthorised-access question starts by identifying the owner or person in charge and the scope of what they permitted.

quiz.concept: Section 65 needs code required by law
quiz.q: A prosecutor wants to add a s. 65 charge against an employee who altered his employer's internal source code before leaving. The firm kept the code purely for its own business reasons. What is the weakness in that charge?
quiz.ok: Section 65 applies only to source code that the law requires to be kept or maintained.
no: Section 65 applies only to source code that belongs to a government or public body.
Section 65 applies only where the code is concealed or destroyed, and not where it is merely altered.
Section 65 applies only where the employee had no authorised access to the code.
quiz.why: The ingredients of s. 65 are knowing or intentional concealment, destruction or alteration of source code used for a computer resource, where the code is required by law to be kept or maintained. The legal requirement is the ingredient most often missed, and code kept for business reasons alone does not meet it. Alteration is expressly covered, so that is not the problem.

quiz.q: While installing an update, a developer accidentally overwrites source code that a regulation required his firm to keep. Is s. 65 made out?
quiz.ok: No, because s. 65 requires the code to be concealed, destroyed or altered knowingly or intentionally.
no: Yes, because altering code required by law is punishable whatever the developer's state of mind.
Yes, because a firm required to keep code is strictly liable for its loss under s. 65.
No, because s. 65 requires the code to be stolen and taken outside the firm.
quiz.why: Section 65's ingredients are knowledge or intention; concealment, destruction or alteration; source code used for a computer resource; and a legal requirement to keep that code. Here the legal requirement is met, but an accidental overwrite lacks the knowledge or intention the section demands. Alteration, not only theft, is covered, so the absence of theft is not the reason.

quiz.q: A repair shop buys phones it has reason to believe are stolen and changes their device identifiers so they can be resold. Which statement best captures its liability under the IT Act?
quiz.ok: Section 66B for receiving the stolen phones, and s. 65 too if the law requires the identifiers to be maintained.
no: Only s. 66B applies, because altering identifiers on a phone can never amount to tampering with source code.
Section 65 applies but not s. 66B, because s. 66B requires the shop to have stolen the phones rather than bought them.
No offence applies, because the shop merely had reason to believe, and did not know, that the phones were stolen.
quiz.why: Section 66B covers dishonestly receiving or retaining a stolen device knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen, so the shop need not be the thief. On the Syed Asifuddin reasoning, device identifiers can be source code, but s. 65 still needs a legal requirement to maintain them. The notes add ss. 43 and 66 for altering the devices.

quiz.concept: Section 66 adds only the mental element
quiz.q: A student says that to convict under s. 66, the prosecution must prove some act different from those listed in s. 43. What is wrong with that view?
quiz.ok: Section 66 punishes the very acts in s. 43 when done dishonestly or fraudulently, adding only a mental element.
no: Section 66 punishes only the old offence of hacking, so acts listed in s. 43 never fall within it.
Section 66 punishes acts in s. 43 only when the loss they cause is above the adjudicating officer's pecuniary limit.
Section 66 punishes acts in s. 43 only when they are done against government or protected systems.
quiz.why: Sections 43 and 66 cover the same conduct and differ only in the mental element: s. 43 is a civil contravention leading to compensation, while s. 66 makes the act an offence when done dishonestly or fraudulently. Analysis therefore starts with the relevant s. 43 clause and then asks whether dishonesty or fraud is proved. Treating s. 66 as needing a separate act is a listed examination error.

quiz.q: An employee deletes his employer's files so that the employer loses a contract to a rival who has promised him a job. Why does this conduct cross from s. 43 into s. 66?
quiz.ok: Because he acted dishonestly, intending wrongful loss to his employer and wrongful gain to himself.
no: Because deleting files is a more serious act than accessing them, whatever his state of mind.
Because the loss of a contract exceeds what an adjudicating officer is able to award.
Because a rival business benefited, which makes the deletion a form of cyber terrorism.
quiz.why: Section 66 applies when a s. 43 act is done dishonestly, meaning with intent to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss, or fraudulently, meaning with intent to defraud. Deleting files is a s. 43 act; what makes it criminal here is his intention to cause his employer wrongful loss for his own gain. The seriousness of the act and the size of the loss do not change the track.

quiz.q: A buyer pays a quarter of the market price for a new iPhone from a stranger at a bus stop, with no box or bill. It turns out to be stolen. The buyer says he never knew it was stolen. Why may s. 66B still apply?
quiz.ok: Section 66B is satisfied by reason to believe the device was stolen, not only by actual knowledge.
no: Section 66B applies to any person found holding a stolen device, whatever he knew or believed.
Section 66B applies because buying a device below market price is itself an offence under the Act.
Section 66B applies only to the thief, so the buyer would instead be liable under s. 66C.
quiz.why: Section 66B punishes whoever dishonestly receives or retains a stolen computer resource or communication device, knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen. The circumstances here give reason to believe, so a claim of ignorance is not decisive. It is not strict liability: dishonesty and knowledge or reason to believe are still required.

quiz.concept: SIM swapping and the reach of s. 66B
quiz.q: A fraudster persuades a mobile operator to move a victim's number to a new SIM and uses the one-time passwords to empty her bank account. No stolen SIM or device is involved. Which analysis is best?
quiz.ok: Cheating by personation (s. 66D) and use of her one-time passwords (s. 66C), with ss. 43 and 66.
no: Receiving a stolen device (s. 66B), because the victim's mobile number counts as a stolen communication device.
Only a civil s. 43 claim, because the fraudster used the operator's ordinary process and broke into no computer.
Cyber terrorism (s. 66F), because moving numbers between SIM cards attacks the country's telecommunications infrastructure.
quiz.why: SIM swapping mainly engages ss. 66C and 66D, together with ss. 43 and 66: the fraudster misrepresents identity to the operator and then uses the victim's one-time passwords. Section 66B is engaged only where a stolen SIM or device is actually received or retained. A number is not a device, and there is no terrorist intent for s. 66F.

quiz.concept: ATM skimming: copying versus using data
quiz.q: A gang fits a skimmer to an ATM, copies card data, and later uses the copied data to withdraw money. How do the IT Act provisions divide this conduct?
quiz.ok: Copying the card data is a s. 43(b) copying contravention, and using it to withdraw money is identity theft under s. 66C.
no: Copying the card data is identity theft under s. 66C, and using it to withdraw money is only a s. 43 contravention.
The whole scheme is receiving a stolen device under s. 66B, because copied card data counts as a stolen device.
The whole scheme is a privacy violation under s. 66E, because the card data is the holders' private information.
quiz.why: Skimming involves s. 43(b) for copying data and s. 66C for using another person's unique identification feature to withdraw money. Section 66C needs the credential to be used, not merely held, which is why the copying stage sits under s. 43(b) (and s. 66 if dishonest). Section 66B enters only where stolen cards or skimming devices are received.

quiz.concept: Phishing with a cloned bank page
quiz.q: A fraudster emails customers a link to a cloned copy of their bank's login page. Several customers type in their passwords, and the fraudster then logs in to their accounts and transfers money. Which provisions best fit the two stages?
quiz.ok: Posing as the bank is cheating by personation (s. 66D); logging in with their passwords is identity theft (s. 66C).
no: Posing as the bank is identity theft (s. 66C); logging in with their passwords is cheating by personation (s. 66D).
Both stages are identity theft (s. 66C), because cloning the bank's page is a use of the bank's own identity.
Both stages are privacy violations (s. 66E), because the passwords are the customers' private information.
quiz.why: Section 66D punishes cheating by personation through a communication device or computer resource, which is what the cloned page does; phishing is its paradigm. Section 66C punishes fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's password or unique identification feature, which happens when the fraudster logs in. Section 66D is pretending to be someone in order to cheat, while s. 66C is using someone's credential.

quiz.concept: Identity theft needs use, not holding
quiz.q: Police find a list of stolen net banking passwords on a suspect's laptop, but there is no evidence that he ever used any of them. Why is a s. 66C charge weak on these facts?
quiz.ok: Section 66C requires the credentials to be fraudulently or dishonestly used, not merely held.
no: Section 66C requires the victims to have suffered a financial loss above a fixed amount.
Section 66C requires the suspect to have pretended to be the victims while dealing with others.
Section 66C requires the credentials to have been obtained by hacking rather than bought.
quiz.why: Section 66C punishes whoever fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of another person's electronic signature, password or other unique identification feature, so the credential must be used, not merely held. Pretending to be someone in order to cheat is the different offence in s. 66D. How the list was obtained may raise other questions, but possession alone does not satisfy s. 66C.

quiz.concept: Impersonating officials on a video call
quiz.q: Callers posing as enforcement officers keep a retired teacher on a video call for two days, show her a forged warrant and persuade her to transfer her savings. She never shares any password. Which IT Act offence is the core charge?
quiz.ok: Cheating by personation by means of a communication device or computer resource under s. 66D.
no: Identity theft under s. 66C, because the callers made use of the real officers' names and official identities.
Violation of privacy under s. 66E, because she was watched on camera throughout the call.
Cyber terrorism under s. 66F, because the callers misused the authority of the State.
quiz.why: Section 66D covers cheating by pretending to be another person through a communication device or computer resource, and it reaches impersonation of officials by video call. Section 66C needs the use of someone's password, signature or unique identification feature, and no credential was used here. Section 66E concerns images of private areas, and nothing suggests terrorist intent.

quiz.concept: Card misuse and charging another's account
quiz.q: A banker's unused credit card details are stolen from his records. A fraudster uses the details to buy goods and tampers with a system so that the purchases are charged to the banker's account. Which pairing fits best?
quiz.ok: Using his credentials is identity theft (s. 66C); charging his account by tampering is s. 43(h), and s. 66 if dishonest.
no: Using his credentials is cheating by personation (s. 66D); charging his account by tampering is a privacy violation (s. 66E).
Using his credentials is receiving stolen property (s. 66B); charging his account by tampering is a privacy violation (s. 66E).
Using his credentials is only a s. 43 contravention; charging his account by tampering needs no separate provision.
quiz.why: In the classroom illustration, using another person's card credentials is s. 66C, and charging purchases to his account by manipulating a system is clause (h) of s. 43, aimed at misuse of access codes and IDs, which becomes s. 66 if done dishonestly. Section 66D needs personation in order to cheat, and s. 66E concerns images of private areas. Nothing here touches source code or terrorist intent.

quiz.q: A gym employee secretly films a male customer changing in the locker room and sends the clip to friends. The defence argues that s. 66E protects only women. How should the court respond?
quiz.ok: Section 66E is gender neutral and protects any person whose private area is captured or transmitted.
no: Section 66E protects only women, so the conduct must be charged under some other provision instead.
Section 66E protects men only where the clip is published to the public rather than sent to friends.
Section 66E protects men only where they are minors, because the section is aimed at child abuse.
quiz.why: Section 66E applies to whoever captures, publishes or transmits the image of a private area of any person without consent in circumstances violating privacy; it is gender neutral. "Transmit" means electronically sending an image intending it to be viewed, so sending the clip to friends is enough. Confining s. 66E to women is a listed examination error.

quiz.concept: Privacy expectation inside a public building
quiz.q: A hidden camera in a shopping mall's public restroom records users' private areas. The accused argues that no one has privacy in a public building. Why does that argument fail under s. 66E?
quiz.ok: The test is a reasonable expectation of disrobing without being captured, which can exist in a public place.
no: The test is whether the building is privately owned, and a shopping mall is private property.
The test is whether the images were later published, and a hidden camera always leads to publication.
The test is whether the victims were women, and restrooms used by women are treated as private places.
quiz.why: "Circumstances violating privacy" means circumstances in which a person has a reasonable expectation that she could disrobe privately without being captured, or that her private area would not be publicly visible, whether in a public or a private place. A restroom gives that expectation even inside a public building. Capture alone is enough; publication is not required.

quiz.concept: Watching without recording is not s. 66E
quiz.q: A neighbour watches through a window, without any camera or phone, as a person undresses. Is s. 66E engaged by this watching?
quiz.ok: No, because s. 66E is engaged only by capturing, publishing or transmitting an image, and watching records nothing.
no: Yes, because s. 66E punishes any intrusion on a person's reasonable expectation of privacy.
Yes, because watching a private area is treated as capturing it under the Explanation.
No, because s. 66E applies only where the victim is in a public place rather than at home.
quiz.why: Section 66E's conduct element is capturing, publishing or transmitting the image of a private area, and "capture" means videotaping, photographing, filming or recording by any means. Mere watching creates no image, so s. 66E is not engaged. The section protects against images being made or spread, and it applies in private places as well as public ones.

quiz.concept: Sending a former partner's intimate video
quiz.q: After a breakup, a man sends his former partner's intimate video, showing her private areas, to a large group chat without her consent. Which analysis fits best?
quiz.ok: Transmitting a private-area image without consent (s. 66E), and s. 67A as well if it shows a sexually explicit act.
no: No offence, because the video went only to a private group chat rather than being published to the public.
Section 67 rather than s. 66E, because intimate videos are judged by whether they tend to deprave and corrupt those who view them.
Section 66C rather than s. 66E, because her image is a unique identification feature that he used dishonestly.
quiz.why: Section 66E punishes capturing, publishing or transmitting an image of a private area without consent in circumstances violating privacy, and "transmit" includes electronically sending an image intending it to be viewed, so a private group is enough. Where the video shows a sexually explicit act, s. 67A also applies without any need to show a tendency to deprave. The notes treat the person who shares such a video in this way as committing both offences.

quiz.concept: Digital arrest with a captured OTP
quiz.q: Callers posing as police officers on a video call tell a retiree she is under "digital arrest" and make her read out a one-time password sent to her phone. They use it to log in to her bank account and move her savings. What does her reading out the password add to the analysis?
quiz.ok: Identity theft by use of her credential (s. 66C), on top of cheating by personation (s. 66D).
no: Nothing, because she handed over the password herself, so only cheating by personation (s. 66D) remains.
It replaces cheating by personation (s. 66D) with identity theft (s. 66C), as the two cannot run together.
It makes the matter a civil s. 43 claim only, because the bank's system was accessed with a genuine password.
quiz.why: Pretending to be police on a video call to cheat her is cheating by personation through a communication device, s. 66D. Logging in with her one-time password is a fraudulent use of another person's unique identification feature, s. 66C, so both offences are committed, just as a fake bank caller who then uses a captured password commits both. Her handing over the password under deception does not make the callers' use of it honest.

quiz.concept: Consent to capture is not dissemination
quiz.q: During their relationship, a woman agreed to her partner photographing her privately. After they separate, he sends the photographs, which show her private areas, to his friends without her consent. Does her consent to the photographs protect him?
quiz.ok: No, because consent to capturing an image is not consent to sending it on, which is a separate act.
no: Yes, because consent given at the time of capture extends to every later use of the same image.
No, but only if the photographs reach the public at large, since sending them to friends is not transmission.
No, because her later withdrawal of consent makes the original photographing unlawful as well.
quiz.why: Section 66E treats capturing, publishing and transmitting as separate acts, each punishable when done without consent in circumstances violating privacy, and "transmit" covers electronically sending an image intending it to be viewed. The voyeurism provision reproduced on class slide 26 made the same point expressly: consent to capture is not consent to dissemination. His sending the images is therefore an offence even though the photographing itself was consensual.

quiz.q: A group introduces malware into a State power grid's control systems, blacking out several districts, and announces that it wants to show people the State cannot protect them. Why does this satisfy s. 66F(1)(A)?
quiz.ok: It combines an intent to strike terror, a listed cyber act, and disruption of supplies essential to the community.
no: It involves a power grid, and any attack on critical infrastructure is cyber terrorism whatever the intent.
It caused damage of high value, and s. 66F applies wherever the loss exceeds the civil compensation limit.
It was carried out by a group, and s. 66F is aimed at computer offences committed by organised groups.
quiz.why: Limb (A) needs three elements: a specific terrorist intent, one of three cyber acts (denying access, unauthorised access or attempted penetration, or introducing a contaminant), and actual or likely serious harm such as disruption of essential supplies or services. The declared aim supplies the intent, the malware is a contaminant, and the blackout is the harm. Neither the target nor the size of the loss alone makes an attack terrorism.

quiz.concept: No terrorist intent: the fallback charges
quiz.q: Ransomware shuts down a city's power supply for a day, but the prosecution cannot prove any intent to threaten the State or strike terror; the attackers appear to want only money. What is the best approach?
quiz.ok: Treat it as s. 43 acts done dishonestly, so s. 66 applies, not cyber terrorism under s. 66F.
no: Charge cyber terrorism (s. 66F) anyway, because disrupting a city's power supply is enough without terrorist intent.
Charge Limb (B) of s. 66F, because that limb covers attacks that are motivated by money rather than terror.
Treat it as a purely civil matter, because a demand for money excludes every criminal provision of the Act.
quiz.why: Limb (A) requires a specific intent to threaten India's unity, integrity, security or sovereignty or to strike terror; serious harm alone is not enough. Without that intent the conduct remains a set of s. 43 acts (introducing a contaminant, disruption, denial of access) done dishonestly, so s. 66 applies, together with extortion under the general law. Limb (B) concerns obtaining restricted information, not disruption.

quiz.q: An attacker tries to penetrate a railway signalling system with intent to strike terror, but the system's defences stop the attack before any harm occurs. Can s. 66F(1)(A) still apply?
quiz.ok: Yes, because attempted penetration satisfies the conduct element and "likely to cause" covers failed attacks.
no: No, because Limb (A) requires actual death, injury or destruction of property to have occurred.
No, because an attempt is punishable only under the general law and never under the IT Act.
Yes, but under Limb (B) rather than Limb (A), because Limb (B) deals with unsuccessful access.
quiz.why: Limb (A)'s conduct element includes attempting to penetrate a computer resource without authorisation, and its harm element is met if the act causes or is likely to cause the specified harm. So an attack stopped before any harm can still be cyber terrorism if the terrorist intent is proved. Forgetting "likely to cause" is a listed examination error.

quiz.q: A contractor knowingly exceeds his authorised access to a defence ministry network and copies restricted files on foreign relations, with reason to believe they may benefit a foreign nation. He has no intent to strike terror. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Limb (B) of s. 66F can apply, because it needs no terrorist intent; it is in substance espionage.
no: Section 66F cannot apply, because every form of cyber terrorism requires a specific intent to strike terror in the people.
Section 43 applies but not s. 66F, because exceeding authorised access differs from access without authorisation.
Limb (A) of s. 66F applies, because copying restricted files disrupts services essential to the community.
quiz.why: Limb (B) applies to whoever knowingly or intentionally accesses a computer resource without or beyond authorisation and obtains restricted information, with reason to believe it may be used to injure State security or friendly relations or to benefit a foreign nation. No terrorist intent is needed, which is why the notes call it in substance an espionage offence. Limb (A) is the limb that turns on terrorist intent.

quiz.q: Two people plan a terrorist cyber attack on a telecom network and buy the malware, but are arrested before launching it. Their lawyer argues that nothing was even attempted. What is the strongest response under s. 66F?
quiz.ok: Section 66F(2) punishes whoever commits or conspires to commit cyber terrorism, so conspiracy is expressly covered.
no: Section 66F(2) punishes a completed or attempted attack, so the lawyer is right that no offence was committed.
Section 66F(2) punishes buying malware as such, so the purchase itself is the offence to charge.
Section 66F(2) punishes planning only where the target is notified as a protected system under s. 70.
quiz.why: Section 66F(2) makes whoever commits or conspires to commit cyber terrorism punishable with imprisonment which may extend to life, so conspiracy is expressly covered. The agreement to carry out an attack with terrorist intent is therefore enough, even though no penetration was attempted. Buying malware is not itself the offence; the conspiracy to commit cyber terrorism is.

quiz.concept: Why s. 66F cannot be bailed or settled
quiz.q: An accused charged under s. 66F, which can carry life imprisonment, claims bail as of right and offers to settle with the affected utility. Why do both requests fail under the IT Act's scheme?
quiz.ok: Because its punishment exceeds three years, s. 66F is non-bailable and can never be compounded.
no: Because s. 66F is a civil contravention, the utility's consent to settle is legally irrelevant.
Because s. 66F is investigated by the CBI, bail and compounding need that agency's consent.
Because s. 66F is committed through a computer, and every such offence is non-bailable and non-compoundable.
quiz.why: Under s. 77B only offences punishable with three years are bailable, and s. 66F carries up to life, so it is cognizable and non-bailable. Section 77A bars compounding of offences punishable with life or more than three years. Many IT Act offences, such as ss. 66 and 66C, are bailable and compoundable, so computer involvement alone decides nothing.

quiz.q: An attacker based abroad, who has never visited India, deploys malware against computers that control an Indian city's water supply. Why can the IT Act reach him, and what practical limit remains?
quiz.ok: The Act applies to conduct abroad involving computers in India, but trial depends on extradition and cooperation.
no: The Act applies to Indian citizens abroad, so a foreign national falls outside its reach.
The Act applies abroad only if the attacker's own computer is located in India at the time.
The Act applies everywhere without limit, so a trial in India needs no help from other States.
quiz.why: Section 75 extends the Act to offences and contraventions committed outside India by any person if they involve a computer, system or network located in India. Nationality is irrelevant, and the Indian computers here are the targets. Because the attacker is abroad, bringing him to trial still depends on extradition and international cooperation.

quiz.q: Which feature of s. 66F makes Limb (B) more open to criticism than Limb (A)?
quiz.ok: It can carry life for accessing restricted information linked to decency, morality or defamation, with no terrorist intent.
no: It requires a specific intent to strike terror, which prosecutors can rarely prove in a real case.
It requires actual death or injury to have occurred, which makes the offence almost impossible to prove in practice.
It applies only to systems declared as protected, which leaves most government networks without protection.
quiz.why: Limb (B) reaches unauthorised access to "any restricted information" where it may be used in relation to decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation or incitement, grounds borrowed from Article 19(2). Read literally, it could catch a researcher or journalist who exceeds authorised access, yet it carries up to life. Limb (A), which needs terrorist intent and serious harm, is far more defensible.

quiz.q: A privately owned payment network handles most card transactions in the country. Its owner argues that only government-owned systems can be critical information infrastructure under s. 70. What test answers the argument?
quiz.ok: Whether its incapacitation or destruction would debilitate national security, the economy, public health or safety.
no: Whether the resource is owned by the government, whatever the effect of its failure on the public.
Whether the resource holds the personal data of more than a notified number of individuals in India.
Whether the resource has previously been attacked or targeted by persons located outside India.
quiz.why: Critical information infrastructure is a computer resource whose incapacitation or destruction would have a debilitating impact on national security, the economy, public health or safety, such as power grids, telecommunications, banking and transport. The test looks to the impact of failure, not to ownership, data volume or past attacks. The appropriate Government may then declare such a resource a protected system.

quiz.q: A literary novel explores a sexual relationship in explicit detail but is written mainly as serious literature, not to arouse. How do the content categories treat it?
quiz.ok: As erotica, which is not mainly for arousal and is protected by the public good exception.
no: As pornography, because an explicit sexual theme shows the material was produced for arousal.
As extreme content, because explicit detail places the novel alongside violent and extreme obscenity.
As obscene material, because explicit sexual writing is always likely to deprave and corrupt its readers.
quiz.why: The class slides distinguish erotica (art or literature on a sexual theme, not mainly for arousal), pornography (produced solely for arousal), obscene material (likely to deprave and corrupt) and extreme content. Genuine erotica is protected by the public good exception for literature and art. Explicitness alone does not decide the category; purpose and effect do.

quiz.concept: Community standards, not the vulnerable reader
quiz.q: A magazine publishes a nude photograph of a famous couple as part of a campaign against racism. A complainant says it would corrupt an impressionable teenager who saw it. Under current Indian law, how is obscenity judged?
quiz.ok: By contemporary community standards, looking at the work as a whole and its message in context.
no: By its likely effect on the most vulnerable person into whose hands the material might fall.
By whether any single passage or image in the work, taken in isolation, could arouse lustful thoughts.
By the personal moral standards of the magistrate before whom the complaint is brought.
quiz.why: Aveek Sarkar replaced the Hicklin test, which judged by the most vulnerable reader, with the community standards test, and held that this kind of photograph, published to oppose racism, was not obscene. The work is judged as a whole and in context, so its anti-racism message matters. The complainant's argument applies the discarded vulnerable-reader approach.

quiz.q: A man "likes" another user's provocative post, which is followed by an unauthorised gathering of several hundred people. He is charged under s. 67. Why should the proceedings be quashed?
quiz.ok: Liking is neither publishing nor transmitting, and s. 67 targets obscene material, not merely provocative content.
no: Liking is a form of publishing, but s. 67 applies only where the material shows a sexually explicit act.
Liking is transmitting, but s. 67 is aimed only at material that is shared on pornographic websites.
Liking amounts to transmitting, but only the author of the original post can be charged under s. 67.
quiz.why: In Imran Khan v State of Uttar Pradesh, the Allahabad High Court quashed the proceedings because a like is neither publication nor transmission, and s. 67 punishes lascivious or prurient material, not content that is merely provocative. Both ingredients therefore failed. A sexually explicit act is the test for s. 67A, not s. 67, and nothing in s. 67 confines liability to the author.

quiz.concept: Why obscenity case law governs s. 67
quiz.q: In a s. 67 prosecution over an online video, the defence argues that obscenity rulings on books and films decided under the general criminal law are irrelevant, because s. 67 is a separate IT Act offence. Why does the argument fail?
quiz.ok: Section 67's ingredients mirror those of the general obscenity offence, differing only in punishment, so that case law applies.
no: Section 67 incorporates the general obscenity offence, so a s. 67 charge is in law a charge under the general law.
Section 67 applies only after a court has found the same material obscene under the general criminal law.
Section 67 uses the sexually explicit act test, which those rulings on books and films first developed.
quiz.why: Section 67 punishes publishing or transmitting electronic material that is lascivious, appeals to the prurient interest or tends to deprave and corrupt its likely audience, ingredients that mirror the general obscenity offence except for punishment. The obscenity case law, including the community standards test in Aveek Sarkar, therefore applies to s. 67. It remains a separate offence, and the sexually explicit act test belongs to s. 67A.

quiz.concept: Section 67A needs no tendency to deprave
quiz.q: A man uploads a video of an explicit sexual act to a website. His lawyer argues that the prosecution must prove the video tends to deprave and corrupt viewers. Under s. 67A, is that right?
quiz.ok: No, because s. 67A requires a sexually explicit act or conduct, and no tendency to deprave need be shown.
no: Yes, because every electronic content offence under the Act uses the deprave-and-corrupt test borrowed from obscenity law.
Yes, because s. 67A is the repeat-offence form of s. 67 and so carries over its test.
No, because s. 67A requires proof instead that the video was viewed by a child under the age of eighteen.
quiz.why: Section 67A punishes publishing or transmitting in electronic form material containing a sexually explicit act or conduct, and no tendency to deprave need be shown. The deprave-and-corrupt and prurient interest tests belong to s. 67. Section 67A is a separate offence, not a repeat-offence version of s. 67, and children are protected separately by s. 67B.

quiz.concept: Public good exception and its burden
quiz.q: A medical college publishes online an anatomy textbook with explicit diagrams of the human body. Prosecuted under s. 67, it relies on the exception. Who must prove what?
quiz.ok: The college must prove the publication is justified for the public good, for example in the interest of science.
no: The prosecution must first prove that the textbook lacks scientific value before the exception can be denied to it.
The college need prove nothing, because medical material is automatically excluded from the scope of s. 67.
The prosecution must prove the college intended to arouse readers, since the exception is otherwise presumed to apply.
quiz.why: The exception covers electronic books, writings, drawings and representations proved to be justified as being for the public good in the interest of science, literature, art, learning or other objects of general concern, or kept for bona fide heritage or religious purposes. Medical texts are a classic example. The person relying on the exception bears the burden of proving it.

quiz.q: A man downloads child sexual abuse material and keeps it on his phone, but never shares it. He asks the court to quash the case because nothing was published or transmitted. What is the correct position?
quiz.ok: The case continues, because s. 67B covers seeking, browsing and downloading such material, not only publication.
no: The case is quashed, because s. 67B, like s. 67, punishes only publishing or transmitting material.
The case is quashed, because possession is a matter for the POCSO Act and never for the IT Act.
The case continues, but only under s. 66E, because the images show the private areas of children.
quiz.why: In Just Rights for Children Alliance v S. Harish, the Supreme Court restored the proceedings: s. 67B covers creating, collecting, seeking, browsing and downloading, and storage without deleting or reporting can indicate the intention POCSO s. 15 requires. Treating s. 67B as requiring publication was the High Court's error. It is the leading authority on possession and viewing offences.

quiz.concept: Online grooming before any image exists
quiz.q: An adult befriends a sixteen-year-old online over several weeks and induces the child into a relationship aimed at sexually explicit acts. No image has yet been created or shared. Is s. 67B engaged?
quiz.ok: Yes, because s. 67B criminalises cultivating or enticing children into such online relationships, before any image exists.
no: No, because s. 67B is engaged only once sexually explicit material depicting the child exists.
No, because a sixteen-year-old is above the age at which s. 67B protects children online.
Yes, but only as s. 67A, because the conduct relates to sexually explicit acts with another person.
quiz.why: Clause (c) of s. 67B punishes whoever cultivates, entices or induces children into online relationships for sexually explicit acts, so grooming is criminal before any image exists. "Children" means persons under eighteen, so a sixteen-year-old is protected. Section 67A concerns publishing or transmitting sexually explicit material, which has not happened here.

quiz.concept: Morphed images that appear to show children
quiz.q: A man uses software to modify ordinary photos of an adult so that they appear to depict a child in sexually explicit conduct, and circulates them online. He argues that no real child was involved. How does the law treat this?
quiz.ok: The material can be child pornography, because the definition includes images modified to appear to depict a child.
no: The material falls outside child protection law, because the definition requires a real, identifiable child.
The material is covered only if the person shown was under eighteen when the original photo was taken.
The material falls under s. 67 instead, because modified images are judged by the general obscenity test.
quiz.why: The POCSO definition of child pornography, as amended in 2019, covers any visual depiction of sexually explicit conduct involving a child, including digital or computer-generated images indistinguishable from, or modified to appear to depict, a child. A morphed image therefore falls within it even though no real child was photographed. What matters is what the image appears to depict, not the age of the person in the original.

quiz.concept: Electronic obscenity and the special scheme
quiz.q: An online marketplace lists an obscene video clip for sale. The prosecution wants to charge one of its officers under the general criminal law's obscenity offence for that same electronic listing. Following Sharat Babu Digumarti, what is the position?
quiz.ok: The general obscenity offence is excluded for the same conduct, as s. 67 with ss. 79 and 81 is a special scheme.
no: The general obscenity offence can be added, because the IT Act operates in addition to the other criminal laws.
