The general obscenity offence must be used instead, because s. 67 applies only to individuals and never to companies or their officers.
The general obscenity offence applies, because listing a clip for sale is not a publication or transmission under s. 67.
quiz.why: Sharat Babu held that where the offence concerns obscene material in electronic form, s. 67, read with ss. 79 and 81, is a special scheme that excludes the general obscenity offence for the same conduct; s. 67's ingredients mirror that offence, so the two cover identical ground. Section 81 gives the IT Act overriding effect, which is the basis of the decision. So an officer discharged under s. 67 could not still be prosecuted under the general law for the same act.

quiz.concept: Applying s. 77B to a stated punishment
quiz.q: Under s. 77B, offences punishable with three years and above are cognizable, and those punishable with three years are bailable. An IT Act offence carries up to five years on a first conviction. How is it classified?
quiz.ok: Cognizable and non-bailable, because the punishment exceeds three years.
no: Cognizable and bailable, because every offence under the IT Act is bailable by default.
Non-cognizable and bailable, because a first conviction is treated more leniently than a repeat one.
Non-cognizable and non-bailable, because the punishment exceeds the three-year threshold.
quiz.why: Section 77B makes offences punishable with three years and above cognizable, and only those punishable with three years bailable. Five years crosses the bail line, so the offence is cognizable and non-bailable, which is why s. 67A is non-bailable. Treating IT Act offences as uniformly bailable is wrong.

quiz.q: Section 67 carries up to three years on a first conviction and up to five years on a subsequent one. A man already convicted once under s. 67 is charged again. Why does the second charge stand on a different procedural footing?
quiz.ok: The higher punishment makes it non-bailable, and an enhanced punishment for a repeat offence bars compounding.
no: The second charge becomes a civil contravention, because repeated conduct is dealt with by compensation.
The second charge stays bailable and compoundable, because the content offence itself is unchanged.
The second charge is non-bailable only if the victim is a woman, because s. 77A turns on the victim.
quiz.why: A first s. 67 offence carries three years, so it is cognizable and bailable; a subsequent offence carries five years, so it becomes non-bailable under s. 77B. Section 77A also bars compounding where a previous conviction attracts enhanced or different punishment. The victim's gender affects compounding, not bail.

quiz.q: A man captured images of a woman's private area without consent and is charged under s. 66E, which carries up to three years. She agrees to settle, and the parties apply to compound the offence. What should the court do?
quiz.ok: Refuse, because s. 77A bars compounding any offence committed against a woman or a child.
no: Allow it, because offences punishable with three years or less are always compoundable by a court.
Allow it, because the victim's consent to settle overrides the statutory bar on compounding.
Refuse, because s. 66E is non-bailable and non-bailable offences can never be compounded.
quiz.why: Section 77A lets courts compound offences other than those punishable with life or more than three years, but not where the offence is committed against a woman or a child under eighteen. Section 66E is therefore compoundable only where the victim is neither, so this case cannot be settled by compounding. Section 66E is bailable, so the non-bailability reason is wrong.

quiz.concept: When identity theft can be compounded
quiz.q: A man fraudulently used a male colleague's net banking password to move ₹20,000, an offence under s. 66C carrying up to three years. He has repaid the colleague and both wish to settle. Can the offence be compounded?
quiz.ok: Yes, because it carries three years, the victim is a man, and no s. 77A bar applies.
no: No, because compounding is available for civil contraventions under s. 63 but not for criminal offences.
No, because identity theft offences under the IT Act are excluded from compounding by s. 77A.
Yes, but only before the adjudicating officer, because compounding of offences is a civil remedy under s. 63.
quiz.why: Section 77A permits compounding of offences other than those punishable with life or more than three years, unless a previous conviction attracts enhanced punishment, the offence affects socio-economic conditions, or it is committed against a woman or a child. Section 66C carries three years and none of the bars applies, so the notes list it as compoundable. Contraventions are compounded under s. 63, while courts compound offences under s. 77A.

quiz.concept: Territorial reach needs an Indian computer
quiz.q: A foreign national in another country hacks a foreign company's server located abroad and steals its data. No computer, system or network in India is involved. Can the IT Act reach this conduct?
quiz.ok: No, because s. 75 reaches conduct abroad only where it involves a computer, system or network in India.
no: Yes, because s. 75 applies the Act to every computer offence, wherever and by whomever committed.
Yes, because s. 75 applies the Act to any data theft from a company that also does business in India.
Yes, because the Act applies to any person who could later be extradited to India for a trial.
quiz.why: Section 75 extends the Act to offences and contraventions committed outside India by any person, but only if they involve a computer, computer system or network located in India. Here no Indian computer is involved, so the Act does not reach the conduct. Extradition is a practical step for bringing someone to trial, not a source of jurisdiction.

quiz.concept: Liability of persons in charge of companies
quiz.q: A company's servers are used to commit an offence under the IT Act. Its managing director, who is in charge of the business, says he knew nothing about it. How does s. 85 treat his defence?
quiz.ok: He is deemed guilty unless he proves that he lacked knowledge or exercised due diligence to prevent it.
no: He cannot be liable, because it is the company that commits an offence under the Act.
He is liable only if the prosecution proves he personally committed the offence with dishonest intent.
He is strictly liable, because a person in charge is treated as having known of the company's offences.
quiz.why: Under s. 85, persons in charge of and responsible to a company for its business are deemed guilty of its offences unless they prove lack of knowledge or due diligence. His claimed ignorance is therefore relevant, but the burden is on him to prove it. Directors and officers whose consent, connivance or neglect is proved are also liable.

quiz.concept: Intermediary safe harbour and actual knowledge
quiz.q: A video platform hosts a user's unlawful upload. It did not initiate the transmission or modify the content, and it observes due diligence. A private complainant emails demanding removal. When does the platform lose s. 79 protection for failing to act?
quiz.ok: When it fails to act on actual knowledge, read as receipt of a court order or government notification.
no: As soon as it receives the private complaint, because any notice from a complainant gives it actual knowledge.
Never, because s. 79 protects intermediaries for third-party content in all circumstances, whatever notice they receive.
As soon as the content is uploaded, because hosting unlawful content itself destroys the protection.
quiz.why: Section 79 protects intermediaries for third-party content if they observe due diligence, do not initiate transmissions, select receivers or modify content, and act on actual knowledge. Shreya Singhal read "actual knowledge" down to mean a court order or government notification, so a private email alone does not trigger the duty. The protection is conditional, not absolute.

quiz.concept: IT Act offences survive the new codes
quiz.q: Since 1 July 2024 the BNS, BNSS and BSA have replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act. A student concludes that identity theft through a stolen password must now be charged under the BNS rather than under s. 66C. What is the correct view?
quiz.ok: The IT Act's offences are unchanged by the new codes, so identity theft is still charged under s. 66C.
no: The IT Act's offences were absorbed into the BNS, so identity theft must now be charged under the new code.
The IT Act's offences survive only for conduct committed before 1 July 2024, after which the BNS applies.
The IT Act's offences survive, but they now carry the BNS's punishments in place of the Act's own.
quiz.why: The new codes replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act, but IT Act offences are unchanged, so s. 66C remains the identity theft offence with its own punishment. What changed is the general criminal law around the Act, not the Act's own offences. Nothing in the new codes moves IT Act offences into the BNS or alters their punishments.

quiz.concept: Hash values and chain of custody
quiz.q: A forensic examiner seizes a laptop, makes a forensic image, records its hash value and logs everyone who handles the device. At trial, what does each step help to show?
quiz.ok: The hash value shows the evidence was not altered, and the custody log shows who handled it.
no: The hash value shows who created the files, and the custody log shows that the files are genuine and authentic.
The hash value makes the evidence admissible, and the custody log fixes the weight it must carry.
The hash value anonymises the suspect's data, and the custody log protects the suspect's privacy.
quiz.why: Forensic imaging and hash values show that evidence has not been altered, and a recorded chain of custody shows who handled it. Neither step settles everything, because admissibility, authenticity and weight remain distinct questions. Hashing detects alteration; it is not a means of anonymisation.

quiz.q: A chat log from the accused's phone is admitted in evidence. The defence then argues that the messages were fabricated and that, even if genuine, they prove little. The prosecution replies that admitting the log has settled both points. Who is right?
quiz.ok: The defence, because admissibility, authenticity and weight are distinct questions, and admission decides only the first.
no: The prosecution, because a court admits an electronic record only after finding it both genuine and conclusive.
The prosecution, because an electronic record cannot be fabricated once it has been seized by the police.
The defence on authenticity only, because the weight of an admitted record is then fixed by law.
quiz.why: Prosecutions rest on electronic records such as chats and logs, but whether a record may be received (admissibility), whether it is genuine (authenticity) and how much it proves (weight) remain distinct questions. Admitting the log does not stop the defence from challenging its authenticity or arguing that it proves little. Forensic imaging, hash values and a recorded chain of custody are the tools for meeting such challenges.

quiz.q: A defendant argues that because s. 81 gives the IT Act overriding effect, a software company cannot sue under the Copyright Act for code he copied from its servers. Why is that wrong?
quiz.ok: Section 81 gives the Act overriding effect but expressly saves rights under the Copyright Act and the Patents Act.
no: Section 81 gives the Act overriding effect over criminal laws but leaves civil statutes untouched.
Section 81 gives the Act overriding effect where the conduct is an offence, not where it is a contravention.
Section 81 gives the Act overriding effect only after the copyright owner has first exhausted s. 43.
quiz.why: Section 81 gives the IT Act overriding effect while saving rights under the Copyright Act, 1957 and the Patents Act, 1970, with the DPDP Act added from 13 May 2027. A copyright claim therefore survives alongside any s. 43 claim; the classroom problem on copied trading code notes that copyright and breach of confidence claims remain. The same override is the basis of Sharat Babu.

quiz.q: DPDP s. 44(2) omits IT Act s. 43A from 13 May 2027. A private hospital company's negligent security lets hackers leak patients' sensitive personal data, and a patient suffers financial loss. Compare a leak in January 2027 with an identical leak in July 2027. What changes for the patient's remedy?
quiz.ok: In January s. 43A compensates her; in July the Board can only penalise, leaving her tort or contract.
no: In July the Board can award her compensation, having taken over the adjudicating officer's role in data cases.
In July she can claim under s. 43 instead, which absorbs s. 43A's negligence liability after the omission.
In January she must first exhaust the Board's grievance route before the adjudicating officer can hear her.
quiz.why: Until 13 May 2027 a negligent body corporate holding sensitive personal data must compensate the person affected through the adjudicating officer. After that date the Board penalises, its penalties are credited to the Consolidated Fund, and the DPDP Act provides no compensation, so the victim must rely on tort or contract. Section 43 is unaffected but covers unauthorised acts, not a holder's negligence.

quiz.concept: Ransomware lockout is a personal data breach
quiz.q: In August 2027, after the DPDP Act's breach duties took effect on 13 May 2027, ransomware encrypts a clinic's patient database. Nothing is copied out, and the clinic says it has no breach to report because no data left its systems. Why is the clinic wrong?
quiz.ok: A personal data breach includes loss of access compromising availability, so it must intimate the Board and every affected patient.
no: A personal data breach covers only disclosure to outsiders, but ransomware is always treated as a disclosure.
A personal data breach must be reported, but only where it is likely to cause a high risk to patients.
A personal data breach must be reported to the police under the IT Act, not to the Data Protection Board.
quiz.why: Section 2(u) defines a personal data breach to include loss of access that compromises confidentiality, integrity or availability, so a ransomware lockout qualifies. From 13 May 2027, s. 8(6) and Rule 7 require intimation to each affected Data Principal and to the Board without delay, with a detailed report within 72 hours. Unlike the GDPR, the DPDP regime has no risk threshold.

quiz.concept: Crime victim still a liable fiduciary
quiz.q: In September 2027, after the DPDP Act's duties took effect on 13 May 2027, a ransomware group abroad encrypts a city water utility's systems, including its customer records, cutting supply for two days, and declares that it wants to show the State cannot protect its people. The utility's safeguards were unreasonable. Which statement best captures the consequences?
quiz.ok: The attackers face cyber terrorism (s. 66F), and the utility must still intimate the breach and risks a penalty for weak safeguards.
no: The attackers face cyber terrorism (s. 66F), and the utility, as the victim of a crime, is excused from every DPDP duty.
The attackers face only civil s. 43 liability, because conduct abroad falls outside the IT Act's criminal provisions.
The utility alone is liable, because its unreasonable safeguards displace the responsibility of the foreign attackers for the outage.
quiz.why: A contaminant and unauthorised access that disrupt essential services, with a declared intent to strike terror, satisfy s. 66F(1)(A), and s. 75 reaches the attackers abroad. Being a victim does not excuse the utility: from 13 May 2027 it must intimate the Board and its customers under s. 8(6) and Rule 7, and it risks penalties if its safeguards were unreasonable. Criminal and regulatory liability run side by side.

quiz.q: In June 2027, after the DPDP Act's breach duties took effect on 13 May 2027, a bank employee accidentally emails a spreadsheet of customers' account details to the wrong outside address. There is no dishonest intent. Which analysis is correct?
quiz.ok: It is a personal data breach the bank must intimate, even though no s. 66 offence arises without dishonesty.
no: It is a s. 66 offence by the employee, because disclosing financial data is criminal without proof of intent.
It is not a personal data breach, because an accidental disclosure is not unauthorised processing.
It is not reportable, because the bank must intimate only breaches caused by outside attackers.
quiz.why: The DPDP definition of a personal data breach includes accidental disclosure, so a misdirected email qualifies, and every breach must be intimated to the Board and each affected Data Principal. Section 66 needs dishonesty or fraud, which is absent here. The duty to intimate does not depend on anyone having committed a crime.

quiz.concept: Insider data theft: crime plus breach
quiz.q: In October 2027, after the DPDP Act's duties took effect on 13 May 2027, an employee of an online retailer dishonestly copies customers' personal data, without the retailer's permission, to sell to a rival. Who bears which consequences?
quiz.ok: The employee's dishonest copying is a s. 43 act and a s. 66 offence; the retailer must intimate the breach.
no: The employee is liable only under s. 43A, because that section deals specifically with leaks of personal data by insiders.
The retailer commits the s. 66 offence, because an employee's dishonesty is attributed to the employer under the IT Act.
The employee commits a s. 66 offence, and the retailer owes no duty because its own staff caused the breach.
quiz.why: Copying data without the owner's permission is a s. 43 contravention, and doing it dishonestly makes it a s. 66 offence. Unauthorised processing is a personal data breach under the DPDP Act, so the retailer must intimate the Board and each affected customer whoever caused it. Section 43A, which ran only until 13 May 2027, made a negligent body corporate compensate; it never targeted the insider.

quiz.q: A company hashes customers' phone numbers and claims the data is now anonymous and outside the DPDP Act. Its forensic team also records hash values of seized disk images for a cybercrime complaint. Which statement is right?
quiz.ok: Hashing helps prove evidence was unaltered, but hashed phone numbers can be reversed and are not reliably anonymous.
no: Hashing makes the phone numbers anonymous, but it cannot help to prove that seized evidence is still unaltered.
Hashing serves both purposes equally, making the numbers anonymous and the disk images unalterable.
Hashing serves neither purpose, because any hash can be decrypted with a key that the company holds.
quiz.why: A hash is a one-way function useful to detect alteration of evidence, which is why forensic teams record hash values. But a hash of a phone number can be reversed by hashing every possible number, so hashing alone rarely anonymises; the DPDP Act still covers data about an individual identifiable by or in relation to it (s. 2(t)), and Rule 6 treats obfuscation and masking as security safeguards, not exits from the Act. Decrypting with a key describes encryption, not hashing.

quiz.q: In 2028, with s. 3 of the DPDP Act in force since 13 May 2027, a Singapore firm with no customers in India profiles Indian users' online behaviour on its servers in Singapore, and also hacks into a server in Mumbai to obtain more data. How do the IT Act and the DPDP Act reach it?
quiz.ok: Section 75 reaches the hacking via the Mumbai server, but the DPDP Act has no monitoring limb for the profiling.
no: Both are reached under the DPDP Act, because it covers any processing abroad of the data of Indian residents.
Neither is reached, because both Acts require the wrongdoer to be located or incorporated in India.
The profiling is reached under s. 75, and the hacking is reached under the DPDP Act's limb on monitoring behaviour.
quiz.why: Section 75 extends the IT Act to conduct abroad by any person that involves a computer in India, so hacking the Mumbai server is covered. The DPDP Act reaches processing abroad only when connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India, and it has no monitoring limb, so profiling Indians without selling to them escapes it. The GDPR, by contrast, covers monitoring of behaviour.

quiz.concept: Under-eighteens in data and content law
quiz.q: In 2028, with the DPDP Act's duties in force since 13 May 2027, a gaming app shows targeted advertisements to its 17-year-old users, and an adult player grooms a 17-year-old into an online relationship aimed at sexually explicit acts. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Both laws treat under-eighteens as children: the ads breach the ban on targeting children, and the grooming falls under s. 67B.
no: Neither law protects a 17-year-old, because both laws treat sixteen as the age at which childhood ends for these purposes.
Only the grooming is unlawful, because targeted advertising to minors is permitted once a parent has given verifiable consent.
Only the advertising is unlawful, because the s. 67B grooming offence requires sexually explicit images of the child to exist already.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act defines a child as a person under eighteen and prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children (s. 9(3)). Section 67B also treats persons under eighteen as children, and its clause (c) criminalises online grooming before any image exists. Setting the age at sixteen is a listed examination error.

quiz.q: In 2028, with the DPDP Act's duties in force since 13 May 2027, a man signs up for a loan app with his cousin's identity details and the one-time password sent to the cousin's phone, intending to take a loan in the cousin's name. Which pairing of consequences fits best?
quiz.ok: Identity theft by using the OTP (s. 66C), and a breach of the Data Principal's duty not to impersonate another person.
no: Identity theft by using the OTP (s. 66C), but no DPDP consequence, because only Data Fiduciaries owe duties under that Act.
Only a civil s. 43 contravention, because the OTP was obtained from a relative without hacking into any computer.
A privacy violation under s. 66E for using the OTP, and a breach of the app's duty to verify each user's identity.
quiz.why: Section 66C punishes fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's password or unique identification feature, which includes a captured one-time password. Section 15 of the DPDP Act separately requires a Data Principal not to impersonate another person when providing personal data, a duty backed by a penalty of up to ₹10,000, so the Act does impose duties on individuals. Pretending to be the cousin to obtain the loan may also be cheating by personation under s. 66D.

quiz.concept: Two tracks against a departing employee
quiz.q: On leaving a software company, Riya logs in to its cloud account with her manager's password and deletes client files. The company wants money for its loss, a claim below the adjudicating officer's ₹5 crore limit, and also wants her prosecuted. Which plan is correct?
quiz.ok: Claim compensation from the adjudicating officer under s. 43, and prosecute identity theft (s. 66C) and, if dishonest, s. 66.
no: Prosecute only, because once the conduct is an offence the civil claim under s. 43 is no longer available to the company.
Claim only, because what a departing employee does with her access is a civil matter that cannot be prosecuted.
Seek compensation from the Data Protection Board, because the deleted client files contain the clients' personal data.
quiz.why: Using the manager's password is unauthorised access under s. 43(a) and identity theft under s. 66C, and deleting the files is a s. 43(d) and (i) contravention that becomes a s. 66 offence if done dishonestly. The civil and criminal tracks run side by side: compensation before the adjudicating officer (a civil court above ₹5 crore) and prosecution in the criminal courts. The Data Protection Board penalises but never awards compensation.

quiz.concept: Security is not the whole of protection
quiz.q: A company uses strong encryption and access controls and has never been hacked, but it collects far more customer data than it needs and reuses it for unrelated purposes. A director says it cannot be in breach of data protection law because its data is secure. What is wrong with this?
quiz.ok: Data security is only one component of data protection; secure processing can still breach minimisation and purpose rules.
no: Nothing is wrong, because data protection law is concerned only with keeping data safe from unauthorised access.
The company breaches only the IT Act, because over-collection is a s. 43 contravention against its customers.
The company is in breach only if a hacker exploits the excess data, which would then make it negligent.
quiz.why: Data security is the technical and organisational measures that keep data confidential, intact and available; it is one component of data protection. A perfectly secure organisation can still breach data protection law by collecting too much or misusing data. Cybercrime law targets unauthorised access and misuse by others, while data protection also regulates what a lawful holder does with data.

quiz.q: From 13 May 2027, Rule 6 requires fiduciaries to log, monitor and review access to personal data and to retain logs for one year. Why does this security duty also matter for cybercrime prosecutions?
quiz.ok: Logs are electronic records that help detect and investigate unauthorised access and show who did what.
no: Logs replace the need for a police investigation, because the Board prosecutes offences on their basis.
Logs make every unauthorised access a s. 66F offence, because they show the system is critical infrastructure.
Logs matter for breach reports rather than prosecutions, because electronic records cannot prove criminal offences.
quiz.why: Rule 6 requires logging, monitoring and review to detect and investigate unauthorised access, with logs retained for a year. Cyber prosecutions rest on electronic records such as logs, emails, chats and device images, so the same records serve both purposes. The Board does not prosecute offences; it inquires and penalises under the DPDP Act.

quiz.q: In 2028, with the DPDP Act's duties in force since 13 May 2027, a private hospital company stores patient records with a cloud processor. A hacker breaks into the processor's servers and copies the records. The contract says the processor bears all data protection responsibility. Who must deal with the breach, and what of the hacker?
quiz.ok: The hospital stays responsible and must intimate the breach; the hacker is liable under s. 43 and, if dishonest, s. 66.
no: The processor alone is responsible, because the contract validly shifts all the data protection duties onto it.
No one under the DPDP Act, because a criminal intrusion by a hacker ends the hospital's responsibility for the data.
The hacker, because s. 43A makes the person who actually causes a leak compensate the affected patients.
quiz.why: Under s. 8(1) a Data Fiduciary is responsible for all processing by it or its processors regardless of any contract, and the duty to intimate a breach under s. 8(6) falls on the fiduciary. The hacker's copying is a s. 43 act and, if dishonest, a s. 66 offence. Section 43A, while it lasted, made a negligent body corporate compensate; it never made the intruder liable under that section.

quiz.concept: Monitoring staff to prevent data theft
quiz.q: In 2028, with the DPDP Act's duties in force since 13 May 2027, a software company worried about employees copying source code before leaving wants to monitor activity on work accounts without seeking each employee's consent. What is its best ground under the DPDP Act?
quiz.ok: The legitimate use for employment, including protecting the employer from loss such as trade secret leaks.
no: A general legitimate interests ground, which allows any processing where the employer's interests outweigh the employees'.
No ground exists, because processing employee data always needs each employee's fresh consent on each occasion.
The exclusion for personal or domestic processing, because the monitoring happens on the company's own systems.
quiz.why: Section 7(i) allows processing without consent for employment, or to protect the employer from loss or liability such as espionage, trade secrets and confidentiality. The DPDP Act has no general legitimate interests ground, so the GDPR-style argument fails. Copying code before leaving would itself be a s. 43 act and, if dishonest, a s. 66 offence.
